The translation renders it consistently as "a people behaving ignorantly," which stresses conduct rather than mere lack of information. The occasions are a demand for an idol (7:138), contempt for humble believers (11:29), homosexual desire (27:55), and challenging a prophet about the timing of punishment (46:23). In 46:23 the verdict is contrasted with "Knowledge [of its time] is only with Allah." 6:111 is similar in using an imperfect verb for disbelievers: "But most of them, [of that], are ignorant." There, however, it is a divine statement, not a prophet's speech.

- 7:138, 11:29, 27:55, 46:23, 6:111

### The ignorant as antagonists whom the believers turn from

In this group "the ignorant" are hostile or provocative people, and the believer's response is restraint. The root is paired with **أَعۡرِضۡ / أَعۡرَضُواْ** (turning away) in 7:199 and 28:55, and with **سَلَٰم** (peace) in 25:63 and 28:55. In 28:55 the ignorant are linked to **ٱللَّغۡوَ** ("ill speech"). 39:64 uses the vocative **أَيُّهَا ٱلۡجَٰهِلُونَ** for those who urge the Prophet to worship other than Allah.

>> وَإِذَا خَاطَبَهُمُ ٱلۡجَٰهِلُونَ قَالُواْ سَلَٰمٗا

- 7:199, 25:63, 28:55, 39:64

### Al-Jāhiliyya: the era or order of ignorance

The abstract noun **ٱلْجَٰهِلِيَّةِ** always appears as the second term of a genitive construct. It names a thought pattern, a mode of judgement, a form of display, or a kind of zeal: "the thought of ignorance" (3:154), "the judgement of [the time of] ignorance" (5:50), "the former times of ignorance" (33:33), "the chauvinism of the time of ignorance" (48:26). In three of the four, the head noun echoes a preceding verb or noun from its own root:

- **يَظُنُّونَ … ظَنَّ**
- **تَبَرَّجۡنَ تَبَرُّجَ**
- **ٱلۡحَمِيَّةَ حَمِيَّةَ**

It is contrasted with "the truth" (3:154), with Allah's judgement (5:50), and with divine tranquillity and "the word of righteousness" (48:26).

- 3:154, 5:50, 33:33, 48:26

### Simple unawareness of the facts

In 2:273 the singular participle has no evident moral censure. "An ignorant [person] would think them self-sufficient because of their restraint". It is contrasted with "you will know them by their [characteristic] sign." Here the word means someone who lacks particular information.

- 2:273

### Ignorance as a trait of human nature

The intensive form **جَهُولًا** occurs once, paired with **ظَلُومٗا**, to describe the human being who took on the Trust: "Indeed, he was unjust and ignorant." It names a disposition of humankind as a whole, not an act or a group.

- 33:72

## Patterns worth attention

- **Form and context:** **ٱلْجَٰهِلِيَّةِ** occurs only in Madani surahs. **تَجْهَلُونَ** and **ٱلْجَٰهِلُونَ** occur only in Makki surahs. Of the six **ٱلْجَٰهِلِينَ**, five are Makki; the exception is 2:67. **بِجَهَٰلَةٍ** is divided evenly: 6:54 and 16:119 are Makki, 4:17 and 49:6 are Madani.
- **Prophetic speech:** the "people behaving ignorantly" formula and the "among the ignorant" formula are concentrated in Makki narratives about prophets.
- **Turning away from the ignorant:** the motif of turning away with words of peace is entirely Makki (7:199, 25:63, 28:55).
- **The Madani profile:** the Madani occurrences lean toward the historical-social label **ٱلْجَٰهِلِيَّةِ**, toward legal or ethical instruction (4:17, 49:6), and toward general statements about human nature (33:72).
- **Opposition to knowledge:** the root is repeatedly set against knowledge or truth: 11:46 ("no knowledge"), 12:89 ("Do you know"), 46:23 ("Knowledge … is only with Allah"), 2:273 ("you will know them"), 3:154 ("other than the truth").
- **Association with desire:** in 12:33 and 27:55 the root is linked with yielding to desire (**أَصۡبُ إِلَيۡهِنَّ**; **شَهۡوَةٗ**). This supports reading **جهل** as reckless conduct and not only as missing information.
- **The بِجَهَٰلَةٍ formula:** in three of four cases it follows **عمل السوء**. The sequence is wrongdoing, then repentance (**تاب**), then forgiveness. 6:54 and 16:119 share almost the same wording: **ثُمَّ تَابَ / تَابُواْ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ…**, **وَأَصۡلَحَ / وَأَصۡلَحُوٓاْ**, and the closing **غَفُورٞ رَّحِيمٞ**.

## The use in 16:119

16:119 belongs to the first group: wrongdoing committed in a state of ignorance and then remedied by repentance.

>> ثُمَّ إِنَّ رَبَّكَ لِلَّذِينَ عَمِلُواْ ٱلسُّوٓءَ بِجَهَٰلَةٖ ثُمَّ تَابُواْ مِنۢ بَعۡدِ ذَٰلِكَ وَأَصۡلَحُوٓاْ إِنَّ رَبَّكَ مِنۢ بَعۡدِهَا لَغَفُورٞ رَّحِيمٌ

The translation reads: "Then, indeed your Lord, to those who have done wrong out of ignorance and then repent after that and correct themselves - indeed, your Lord, thereafter, is Forgiving and Merciful."

Its closest parallel is the Makki 6:54. The two share the verb **عمل** with **السوء**, the sequence of repenting and then correcting oneself (**أصلح**), and the closing pair **غَفُورٞ رَّحِيمٞ**. The Madani 4:17 has the same opening structure but stresses repenting "soon after," not "correcting themselves."

Within the verse itself, **جَهَٰلَة** describes a condition that is temporary and can be repaired. This sets it apart from the fixed traits of the "people behaving ignorantly," from the intensive **جَهُول** of 33:72, and from the abstract **ٱلْجَٰهِلِيَّةِ**.

The exact sense of the phrase cannot be settled from the data alone. 49:6 points toward acting without verified knowledge. 12:89, 12:33 and 27:55, together with the gloss "[or carelessness]" at 4:17, point toward heedless or impulsive wrongdoing. The wording of 16:119 is consistent with either reading.

## Usage across the Qur'an

The lemma طائِر (root ط ي ر, active participle) occurs **5 times in 5 surahs**, all in Makki surahs (6:38, 7:131, 17:13, 27:47, 36:19), with no occurrences in Madani surahs. It appears in four forms: the unsuffixed indefinite طئر (×1), and three forms with pronoun suffixes: طئركم (×2), طئرهم (×1), and طئره (×1). The occurrences divide into a single literal use, "bird", and a figurative cluster concerned with omen, fortune, and fate.

### A bird (literal sense)

In its one unsuffixed occurrence, the word denotes a flying creature. It is paired with دَآبَّةٖ ("creature") on the earth, and the two together cover the animal world, which is said to consist of "communities like you." The literal sense is reinforced by the cognate verb and the mention of wings in the same phrase:

>> وَلَا طَـٰٓئِرٖ يَطِيرُ بِجَنَاحَيۡهِ

The translation renders this as "or bird that flies with its wings."

- 6:38

### Omen or fortune, in disputes between a people and those sent to them

In three occurrences, the word carries a pronoun suffix and refers to an omen or a person's fortune. In each case it appears where an ill outcome is being blamed on someone. In 7:131 and 27:47 it answers an accusation expressed with the related verb of omen-taking (يَطَّيَّرُواْ, ٱطَّيَّرۡنَا). The reply moves the source of the omen from the accused to God:

>> أَلَآ إِنَّمَا طَـٰٓئِرُهُمۡ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ

>> قَالَ طَـٰٓئِرُكُمۡ عِندَ ٱللَّهِۖ

In 36:19 the omen is instead located with the accusers themselves:

>> قَالُواْ طَـٰٓئِرُكُم مَّعَكُمۡ

The translation gives this as "Your omen is with yourselves." In 7:131 the gloss reads "their evil omens" but the translation reads "their fortune." The sense therefore seems to sit between "bad omen" and a more neutral "lot" or "fortune", and the data does not settle which is primary.

- 7:131
- 27:47
- 36:19

### One's fate, bound to the individual

In one occurrence, the word refers to the destiny or account attached to each individual. It is joined to the image of the neck and followed directly by the mention of a record produced on the Day of Resurrection:

>> وَكُلَّ إِنسَٰنٍ أَلۡزَمۡنَٰهُ طَـٰٓئِرَهُۥ فِي عُنُقِهِۦۖ

The translation renders this as "And [for] every person We have imposed his fate upon his neck." The word here describes every human being, not a particular people in dispute. The pairing with كِتَٰبٗا ("a record") suggests that the "fate" is closely tied to what is recorded of the person. How far the two are equated cannot be determined from the text alone.

- 17:13

## Patterns worth a researcher's attention

- **Form and sense align closely.** The only unsuffixed, indefinite form (6:38) carries the literal sense "bird." Every pronoun-suffixed form (7:131, 17:13, 27:47, 36:19) carries the figurative sense of omen, fortune, or fate. Possession attached to a person appears to mark the figurative use.
- **Locative collocations.** The figurative uses are regularly followed by a phrase saying where the omen or fate lies: عِندَ ٱللَّهِ (7:131, 27:47), مَعَكُمۡ (36:19), and فِي عُنُقِهِۦ (17:13). The question of where one's "omen" resides appears to be central to these passages.
- **Cognate verbs.** The root appears verbally alongside the noun. In the literal sense it is يَطِيرُ (6:38). In the omen sense it is the form يَطَّيَّرُواْ / ٱطَّيَّرۡنَا (7:131, 27:47), which the translations render as seeing or considering someone "an evil omen" or "a bad omen."
- **Dialogue setting.** Three of the figurative uses (7:131, 27:47, 36:19) occur in reported speech, in exchanges between a people and those who brought them a message. 17:13 is the exception: it is a divine statement in the first person plural (أَلۡزَمۡنَٰهُ) about every person.
- **Makki and Madani.** All five occurrences are Makki, so no Makki and Madani contrast can be drawn from this data.

## The use in 17:13

17:13 belongs to the figurative cluster: it shares the possessive suffix and the locative construction seen in 7:131, 27:47, and 36:19. It also stands apart from them. In the dispute passages, the word is a charge traded between opposing parties and then reassigned, either to God or back to the accusers. In 17:13, God states that each person's طائر is fastened to them, "upon his neck," and links it to the record encountered on the Day of Resurrection. The verse thus extends the dispute passages' question of where an omen lies into a general statement: every human being carries their own fate. Its closest parallel in the data is 36:19, "Your omen is with yourselves," which also places the omen with the person concerned.

## Fisq in the Qur'an: Acts Identified in the Occurrences of the Root ف س ق

### Scope of the Evidence

The 54 occurrences do not provide a closed or exhaustive catalogue of acts that constitute *fisq*. In most places the root names **persons or peoples** (*al-fāsiqūn*, *qawm fāsiqīn*) and attaches consequences to them, without listing acts. A list drawn from these texts is therefore **conclusive only for what the texts state**. It cannot claim to cover everything *fisq* includes.

The material falls into three tiers of directness:

1. **Acts explicitly called *fisq*/*fusūq***, where the noun is predicated of the act itself.
2. **Acts whose doers are directly declared *fāsiqūn*** in the same ayah.
3. **Conduct contextually associated with *fisq***, either as the stated cause of punishment or in narrative description.

---

### Tier 1: Acts Explicitly Termed *Fisq* or *Fusūq*

**1. Consuming prohibited categories of meat, and seeking decisions by divining arrows (5:3)**

>> ذَٰلِكُمۡ فِسۡقٌۗ

The list covers "dead animals, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to other than Allah, and [those animals] killed by strangling or by a violent blow or by a head-long fall or by the goring of horns, and those from which a wild animal has eaten… and those which are sacrificed on stone altars, and [prohibited is] that you seek decision through divining arrows. That is grave disobedience."

**2. Eating that over which Allah's name has not been mentioned (6:121)**

>> وَلَا تَأۡكُلُواْ مِمَّا لَمۡ يُذۡكَرِ ٱسۡمُ ٱللَّهِ عَلَيۡهِ وَإِنَّهُۥ لَفِسۡقٞۗ

"And do not eat of that upon which the name of Allah has not been mentioned, for indeed, it is grave disobedience."

**3. Slaughter dedicated to other than Allah (6:145)**

>> أَوۡ فِسۡقًا أُهِلَّ لِغَيۡرِ ٱللَّهِ بِهِۦۚ

"or it be [that slaughtered in] disobedience, dedicated to other than Allah."

**4. Harming a scribe or a witness in a contract (2:282)**

>> وَلَا يُضَآرَّ كَاتِبٞ وَلَا شَهِيدٞۚ وَإِن تَفۡعَلُواْ فَإِنَّهُۥ فُسُوقُۢ بِكُمۡۗ

"Let no scribe be harmed or any witness. For if you do so, indeed, it is [grave] disobedience in you."

**5. Ridicule, insult and offensive nicknaming among believers (49:11)**

>> بِئۡسَ ٱلِٱسۡمُ ٱلۡفُسُوقُ بَعۡدَ ٱلۡإِيمَٰنِۚ

This follows directly on the prohibitions: "let not a people ridicule [another] people… nor let women ridicule [other] women… And do not insult one another and do not call each other by [offensive] nicknames. Wretched is the name of disobedience after [one's] faith."

**6. *Fusūq* during Hajj (2:197)**

*Fusūq* is prohibited alongside sexual relations and disputing: "there is [to be for him] no sexual relations and no disobedience and no disputing during Hajj." The ayah forbids *fusūq* but does **not** specify its content.

---

### Tier 2: Acts Whose Doers Are Declared *Fāsiqūn*

**7. Departing from a direct divine command (18:50)**

>> فَفَسَقَ عَنۡ أَمۡرِ رَبِّهِۦٓۗ

This is Iblees's refusal to prostrate: "He was of the jinn and departed from the command of his Lord."

**8. Defiance by the affluent of a command given to them (17:16)**

>> أَمَرۡنَا مُتۡرَفِيهَا فَفَسَقُواْ فِيهَا

"We command its affluent but they defiantly disobey therein." The pattern is the same as in 18:50: a command (*amr*) followed by *fisq*. The ayah does not name the specific acts committed.

**9. Not judging by what Allah has revealed (5:47)**

"And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed - then it is those who are the defiantly disobedient." 5:49 adds following others' inclinations and turning away from such judgement.

**10. Accusing chaste women without producing four witnesses (24:4)**

"And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses… And those are the defiantly disobedient."

**11. Turning away or disbelieving after a covenant or divine promise (3:82; 24:55)**

- 3:82: "And whoever turned away after that - they were the defiantly disobedient."
- 24:55: "But whoever disbelieves after that - then those are the defiantly disobedient."

**12. Denying clear revealed verses (2:99; 6:49)**

- 2:99: "no one would deny them except the defiantly disobedient."
- 6:49: "those who deny Our verses - the punishment will touch them for their defiant disobedience."

**13. Hypocrisy: enjoining wrong, forbidding right, withholding, forgetting Allah (9:67)**

"They enjoin what is wrong and forbid what is right and close their hands. They have forgotten Allah… Indeed, the hypocrites - it is they who are the defiantly disobedient."

**14. Forgetting Allah (59:19)**

"And be not like those who forgot Allah, so He made them forget themselves. Those are the defiantly disobedient."

**15. Preferring kin, wealth, trade and dwellings over Allah, His Messenger and jihad (9:24)**

The ayah concludes: "And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people."

**16. Disbelief in Allah and His Messenger (9:80; 9:84)**

- 9:80: "That is because they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people."
- 9:84: "they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger and died while they were defiantly disobedient."

**17. Breaking pacts and false verbal assurance (9:8; 7:102)**

- 9:8: "they do not observe concerning you any pact of kinship or covenant of protection? They satisfy you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse [compliance], and most of them are defiantly disobedient."
- 7:102: "We did not find for most of them any covenant; but indeed, We found most of them defiantly disobedient."

**18. Taking the wrong parties as allies (5:81)**

"if they had believed in Allah and the Prophet… they would not have taken them as allies; but many of them are defiantly disobedient."

---

### Tier 3: Conduct Contextually Associated with *Fisq*

In these ayat, *fisq* is the stated cause (*bimā kānū yafsuqūn*) or a description of the people, and the surrounding text describes their conduct.

- **Altering a divinely given wording (2:59):** "those who wronged changed [those words] to a statement other than that which had been said to them… because they were defiantly disobeying."
- **Violating the sabbath (7:163):** "when they transgressed in [the matter of] the sabbath… because they were defiantly disobedient."
- **Forgetting a reminder (7:165):** "when they forgot that by which they had been reminded… because they were defiantly disobeying."
- **Committing wicked deeds, said of Lot's city (21:74):** "the city that was committing wicked deeds. Indeed, they were a people of evil, defiantly disobedient."
- **Obeying a deceiving ruler (43:54):** "So he bluffed his people, and they obeyed him. Indeed, they were [themselves] a people defiantly disobedient [of Allah]."
- **Arrogance on earth without right (46:20):** paired with *fisq* as a second cause: "because you were arrogant upon the earth without right and because you were defiantly disobedient."
- **Harming a messenger and deviating (61:5):** "why do you harm me… And when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people."
- **Hardening of hearts over time (57:16).**
- **Failing to observe a self-adopted devotion (57:27):** "they did not observe it with due observance… but many of them are defiantly disobedient."
- **Oaths sworn to win approval (9:96).**

---

### What the Data Does Not Establish

- **No exhaustive definition.** No ayah gives a definition or full enumeration of *fisq*. Many occurrences (e.g. 2:26, 10:33, 32:18, 32:20, 46:35, 51:46, 27:12, 28:32, 63:6) name the *fāsiqūn* without identifying any act.
- ***Fisq* is not simply identical to disbelief.** 49:7 lists it as a distinct item beside disbelief and disobedience:
>> وَكَرَّهَ إِلَيۡكُمُ ٱلۡكُفۡرَ وَٱلۡفُسُوقَ وَٱلۡعِصۡيَانَۚ
  Yet 9:80, 9:84 and 24:55 tie it closely to disbelief. The texts thus show overlap without identity.
- **It can apply to believers' conduct.** 2:197, 2:282 and 49:11 address believers directly. 49:6 shows that a *fāsiq* may be a source of reports requiring verification.
- **On 17:16 specifically,** the data supports reading *fisq* as defiance of a received command. This parallels 18:50, where *fasaqa* is construed with *ʿan amr rabbihi*. The ayah does not itself specify which acts the affluent committed.

### Summary

Strictly on the texts, the acts **explicitly named** as *fisq* are:

- the prohibited foods and divining arrows (5:3)
- eating what was not consecrated with Allah's name (6:121)
- dedication of slaughter to other than Allah (6:145)
- harming a scribe or witness (2:282)
- mutual ridicule, insult and nicknaming (49:11)

The **broader semantic core** that emerges across all occurrences is departure from, or defiance of, a known divine command, covenant or revelation (18:50, 17:16, 3:82, 5:47, 2:99). Any list extending beyond the explicit cases is inference from context, not textual definition.

## Usage across the Qur'an

The lemma أُفّ (root أ ف ف), a verbal noun of the ism fiʿl type, occurs **3 times in 3 surahs**: 17:23, 21:67 and 46:17. All three occurrences are in **Makki** surahs, and none is in a Madani surah. The word has a single form, اف, which appears in each ayah as أُفّٖ, with nunation. The gloss in 17:23 is "a word of disrespect," and in the other two places it is simply "Uff." In every case the word is a spoken utterance, an exclamation addressed to someone, and not a descriptive term.

### Uff addressed to parents

In two of the three occurrences the word is directed at parents, and the two passages mirror each other. In 17:23 the utterance is **prohibited**. It is the smallest expression of disrespect toward aged parents, set within a decree that joins the worship of God alone with "to parents, good treatment":

>> فَلَا تَقُل لَّهُمَآ أُفّٖ وَلَا تَنۡهَرۡهُمَا وَقُل لَّهُمَا قَوۡلٗا كَرِيمٗا

The translation reads: "say not to them [so much as], "uff," and do not repel them but speak to them a noble word." Here أُفّ is paired with a stronger act, نَهَر ("repel"), and contrasted with قَوۡلٗا كَرِيمٗا ("a noble word").

In 46:17 the word is actually **spoken** by a son to his parents. It opens his rejection of their belief in resurrection:

>> وَٱلَّذِي قَالَ لِوَٰلِدَيۡهِ أُفّٖ لَّكُمَآ

The translation reads: "But one who says to his parents, "Uff to you; do you promise me that I will be brought forth [from the earth] when generations before me have already passed on [into oblivion]?"" The utterance stands against the parents' plea, "Woe to you! Believe! Indeed, the promise of Allah is truth," and the son's dismissal, "This is not but legends of the former people." In this passage the word expresses impatient contempt for the parents and for what they urge on him.

- 17:23, 46:17

### Uff addressed to idolaters and their objects of worship

In 21:67 the word is directed at a group of people and, together with them, at what they worship:

>> أُفّٖ لَّكُمۡ وَلِمَا تَعۡبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِۚ

The translation reads: "Uff to you and to what you worship instead of Allah. Then will you not use reason". Here the exclamation voices disgust or repudiation of worship directed to other than God. It is followed by a rebuke appealing to reason. The speaker is not named within the ayah as given, so the data alone does not identify him.

- 21:67

## Patterns worth a researcher's attention

- **Single fixed form.** The word never inflects. It appears only as أُفّٖ, consistent with its status as an ism fiʿl.
- **Construction with lām.** In both cases where the word is actually uttered (21:67, 46:17), it is followed by lām plus a pronoun of the addressee: أُفّٖ لَّكُمۡ and أُفّٖ لَّكُمَآ. In 17:23 the lām phrase precedes the word, as the indirect object of the verb تَقُل: تَقُل لَّهُمَآ أُفّٖ.
- **Embedding in speech verbs.** The word is always framed as speech. It is the object of قَالَ or تَقُل in 17:23 and 46:17, and a direct utterance in 21:67. Its semantic field is verbal conduct.
- **Collocation with worship.** All three ayat bring the word into proximity with the language of worship or faith. In 17:23 the passage opens with أَلَّا تَعۡبُدُوٓاْ إِلَّآ إِيَّاهُ. In 21:67 the word is followed by مَا تَعۡبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ. In 46:17 the parents' appeal is to the truth of God's promise.
- **Parents as recurring addressees.** Two of the three occurrences concern parents (لَّهُمَآ, لِوَٰلِدَيۡهِ, with dual pronouns). The dual pronoun لَّكُمَآ in 46:17 and the plural لَّكُمۡ in 21:67 mark the difference between the two groups.
- **Makki and Madani distribution.** The word is attested only in Makki surahs. With three occurrences, this distribution should not be pressed too far as evidence of a stylistic tendency.

## The use in 17:23 in relation to these groups

17:23 belongs to the group in which the word is addressed to parents. It is the prescriptive counterpart of 46:17: what 17:23 forbids, the son in 46:17 actually says, along with the denial of resurrection. Read together, the two ayat present أُفّ as the minimal verbal mark of disrespect toward parents. 17:23 places it at the lower end of a scale whose next step is نَهَر and whose positive opposite is قَوۡلٗا كَرِيمٗا.

21:67 shows that the same exclamation can also be used in a righteous register, to repudiate what is worshipped instead of God. The force of the word therefore appears to depend on its addressee. Directed at parents it is censured; directed at false objects of worship it expresses legitimate rejection. This reading rests on only three occurrences, so it should be treated as a pattern suggested by the data rather than an established rule.

## Usage across the Qur'an

The lemma **مَوْفُور** (root و ف ر, passive participle) occurs **once** in the Qur'an, at 17:63, in a Makki surah. It has no Madani occurrences. Its single form is the indefinite accusative **موفورا**, glossed "ample." With only one attestation, there is no internal Qur'anic range of usage to compare, and the observations below rest on this one context.

### Recompense described as full or ample

Here the word qualifies the noun **جَزَآء** (recompense) and describes that recompense as complete or abundant, with nothing lacking from it. The recompense is identified as Hell, and it is addressed to the one told "Go" together with "whoever of them follows you." The ayah does not name the addressee. The participle is not paired or contrasted with any other descriptive term. Its force comes from the repetition of the noun it qualifies.

>> قَالَ ٱذۡهَبۡ فَمَن تَبِعَكَ مِنۡهُمۡ فَإِنَّ جَهَنَّمَ جَزَآؤُكُمۡ جَزَآءٗ مَّوۡفُورٗا

Translation: "[Allah] said, "Go, for whoever of them follows you, indeed Hell will be the recompense of you - an ample recompense"

- 17:63

## Patterns worth a researcher's attention

- **Single attestation:** With only one occurrence, no claims can be made from the Qur'anic data about a preferred construction or semantic field for this lemma.
- **Construction:** The participle appears in the phrase **جَزَآءٗ مَّوۡفُورٗا**, where it follows an indefinite accusative repetition of **جَزَآء**. That noun has just appeared as **جَزَآؤُكُمۡ**. The repetition-plus-qualifier pattern intensifies the statement. Read grammatically, **جَزَآءٗ** functions as an emphatic restatement, and **مَّوۡفُورٗا** as its adjective.
- **Passive voice:** As a passive participle, the word presents the recompense as something made full, rather than something that is itself filling or abundant. This is consistent with the gloss "ample," although the precise nuance (complete, undiminished, or abundant) cannot be fixed further from this single context.
- **Makki/Madani distribution:** The sole occurrence is Makki. A single data point does not allow any conclusion about distribution.
- **Collocation:** The only collocate in the data is **جَزَآء**, set within a threat of Hell (**جَهَنَّمَ**) for those who follow the addressee.

## Relation of 17:63 to these groups

Since 17:63 is the only occurrence, it alone constitutes the single sense-group identified here: recompense described as full or ample. The word's meaning must therefore be read entirely from this context. In this ayah it seals a declaration of punishment, stressing that the recompense of Hell for the addressee and his followers will be complete and undiminished.

## The Lemma ʿabd in the Qurʾan: Universal Servanthood or Qualified Designation?

### Summary of the finding

The 131 occurrences show that the Qurʾan uses ʿabd / ʿibād in **two layers that coexist**:

1. **Universal (creaturely) servanthood.** Every being, believer or disbeliever, obedient or sinful, is Allah's ʿabd by creation and subjection.
2. **Qualified (honorific) servanthood.** Allah singles out certain servants and calls them "My servants" or "Our servants" because of named qualities such as sincerity, faith, righteousness, gratitude, turning back to Him, and piety.

So the answer is not either/or. Everyone is an ʿabd of Allah in the first sense, but the Qurʾan reserves the honorific designation, with its protection and promise, for those who have certain qualities. **17:65 belongs to the second, qualified layer.**

A third, separate usage refers to human slaves in social law. It is not part of the theological question.

---

## 1. Evidence for universal servanthood

### All creation comes as a servant

The most comprehensive statement is 19:93:

>> إِن كُلُّ مَن فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ إِلَّآ ءَاتِي ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ عَبۡدٗا

"There is no one in the heavens and earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant"

### Divine sovereignty over the servants

- 6:18 and 6:61: "And He is the subjugator over His servants."
- 39:46: "You will judge between your servants concerning that over which they used to differ."
- 40:48: the arrogant in the Fire say, "Indeed, Allah has judged between the servants."

### Sinners and disbelievers are still called His servants

- **Sins and wrongdoing:** 17:17 and 25:58 speak of "the sins of His servants."
- **Those who mocked the messengers:** 36:30 says "How regretful for the servants. There did not come to them any messenger except that they used to ridicule him."
- **Those facing punishment:** 5:118 says "If You should punish them - indeed they are Your servants."
- **Disbelief:** 39:7 says "If you disbelieve - indeed, Allah is Free from need of you. And He does not approve for His servants disbelief."
- **Transgressors:** 39:53 addresses them directly:

>> ۞قُلۡ يَٰعِبَادِيَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَسۡرَفُواْ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمۡ لَا تَقۡنَطُواْ مِن رَّحۡمَةِ ٱللَّهِۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَغۡفِرُ ٱلذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًاۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلۡغَفُورُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ

"Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves [by sinning], do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful"

- **Contexts of judgment:** the formula "Allah is not ever unjust to [His] servants" appears in 3:182, 8:51, 22:10 and 41:46, and 50:29 has "never will I be unjust to the servants." Each time it follows a statement of recompense for evil deeds, so the servants in view include those being punished.
- **Those who are misled:** 25:17 asks the false objects of worship, "Did you mislead these, My servants, or did they [themselves] stray from the way." Even the possessive "My servants" is applied here to people who strayed.

### Even false objects of worship are servants

- 7:194: "those you [polytheists] call upon besides Allah are servants like you."
- 21:26 and 43:19 call the angels "honored servants" and "servants of the Most Merciful."
- 4:172 says "Never would the Messiah disdain to be a servant of Allah, nor would the angels near [to Him]."

### Iblis takes his share from Allah's servants

4:118:

>> لَّعَنَهُ ٱللَّهُۘ وَقَالَ لَأَتَّخِذَنَّ مِنۡ عِبَادِكَ نَصِيبٗا مَّفۡرُوضٗا

"Whom Allah has cursed. For he had said, "I will surely take from among Your servants a specific portion"

Those whom Satan takes are drawn from among Allah's servants. Being an ʿabd in this universal sense therefore does not by itself guarantee guidance.

---

## 2. Evidence for qualified, honorific servanthood

Alongside the universal sense, the data repeatedly attaches **defining qualities** to the servants Allah honors.

| Quality | References | Translation (from data) |
|---|---|---|
| **Chosen/sincere** (al-mukhlaṣīn) | 12:24; 15:40; 37:40, 74, 128, 160, 169; 38:83 | "Our chosen servants"; "the chosen servants of Allah" |
| **Believing** | 27:15; 37:81, 111, 122, 132 | "Our believing servants"; "His believing servants" |
| **Righteous** | 21:105; 27:19; 66:10 | "My righteous servants"; "Your righteous servants"; "two of Our righteous servants" |
| **Grateful** | 17:3; 34:13 | "he was a grateful servant"; "few of My servants are grateful" |
| **Turning back to Allah** | 34:9; 50:8; 38:17, 30, 44 | "every servant turning back [to Allah]"; "one repeatedly turning back [to Allah]" |
| **Patient** | 38:44 | "We found him patient, an excellent servant" |
| **Fearing Allah** | 19:63; 35:28 | "those of Our servants who were fearing of Allah"; "Only those fear Allah, from among His servants, who have knowledge" |
| **Avoiding Taghut** | 39:17 | "those who have avoided Taghut, lest they worship it, and turned back to Allah … So give good tidings to My servants" |
| **Faith and righteous deeds** | 42:23 | "His servants who believe and do righteous deeds" |
| **Chosen** | 27:59; 35:32 | "His servants whom He has chosen"; "those We have chosen of Our servants" |

### Servanthood defined by conduct

25:63 defines "the servants of the Most Merciful" by how they behave:

>> وَعِبَادُ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ ٱلَّذِينَ يَمۡشُونَ عَلَى ٱلۡأَرۡضِ هَوۡنٗا وَإِذَا خَاطَبَهُمُ ٱلۡجَٰهِلُونَ قَالُواْ سَلَٰمٗا

"And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth easily, and when the ignorant address them [harshly], they say [words of] peace"

### The singular ʿabd as a title of honor for individuals

- **The Prophet Muhammad:** 2:23, 8:41, 17:1, 18:1, 25:1, 39:36, 53:10, 57:9, 72:19.
- **Other individuals:**
  - Noah (17:3, 54:9)
  - Zechariah (19:2)
  - Jesus (19:30, 43:59)
  - David (38:17)
  - Solomon (38:30)
  - Job (38:41)
  - Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (38:45)
  - the servant of 18:65
- The messengers collectively: "Our servants, the messengers" (37:171).

Each individual designation is tied to revelation, favor, mercy, knowledge, or a named virtue.

The exact phrase "servant of Allah" (ʿabd Allāh) in the singular occurs only twice in the data, and both times for specific honored persons:
- Jesus: "Indeed, I am the servant of Allah" (19:30)
- the Prophet: "the Servant of Allah stood up supplicating Him" (72:19)

### Eschatological address

- 43:68: "O My servants, no fear will there be concerning you this Day, nor will you grieve."
- 89:29: "And enter among My [righteous] servants."
- 76:6: "the [righteous] servants of Allah."

---

## 3. The significance of qualifiers

Several addresses add a restrictive clause to "My servants":
- 14:31: "tell My servants who have believed"
- 29:56: "O My servants who have believed"
- 39:10: "O My servants who have believed"
- 39:53: "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves"

The qualifier picks out one group within a wider body of servants. This confirms both layers at once:
- the wider body exists (universal), and
- groups within it are identified by their qualities (qualified).

---

## 4. Application to 17:65

>> إِنَّ عِبَادِي لَيۡسَ لَكَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ سُلۡطَٰنٞۚ وَكَفَىٰ بِرَبِّكَ وَكِيلٗا

"Indeed, over My [believing] servants there is for you no authority. And sufficient is your Lord as Disposer of affairs"

Four pieces of internal evidence show that ʿibādī here is the **qualified** sense:

1. **The parallel in 15:42** separates the deviators from the protected servants:

>> إِنَّ عِبَادِي لَيۡسَ لَكَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ سُلۡطَٰنٌ إِلَّا مَنِ ٱتَّبَعَكَ مِنَ ٱلۡغَاوِينَ

"Indeed, My servants - no authority will you have over them, except those who follow you of the deviators"

2. **Iblis's own exception** in 15:40 and 38:83 is "Except, among them, Your chosen servants." He concedes that only the mukhlaṣīn are beyond his reach.

3. **4:118** shows Iblis taking "a specific portion" from among Allah's servants in the universal sense. Since Satan does gain authority over some of these, the servants over whom he has "no authority" in 17:65 must be a narrower group.

4. **The translation in the data** itself marks this by rendering the word "My [believing] servants."

---

## Conclusion

On the basis of the occurrences given:

- **Everyone is ʿabd of Allah** in the sense of created, owned and subject being. This is shown by 19:93, by the application of the term to sinners, disbelievers, the misled and the punished, and by its use for angels and for false objects of worship.
- **The honorific "My servants / Our servants"**, carrying protection from Satan, divine nearness and the promise of Paradise, is **granted to those with specific qualities**: sincerity, faith, righteousness, gratitude, patience, piety, turning back to Allah, and avoiding Taghut.
- **The word ʿibādī in 17:65 belongs to this qualified category.** It denotes the servants over whom Satan has no authority, as distinct from those who follow him.

One limitation applies: this analysis covers only the noun lemma ʿabd. The data does not include the verbal forms of the root ʿ-b-d (to worship), which would bear further on how servanthood is realized in practice.

## Usage across the Qur'an

The lemma سُلْطان (root س ل ط) occurs **37 times in 26 surahs**. Of these, 31 are in Makki surahs and 6 in Madani surahs (3:151, 4:91, 4:144, 4:153, 22:71, 55:33). It takes six surface forms:

- سلطن ×13
- سلطنا ×11
- بسلطن ×8
- وسلطن ×3
- سلطنه ×1 (16:100)
- سلطنيه ×1 (69:29)

Apart from these two suffixed forms, every occurrence is indefinite. The English translation renders the word mostly as "authority," but also as "authorization," "evidence," "a clear case," and "supremacy." The word therefore ranges between a warrant or proof and power or control over someone.

### Divine warrant denied to associated objects of worship

Here سلطان is a warrant that God would have to "send down" to justify worshipping something besides Him. The ayahs always state or imply that no such warrant exists. The word is paired with association (أشرك), with "[mere] names you have named them," and with the absence of knowledge. In 22:71 it is placed alongside "that of which they have no knowledge," and in 53:23 it is contrasted with following "assumption and what [their] souls desire." A recurring formula is:

>> مَا لَمۡ يُنَزِّلۡ بِهِۦ سُلۡطَٰنٗا

and its variant:

>> مَّآ أَنزَلَ ٱللَّهُ بِهَا مِن سُلۡطَٰنٍۚ

In 30:35 the same idea is put as a rhetorical question: "Or have We sent down to them an authority, and it speaks of what they were associating with Him."

**References:** 3:151, 6:81, 7:33, 7:71, 12:40, 22:71, 30:35, 53:23

### Proof demanded, challenged, or lacking in argument

In these ayahs سلطان is evidence that one party is challenged, or claims, to produce in a dispute. It is typically governed by أتى بـ ("bring") and qualified by مبين or بيّن ("clear").

- Unbelievers demand it of messengers (14:10). The messengers reply that they cannot bring it "except by permission of Allah" (14:11), where the translation renders it "evidence."
- Conversely, those who associate partners with God, or claim knowledge of the unseen, are challenged to produce one (10:68, 18:15, 37:156, 52:38).
- In 40:35 and 40:56 those who "dispute concerning the signs of Allah" do so "without an authority having come to them," and 40:56 contrasts this with the "pride" in their breasts.
- 27:21 uses the same construction in a non-theological setting: "unless he brings me clear authorization." This shows the sense of a justifying reason in an ordinary human (or creaturely) context.

**References:** 10:68, 14:10, 14:11, 18:15, 27:21, 37:156, 40:35, 40:56, 52:38

### Authority conferred by God on a messenger

Here سلطان is something God gives or sends with a messenger. It is most often paired with "Our signs" (آياتنا). Moses is the recipient in most of these ayahs:

>> وَلَقَدۡ أَرۡسَلۡنَا مُوسَىٰ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا وَسُلۡطَٰنٖ مُّبِينٍ

This recurs verbatim in 11:96 and 40:23. 23:45 adds Aaron, and 51:38 has "We sent him to Pharaoh with clear authority." In 28:35 the translation renders it "supremacy," linked to being "the predominant." This leans towards effective power rather than proof alone.

In 17:80 the speaker prays for "a supporting authority" from God. 44:19 shares the formula بِسُلۡطَٰنٖ مُّبِينٖ, but the ayah as given does not name its speaker. Whether the word here means a convincing proof, a commission, or a granted power is not fully determinable from these texts. Several ayahs seem to allow more than one of these readings.

**References:** 4:153, 11:96, 17:80, 23:45, 28:35, 40:23, 44:19, 51:38

### Power over people, asserted or denied, of Satan and misleaders

In this group سلطان means control or sway exercised over persons. It is constructed with عَلَى + the object, and in most instances it is denied.

- Satan states in 14:22 that he "had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me." This separates سلطان (compelling power) from mere invitation.
- 15:42, 16:99 and 17:65 deny such authority over God's servants or over "those who have believed and rely upon their Lord."
- 16:100 states positively where it does operate: "His authority is only over those who take him as an ally."
- In 34:21 and 37:30 the denial again appears with an exception or contrast ("but you were a transgressing people"). In 37:30 the speakers are not identified in the ayah as given.

**References:** 14:22, 15:42, 16:99, 16:100, 17:65, 34:21, 37:30

### Right or authorization granted against another party

In these ayahs سلطان is a sanctioned right to act against someone. It is constructed with جعل لـ … على, or جعل لـ alone.

- In 4:91 God has made for the believers "against them a clear authorization."
- In 4:144 the believers are warned against giving "Allah against yourselves a clear case."
- In 17:33 the heir of one killed unjustly is given "authority," limited by the command "let him not exceed limits."

The sense here is close to a legal entitlement.

**References:** 4:91, 4:144, 17:33

### Power or capacity in general

Two ayahs use the word for power or ability without the contexts above. In 55:33, jinn and mankind "will not pass except by authority." The bracketed "[from Allah]" is the translator's addition. In 69:29 a speaker laments: "Gone from me is my authority." This could be read as worldly power or as the speaker's former proof or standing; the text alone does not settle which.

**References:** 55:33, 69:29

## Patterns worth a researcher's attention

- **Collocation with مبين:** سلطان is qualified by مبين in 12 ayahs: 4:91, 4:144, 4:153, 11:96, 14:10, 23:45, 27:21, 37:156, 40:23, 44:19, 51:38, 52:38. It is qualified by بيّن in 18:15. The qualifier is almost exclusive to the proof-challenge, messenger, and authorization groups. It never occurs in the "sent down" formula or in the denials of Satan's power.
- **Form and construction track sense:**
  - The accusative سلطانا clusters in the "not sent down" formula and in grants with جعل.
  - بسلطان appears mainly with أتى بـ (bring) and أرسل بـ (send with).
  - وسلطان occurs only in the fixed phrase بآياتنا وسلطان مبين about Moses.
  - Partitive من سلطان after negation (7:71, 10:68, 12:40, 14:22, 34:21, 37:30, 53:23) gives an emphatic "any authority at all."
- **عَلَى marks control:** When سلطان takes على of a person, it denotes power over that person. This applies to all of the Satan group and also to 4:91 and 4:144. When it takes بـ of a thing (نزّل به), it denotes a warrant for that thing.
- **Makki and Madani:** All seven ayahs on Satan's or misleaders' power are Makki, as are the proof-challenges. The Madani occurrences include the two legal or military authorizations in Surah 4 (4:91, 4:144). The "not sent down" formula appears in both (Makki 6:81, 7:33; Madani 3:151, 22:71).
- **Possessed forms:** Only two forms carry a pronoun suffix: سلطانه in 16:100 (Satan's) and سلطانيه in 69:29 (the speaker's). Both concern power that is limited or lost.

## The use in 17:65

17:65 belongs to the group on power over people, asserted or denied:

>> إِنَّ عِبَادِي لَيۡسَ لَكَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ سُلۡطَٰنٞۚ وَكَفَىٰ بِرَبِّكَ وَكِيلٗا

Translation: "Indeed, over My [believing] servants there is for you no authority. And sufficient is your Lord as Disposer of affairs."

- **Construction:** The form is the bare indefinite nominative, subject of ليس, with عَلَيۡهِمۡ marking the persons over whom control is denied. The addressee is not named within the ayah. The near-identical wording of 15:42 and the explicit speech of Satan in 14:22 place it in the same frame.
- **Comparison with 15:42:** 15:42 shares the opening إِنَّ عِبَادِي لَيۡسَ لَكَ عَلَيۡهِمۡ سُلۡطَٰنٌ but continues with an exception for "those who follow you of the deviators." 17:65 instead closes on God's sufficiency as وكيل. This echoes 16:99, where the protected are those who "rely upon their Lord."
- **Translation note:** The word "[believing]" in the translation is a bracketed addition. The Arabic has only عِبَادِي.

Read against the whole data set, سلطان in 17:65 denotes effective control rather than proof or warrant. Its unqualified indefiniteness, without مبين, matches the pattern of the other denials of such power.

QUESTION: এই আয়াতের প্রকৃত অর্থ কী? বিজ্ঞানের সাথে সম্পর্কিত করে প্রমাণ করুন

ANSWER:
## শব্দগুলো কী বলছে

>> وَلَـقَدۡ خَلَقۡنَا الۡاِنۡسَانَ مِنۡ صَلۡصَالٍ مِّنۡ حَمَاٍ مَّسۡنُوۡنٍ​ۚ

তিনটি মূল শব্দ পুরো অর্থ বহন করে:

- **صَلْصَال** – ص-ل-ل মূল থেকে উদ্ভূত একটি দ্বিরুক্ত রূপ। প্রধান অভিধানিক অর্থ এটিকে *সালসালাহ*-এর সাথে সংযুক্ত করে, অর্থাৎ ঝনঝন বা টুংটাং শব্দ: শুষ্ক মাটি যা আঘাত করলে ঝনঝন শব্দ করে বা বেজে ওঠে, অর্থাৎ যে মাটি তার পানি হারিয়েছে। দ্বিতীয়, কম প্রচলিত একটি অভিধানিক ধারা ص-ل-ل-কে পচা/দুর্গন্ধযুক্ত হওয়ার সাথে যুক্ত করে (যেমন মাংস পচে গেলে বলা হয়)। উভয় অর্থই অভিধানগুলোতে উল্লেখিত আছে; এখানে কোনটি মুখ্য তা নিয়ে মতভেদ রয়েছে *(যাচাই প্রয়োজন)*।
- **حَمَأ** – কালো বা গাঢ় রঙের, ভেজা কাদা; যে ধরনের কাদা স্থির পানির তলদেশে পাওয়া যায়। শব্দটি নিজেই কালোত্ব ও আর্দ্রতার অর্থ বহন করে, এবং ব্যবহারে প্রায়ই দুর্গন্ধ বা অপবিত্রতার অর্থেও আসে।
- **مَسْنُون** – س-ن-ن মূলের কর্মবাচ্য কৃদন্ত রূপ, এবং এটিই প্রকৃতপক্ষে অস্পষ্ট শব্দ। অভিধানগুলোতে অন্তত তিনটি দিক প্রমাণিত *(যাচাই প্রয়োজন)*:
  1. *ঢেলে দেওয়া / গঠিত*, যেমন তরল কাদা একটি ছাঁচে ঢেলে দেওয়া হয়;
  2. *মসৃণ করা, আকৃতি দেওয়া, পালিশ করা*, পাথরে ধার দেওয়া বা শান দেওয়া থেকে (سنّ المدية);
  3. *কালের অতিবাহনে পরিবর্তিত*, কোনো বস্তুর উপর বছর/কাল অতিবাহিত হওয়ার অর্থ থেকে — যা সহীহ ইন্টারন্যাশনালের "পরিবর্তিত" অনুবাদ অনুসরণ করে।

**ব্যাকরণ:** দ্বিতীয় مِنْ কোনো পৃথক দ্বিতীয় উপাদান নয়। এটি ব্যাখ্যামূলক (বদল/বয়ান): সালসাল হল হামা'ইন মাসনূন *থেকে*। সুতরাং এই আয়াতটি **একটি পদার্থের দুটি ধারাবাহিক অবস্থা** বর্ণনা করছে, দুটি উপাদান নয়: গাঢ় কাদা যা আকৃতি দেওয়া/ছেড়ে দেওয়া/পরিবর্তিত হয়েছিল, এবং যা পরে শুষ্ক, শব্দকারী মাটিতে পরিণত হয়েছিল।

**আয়াতের সরল পাঠ:** আল্লাহ মানুষকে এমন মাটি-পদার্থ থেকে সৃষ্টি করেছেন যা বিভিন্ন স্তর অতিক্রম করেছে — ভেজা গাঢ় কাদা, যা প্রক্রিয়াজাত হয়েছে বা পরিবর্তনের জন্য ছেড়ে দেওয়া হয়েছে, তারপর শুষ্ক মাটি।

## প্রেক্ষাপট

- 15:27 আয়াতে তৎক্ষণাৎ জ্বীনের উৎপত্তির সাথে বৈসাদৃশ্য তুলে ধরা হয়েছে:

>> وَالۡجَـآنَّ خَلَقۡنٰهُ مِنۡ قَبۡلُ مِنۡ نَّارِ السَّمُوۡمِ

মাটি/আগুনের এই জোড়াটিই অনুচ্ছেদের মূল বিষয়: পরবর্তী আয়াতগুলো (15:28–33, শুধুমাত্র রেফারেন্স) আদমের গঠন, রূহ ফুঁকে দেওয়া, সাজদাহর নির্দেশ এবং ইবলীসের অস্বীকৃতির একই বিবরণ পুনরাবৃত্তি করে — তার উল্লেখিত কারণ ছিল তার অগ্নি-উৎসের শ্রেষ্ঠত্ব। সুতরাং প্রেক্ষাপটে 15:26-এর কাজ হল **ধর্মতাত্ত্বিক ও নৈতিক**, পদার্থের অহংকারের বিপরীতে পদার্থের বিনয় প্রতিষ্ঠা করা, রসায়ন বর্ণনা করা নয়।

- কুরআনের অন্যত্র একই উৎসের জন্য ভিন্ন ভিন্ন শব্দ ব্যবহৃত হয়েছে: 55:14 (সালসালকে পোড়া মৃৎপাত্রের সাথে তুলনা করা হয়েছে), 23:12 (তীনের নির্যাস), 32:7–8 (তীন থেকে সূচনা, তারপর তুচ্ছ তরল থেকে বংশধর), 22:5 এবং 3:59 (তুরাব, ধুলো/মাটি), 6:2 (তীন)। সবগুলো একত্রে বিবেচনা করলে শব্দভাণ্ডারটি হল **মাটি, পানি এবং স্তরে স্তরে পরিবর্তন** — সামঞ্জস্যপূর্ণ, কিন্তু ইচ্ছাকৃতভাবে প্রযুক্তিগত নয় *(সকল রেফারেন্স যাচাই প্রয়োজন)*।

## বিজ্ঞানের সাথে সম্পর্ক — এবং "প্রমাণের" সীমাবদ্ধতা

আমি সরাসরি বলব: **এই আয়াতটি বিজ্ঞান দিয়ে "প্রমাণ" করা যায় না, এবং এটি কোনো বৈজ্ঞানিক বিবৃতি হওয়ার দাবিও করে না।** সততার সাথে যা বলা যায়:

**প্রকৃত মিলনবিন্দু (প্রমাণ নয়):**

- মানবদেহের মৌলিক গঠন (অক্সিজেন, কার্বন, হাইড্রোজেন, নাইট্রোজেন, ক্যালসিয়াম, ফসফরাস, এবং সামান্য পরিমাণ ধাতু) সম্পূর্ণভাবে মাটি, পানি ও বাতাসে পাওয়া একই মৌলসমূহ থেকে গৃহীত। দেহের কোনো কিছুই পৃথিবীর কাছে অপরিচিত নয়। এটি পদার্থের স্তরে "মাটি-পদার্থ থেকে সৃষ্ট" ধারণার সাথে মিলে যায় *(সঠিক পরিসংখ্যান উদ্ধৃত করলে তা যাচাই প্রয়োজন)*।
- আয়াতটি **স্তরসমূহ** বর্ণনা করে, শূন্য থেকে চূড়ান্ত রূপের তাৎক্ষণিক আবির্ভাব নয়: কাদা → পরিবর্তিত/আকৃতি দেওয়া → শুষ্ক মাটি। পাঠ্যটির নিজস্ব গঠনই প্রক্রিয়া ও সময়কালের ইঙ্গিত দেয়, যা অন্তত উৎপত্তির স্তরবিন্যাসভিত্তিক যেকোনো বর্ণনার সাথে সাংঘর্ষিক নয়।
- জীবনের উৎপত্তি সংক্রান্ত রসায়নে প্রকৃত এক গবেষণাধারা রয়েছে যা প্রস্তাব করে যে কাদা-খনিজ পদার্থ (মন্টমোরিলোনাইট ও অনুরূপ) নিউক্লিওটাইডের পলিমারাইজেশনকে ত্বরান্বিত করতে এবং জৈব অণুগুলোকে ঘনীভূত করতে পারে, এবং খনিজ পৃষ্ঠতল প্রাথমিক প্রতিলিপন প্রক্রিয়ার টেমপ্লেট হিসেবে কাজ করতে পারে। এটি একটি জীবন্ত প্রকল্পনা, প্রতিষ্ঠিত সত্য নয় *(নাম ও বর্তমান অবস্থা যাচাই প্রয়োজন)*।

**যেখানে এই মিলনবিন্দু থামতে হবে — এবং বাড়াবাড়ি যুক্তিকে কীভাবে ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত করে:**

- এই কাদা-সংক্রান্ত প্রকল্পনাগুলো সাধারণভাবে **জীবনের উৎপত্তি** সম্পর্কিত, নির্দিষ্টভাবে মানুষের উৎপত্তি সম্পর্কিত নয়। আয়াতটি *আল-ইনসান* সম্পর্কে কথা বলে। দুটিকে এক করে ফেলা এমন একটি লাফ যা পাঠ্য নিজে করে না।
- মাটি থেকে প্রথম মানুষ সৃষ্টির কোনো বিবরণ বিজ্ঞানের কাছে নেই, এবং এটি এমন ধরনের দাবি নয় যা পরীক্ষা করার জন্য বিজ্ঞান গঠিত হয়েছে। একটি অপুনরাবৃত্তিযোগ্য, অপর্যবেক্ষিত, একক ঘটনা পদ্ধতির বাইরে অবস্থিত।
- শব্দভাণ্ডারটি (সালসাল, হামা, মাসনূন) পরিচিত পদার্থের জন্য সপ্তম শতাব্দীর সাধারণ আরবি। এতে "কলয়েডাল রসায়ন", "জৈব পলল" বা "পলিমার" পড়া অর্থ আরোপ করা, অর্থ উদ্ধার করা নয়।
- বৈজ্ঞানিক মডেল পরিবর্তিত হয়। একটি আয়াতের সত্যতাকে বর্তমান কোনো প্রকল্পনার সাথে বেঁধে ফেলা আয়াতটিকে পরবর্তী সংশোধনের জিম্মি করে তোলে। এই সতর্কতাই নিজে একটি শক্তিশালী পদ্ধতিগত বক্তব্য।

**আয়াতটি নিজের শর্তে যা প্রতিষ্ঠা করে:** মানুষ তুচ্ছ, সাধারণ মাটি-পদার্থ থেকে তৈরি; মানুষের মর্যাদা পদার্থ থেকে আসে না, বরং 15:29 (শুধুমাত্র রেফারেন্স) পরবর্তীতে যা যোগ করে তা থেকে আসে — গঠন ও রূহ ফুঁকে দেওয়া। বিনয়ী করার উদ্দেশ্যেই সুনির্দিষ্টভাবে বস্তুগত উৎস উল্লেখ করা হয়েছে।

## সৎ সারসংক্ষেপ

- **পাঠ্য থেকে স্পষ্ট:** মানুষের উৎপত্তি মাটি-পদার্থ থেকে; সেই পদার্থ একাধিক অবস্থা অতিক্রম করেছে; জ্বীনের উৎপত্তি আগুন হিসেবে বৈসাদৃশ্যপূর্ণভাবে উপস্থাপিত; বিবৃতিটির উদ্দেশ্য হল বিনয় প্রতিষ্ঠা করা এবং ইবলীসের অস্বীকৃতির প্রেক্ষাপট তৈরি করা।
- **ব্যাখ্যা, বিতর্কিত:** *সালসাল* মানে কি "ঝনঝনে শুষ্ক মাটি" নাকি "দুর্গন্ধযুক্ত মাটি"; *মাসনূন* মানে কি ঢেলে দেওয়া, আকৃতি দেওয়া, নাকি কালের দ্বারা পরিবর্তিত; স্তরগুলো কি দীর্ঘ সময়কালের ইঙ্গিত দেয়।
- **পাঠ্যে নেই:** কোনো প্রক্রিয়া, সময়কাল, রসায়ন, বা এমন কোনো দাবি যা বিজ্ঞান হিসেবে পরীক্ষাযোগ্য। সেই দিকে প্রদত্ত যেকোনো "প্রমাণ" সর্বোচ্চ সামঞ্জস্যের একটি যুক্তি, কখনোই প্রদর্শন নয়।

## সংরক্ষণের আগে যাচাই করতে হবে

- লিসানুল আরব, আস-সিহাহ, মাকায়ীসুল লুগাহ-এ ص-ل-ل / صَلْصَال-এর অভিধানিক ভুক্তি — "ঝনঝন" এবং "পচন" উভয় অর্থ।
- حَمَأ-এর অভিধানিক ভুক্তি এবং مَسْنُون-এর তিনটি প্রমাণিত অর্থের ভুক্তি (ঢেলে দেওয়া / আকৃতি দেওয়া-মসৃণ করা / কালের দ্বারা পরিবর্তিত)।
- দ্বিতীয় مِنْ-কে দ্বিতীয় উপাদান না ধরে বদল বা বয়ান হিসেবে ব্যাকরণগত বিশ্লেষণ — কোনো কুরআনিক ইরাব গ্রন্থে যাচাই করুন।
- শুধুমাত্র সংখ্যা দিয়ে উল্লেখিত রেফারেন্সসমূহ: 15:28–33, 55:14, 23:12, 32:7–8, 22:5, 3:59, 6:2, 15:29 — প্রতিটি আমি যা সারসংক্ষেপ করেছি তা বলে কিনা তা নিশ্চিত করুন।
- 15:33-ই সত্যিই সেই স্থান যেখানে ইবলীস তার কারণ বর্ণনা করেছে, এবং তার যুক্তির সঠিক শব্দাবলি।
- মানবদেহের মৌলিক গঠনের পরিসংখ্যান ও মৌল তালিকা।
- জীবাণুজনিত নয় এমন জীবনোৎপত্তি (abiogenesis)-এ কাদা-খনিজ প্রকল্পনা: উদ্ভাবক, মূল গবেষণাপত্র, এবং গবেষকদের মধ্যে এর বর্তমান অবস্থান।
- সহীহ ইন্টারন্যাশনালের "পরিবর্তিত কালো কাদা" অনুবাদটি অনুবাদকদের মধ্যে مَسْنُون-এর সংখ্যাগরিষ্ঠ নাকি সংখ্যালঘু পাঠকে প্রতিফলিত করে।
ans.en:
## What the words say

>> وَلَـقَدۡ خَلَقۡنَا الۡاِنۡسَانَ مِنۡ صَلۡصَالٍ مِّنۡ حَمَاٍ مَّسۡنُوۡنٍ​ۚ

Three content words carry the whole meaning:

- **صَلْصَال** – a reduplicated form from the root ص-ل-ل. The dominant lexical sense connects it to *ṣalṣalah*, a ringing or clinking sound: dried clay that rattles or rings when struck, i.e. clay that has lost its water. A second, less common lexical line links ص-ل-ل to rotting/stinking (as in meat that has turned). Both senses are reported in the dictionaries; which one is primary here is disputed *(needs verification)*.
- **حَمَأ** – black or dark, wet mud; the kind found at the bottom of standing water. The word itself carries the sense of darkness and dampness, and in usage often of foulness.
- **مَسْنُون** – passive participle of س-ن-ن, and this is the genuinely ambiguous word. At least three directions are attested in the lexicons *(needs verification)*:
  1. *poured out / cast*, as liquid mud poured into a form;
  2. *smoothed, shaped, polished*, from sharpening or honing against a stone (سنّ المدية);
  3. *altered by the passage of time*, from the sense of years/periods passing over a thing — which is what Saheeh International's "altered" follows.

**The grammar:** the second مِنْ is not a second separate material. It is explanatory (badal / bayān): the ṣalṣāl is *from* the ḥamaʾ masnūn. So the ayah describes **one substance in two successive states**, not two ingredients: dark mud that was shaped/left/altered, and which then became dry, sounding clay.

**Reading of the ayah, plainly:** God created the human being out of earth-matter that passed through stages — wet dark mud, worked or left to change, then dried clay.

## Context

- 15:27 immediately contrasts the origin of the jinn:

>> وَالۡجَـآنَّ خَلَقۡنٰهُ مِنۡ قَبۡلُ مِنۡ نَّارِ السَّمُوۡمِ

The pairing clay/fire is the point of the passage: the following ayahs (15:28–33, reference only) repeat the same phrase about the forming of Adam, the breathing of spirit, the command to prostrate, and Iblīs's refusal — his stated reason being the superiority of his fiery origin. So the function of 15:26 in its context is **theological and moral**, setting up humility of substance against arrogance of substance, not describing chemistry.

- Elsewhere the Qur'an uses other terms for the same origin: 55:14 (ṣalṣāl likened to fired pottery), 23:12 (an extract of ṭīn), 32:7–8 (a beginning from ṭīn, then progeny from a despised fluid), 22:5 and 3:59 (turāb, dust), 6:2 (ṭīn). Taken together the vocabulary is **earth, water, and change over stages** — consistent, but deliberately non-technical *(all references need verification)*.

## Relation to science — and the limits of "proof"

I will be direct: **this ayah cannot be "proven" by science, and it does not claim to be a scientific statement.** What can honestly be said:

**Genuine points of convergence (not proof):**

- The elemental composition of the human body (oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, calcium, phosphorus, plus trace metals) is drawn entirely from the same elements found in soil, water and air. Nothing in the body is exotic to the earth. This matches "created from earth-matter" at the level of substance *(needs verification of exact figures if you cite them)*.
- The ayah describes **stages**, not an instantaneous appearance of the final form from nothing: mud → altered/shaped → dried clay. The text's own structure implies process and duration, which is at least not in tension with any staged account of origins.
- There is a real line of research in origin-of-life chemistry proposing that clay minerals (montmorillonite and similar) could catalyse the polymerisation of nucleotides and concentrate organic molecules, and that mineral surfaces may have templated early replication. This is a live hypothesis, not established fact *(needs verification of names and current status)*.

**Where the convergence must stop — and why overreaching damages the argument:**

- Those clay hypotheses concern the origin of **life in general**, not the origin of the human being specifically. The ayah speaks of *al-insān*. Equating the two is a leap the text does not make.
- Science has no account of the creation of a first human from mud, and it is not the kind of claim science is built to test. An unrepeatable, unobserved, singular act is outside the method.
- The vocabulary (ṣalṣāl, ḥamaʾ, masnūn) is ordinary seventh-century Arabic for familiar materials. Reading "colloidal chemistry", "organic sediment" or "polymer" into it is importing meaning, not extracting it.
- Scientific models change. Anchoring the truth of an ayah to a current hypothesis makes the ayah hostage to the next revision. This caution is itself the strongest methodological point you can make.

**What the ayah does establish, on its own terms:** the human being is made of lowly, common earth-substance; the dignity of the human comes not from the material but from what 15:29 (reference only) adds afterwards — the forming and the breathing of spirit. The material origin is stated precisely in order to be humbling.

## Honest summary

- **Clear from the text:** human origin is from earth-matter; that matter passed through more than one state; the jinn's origin is contrasted as fire; the purpose of the statement is to ground humility and to set up the refusal of Iblīs.
- **Interpretation, disputed:** whether *ṣalṣāl* means "ringing dry clay" or "stinking clay"; whether *masnūn* means poured, shaped, or altered-by-time; whether the stages imply a long duration.
- **Not in the text:** any mechanism, timescale, chemistry, or claim that is testable as science. Any "proof" offered in that direction is an argument of compatibility at best, never demonstration.

## To verify before saving

- Lexical entries for ص-ل-ل / صَلْصَال in Lisān al-ʿArab, al-Ṣiḥāḥ, Maqāyīs al-Lugha — both the "ringing" and the "rotting" senses.
- Lexical entries for حَمَأ and for the three attested senses of مَسْنُون (poured / shaped-smoothed / altered by time).
- The grammatical analysis of the second مِنْ as badal or bayān rather than a second material — check in a Qur'anic iʿrāb work.
- References cited by number only: 15:28–33, 55:14, 23:12, 32:7–8, 22:5, 3:59, 6:2, 15:29 — confirm each says what I summarised.
- That 15:33 is indeed where Iblīs states his reason, and the exact wording of his argument.
- Figures and element list for the elemental composition of the human body.
- The clay-mineral hypothesis in abiogenesis: originators, key papers, and its current standing among researchers.
- Whether the Saheeh International rendering "altered black mud" reflects a majority or a minority reading of مَسْنُون among translators.

q.en: What does this ayah actually mean? Relate to science and prove

ans.en:
## How many punishments does the passage name?

Within 15:73–74 the text explicitly names **three** distinct acts:

>> فَاَخَذَتۡهُمُ الصَّيۡحَةُ مُشۡرِقِيۡنَۙ

>> فَجَعَلۡنَا عَالِيـَهَا سَافِلَهَا وَ اَمۡطَرۡنَا عَلَيۡهِمۡ حِجَارَةً مِّنۡ سِجِّيۡلٍؕ

1. **al-ṣayḥah**, the mighty blast or cry, which "seized them" at sunrise.
2. **The overturning**: *jaʿalnā ʿāliyahā sāfilahā*, "We made its highest part its lowest."
3. **The rain of stones** *min sijjīl*, usually rendered as stones of baked or hardened clay.

This is what the text states. Other passages about the same people add details:
- The time is morning (15:66; 11:81).
- The stones are described further, for example as successive and marked (11:82–83) and as being of clay (51:33–34).
- A separate episode involves the blinding of certain men who came after Lūṭ's guests (54:37).

If those passages are counted, some would list more than three. That blinding, however, affected a particular group before the final destruction, so it is a different kind of event. Within this ayah and the one before it, the answer is three.

## Were they already dead from the ṣayḥah?

The question assumes the ṣayḥah killed them. The text does not actually say so.

- **The verb is *akhadhathum*, "it seized/took them."** *Akhdh* in Qur'anic usage often means being overtaken or gripped by punishment. It does not by itself specify death. In the account of Thamūd (11:67), the text adds explicitly that they became lifeless, lying prostrate in their homes. No such statement occurs in 15:73. The cry may therefore be the *onset* of the punishment (terror, stunning, the opening blow) rather than its sole lethal cause. This is an inference from wording, not an explicit statement.
- **The particle *fa-* at the head of 15:74** marks sequence and consequence: the blast, *then* the overturning and stones. Arabic grammarians, however, also recognise a *fa-* that orders things in narration rather than strictly in time. So the text establishes the order of mention firmly, while the exact chronology is less certain.
- **A possible reading of the three as one event.** Some interpreters understand the ṣayḥah as the tremendous sound accompanying the upheaval itself, so that cry, overturning and stones form one catastrophe described from several angles. This view needs verification, and I cannot confirm who held it.

## What is the point of the further punishments?

Even on the assumption that some or all had died from the blast, the text itself suggests several purposes. Points (a) to (c) are drawn from the wording. Point (d) is reported interpretation.

**(a) The objects are different.**
- The overturning has a **feminine singular pronoun**: *ʿāliyahā sāfilahā*, "*its* top, *its* bottom." It refers to the settlement (the "city" mentioned in 15:67), not to the people.
- The stones fall *ʿalayhim*, "upon *them*."

So the punishment is directed at both the inhabitants and the place. Killing people is one thing. Erasing the town as a habitation is another. The second is not redundant after the first.

**(b) The punishment is meant to remain as a sign.** The very next ayah draws the conclusion:

>> اِنَّ فِىۡ ذٰ لِكَ لَاٰيٰتٍ لِّـلۡمُتَوَسِّمِيۡنَ

*al-mutawassimūn* derives from the root *w-s-m*, "mark, trace." It suggests people who read marks and traces. The following ayah (15:76) adds that the site lies on a road still travelled. An overturned land strewn with stones leaves a **visible, lasting trace**, which a silent mass death would not. On this reading, the overturning and stones serve the didactic purpose explicitly stated in 15:75–76. A comparable logic appears in 10:92, where Pharaoh's body is preserved to be a sign for those after him.

**(c) Totality and disgrace.** Overturning the town, then burying it under stones, expresses complete eradication and humiliation, beyond death alone. The scale of the punishment matches the gravity and public character of the crime as the Qur'an presents it. This is an interpretive reading of the narrative's force, not something the ayah states.

**(d) Reported views on the stones.** It is reported that some exegetes held the stones struck those who were outside the town at the time (travellers or absentees), so that none escaped. This needs verification. The text of 15:74 does not say this.

## Summary

- **Clear in the text:** three acts are named (blast, overturning, stones). They are joined in narrative sequence by *fa-* and *wa-*, and 15:75 presents the whole as signs for those who read traces.
- **Not stated in the text:** that the ṣayḥah alone killed everyone.
- **Reasonable inference:** the later acts target the town itself and create a lasting, readable sign, so they are not pointless even if death came with the blast.
- **Uncertain:** the exact chronology, and whether the three are separate stages or aspects of one event.

## To verify before saving

- Wording of 11:67 (Thamūd lying lifeless after the ṣayḥah) as a contrast to 15:73.
- 15:66 and 11:81 (timing at morning).
- 15:67 (reference to "the people of the city", the antecedent of the pronoun *-hā*).
- 15:76 (the site lying on an existing road).
- 11:82–83 and 51:33–34 (descriptions of the stones as successive, marked, and of clay).
- 54:37 (blinding of the men who came for the guests).
- 10:92 (Pharaoh's body preserved as a sign).
- The grammarians' distinction between chronological *fa-* and *fa-* of ordering in narration.
- Derivation of *al-mutawassimīn* from *w-s-m* and its sense of "reading marks."
- Meaning and possible origin of *sijjīl*.
- The view that the ṣayḥah was the sound of the overturning itself (who held it).
- The view that the stones struck those outside the town (who held it).
- The general claim that *akhadha* in Qur'anic usage does not by itself entail death.

q.en: 15:74, how many types of punishment actually fell upon them? If they were already dead by the big cry what the point of the other punishments?

ans.en:
## The phrase in its ayah

>> وَمَا خَلَقۡنَا السَّمٰوٰتِ وَالۡاَرۡضَ وَمَا بَيۡنَهُمَاۤ اِلَّا بِالۡحَـقِّ​ ؕ وَاِنَّ السَّاعَةَ لَاٰتِيَةٌ​ فَاصۡفَحِ الصَّفۡحَ الۡجَمِيۡلَ

The question concerns *fa-ṣfaḥi ṣ-ṣafḥa*, which only makes full sense together with its adjective *al-jamīl*. The sections below take the parts in turn.

## Lexical meaning of the root ṣ-f-ḥ

- The root ṣ-f-ḥ relates to the **broad, flat side or surface of something**. A *ṣafḥa* is a flat surface, the side of the face, or a page.
- From this comes the verb *ṣafaḥa ʿan* (form I, imperfect *yaṣfaḥu*), "to turn aside from" someone or something. Classical lexicography commonly explains it as turning one's side or cheek away, that is, **not dwelling on an offence and passing over it**.
- The verbal noun *ṣafḥ* is therefore the act of overlooking or passing over: a deliberate disengagement from the wrong done, without retaliation.
- The Bengali translation's এড়িয়ে যাও ("pass by / avoid them") reflects this "turning aside" sense directly. Pardon, as a moral meaning, is a natural extension of it.

**Clear from the language:** the core image is turning aside. **Interpretive:** how far *ṣafḥ* also implies inner forgiveness, as opposed to simply refraining from response (see below).

## Grammatical analysis

- **fa-**: a connective of consequence. The command follows from what was just stated, namely that creation has a true purpose and that "the Hour is surely coming."
- **iṣfaḥ**: singular imperative, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ. The final kasra in *fa-ṣfaḥi* is not a case ending. It is added to avoid two consecutive sukūns (*iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn*) before the definite article of *aṣ-ṣafḥ*.
- **aṣ-ṣafḥa**: an absolute object (*mafʿūl muṭlaq*), a cognate noun from the same root as the verb.
- **al-jamīla**: an adjective qualifying it.

A bare cognate object can serve emphasis. Here, because it is **qualified by an adjective**, its main function is generally analysed as **specifying the kind** (*bayān al-nawʿ*): not just any overlooking, but overlooking of a particular, beautiful kind. So the expression means roughly: *"So overlook [them] with a gracious overlooking."*

## What makes the ṣafḥ "jamīl"?

The text does not define *al-ṣafḥ al-jamīl*, so any definition is interpretation. A widely reported explanation in the tafsir tradition is that it is **overlooking without reproach or complaint**: the wrong is let go without lingering blame or resentment, and without the passing-over itself becoming a form of rebuke. This attribution needs verification.

The Qur'an pairs *jamīl* with other forms of restraint in a similar way:

- *ṣabr jamīl* at 12:18, 12:83 and 70:5
- *hajr jamīl* at 73:10
- *sarāḥ jamīl* at 33:28 and 33:49

Across these passages the pattern suggests that *jamīl* marks a restraint or separation carried out **with dignity and without harshness**. This is an inference from usage, not an explicit definition.

## Ṣafḥ and ʿafw

*Ṣafḥ* often occurs alongside *ʿafw* (pardon). Examples include 2:109, 5:13, 24:22 and 64:14, where both verbs appear together. The related command at 43:89 tells the Prophet to turn aside from them and say "peace."

Some scholars distinguish the two terms. On this view, *ʿafw* means forgoing the punishment, while *ṣafḥ* goes further and means not even reproaching, as if "turning the page." This distinction is reported in general terms and needs verification. It is not stated by the ayah itself.

## Contextual meaning

- **Preceding context (15:80–84):** the fate of earlier deniers, ending with:

>> فَمَاۤ اَغۡنٰى عَنۡهُمۡ مَّا كَانُوۡا يَكۡسِبُوۡنَؕ

- **The ayah's logic:** creation was made *bi-l-ḥaqq*, with real purpose, and the Hour will come. Accountability is therefore certain, and it belongs to God. The *fa-* makes the Prophet's gracious overlooking a consequence of this certainty. He need not avenge himself, because final justice is assured.
- **Following ayah:**

>> اِنَّ رَبَّكَ هُوَ الۡخَـلّٰقُ الۡعَلِيۡمُ

This reinforces the point: the Creator, who knows everything, will judge. The Prophet's role here is patient disengagement, not retribution.

## A question of abrogation

Some exegetes held that this and similar Meccan commands to overlook were abrogated by later verses permitting fighting, often linked to 9:5. Others held that the command remains in force as a moral instruction for dealing with personal offence. Both positions are reported here only in general terms and need verification. The ayah itself says nothing about whether it is temporary.

## To verify before saving

- Lexical claims for ṣ-f-ḥ: "broad side/surface," the turning-aside image, and *ṣafḥa* meaning "page" (check classical lexicons)
- The explanation of the kasra in *fa-ṣfaḥi* as avoiding two sukūns
- The analysis of *aṣ-ṣafḥ* as *mafʿūl muṭlaq* for specifying the kind (check *iʿrāb* works)
- The attribution in tafsir works of the definition "overlooking without reproach"
- The reported distinction between *ʿafw* and *ṣafḥ* and who held it
- References: 2:109, 5:13, 24:22, 64:14 (ʿafw/ṣafḥ pairing); 43:89 (turning aside and saying "peace")
- References: 12:18, 12:83, 70:5 (*ṣabr jamīl*); 73:10 (*hajr jamīl*); 33:28, 33:49 (*sarāḥ jamīl*)
- The summary of 15:80–84 as concerning earlier deniers
- The reported abrogation view, its link to 9:5, and the opposing view
- The Meccan setting of Sūrat al-Ḥijr

q.en: Explain the expression فَاصۡفَحِ الصَّفۡحَ

ans.en:
## The phrase in its ayah

>> خَلَقَ الۡاِنۡسَانَ مِنۡ نُّـطۡفَةٍ فَاِذَا هُوَ خَصِيۡمٌ مُّبِيۡنٌ

The phrase *khaṣīmun mubīn* is the predicate of the clause *fa-idhā huwa…*. It describes what the human being "turns out to be" after being created from a *nuṭfa*, a small quantity of fluid. The ayah turns on the contrast between this humble origin and the disputatious figure man becomes.

## Linguistic analysis

**خَصِيم (khaṣīm)**
- **Root:** *kh-ṣ-m*, denoting dispute, contention and adversarial argument, as in *khiṣām* and *mukhāṣama*.
- **Pattern:** *faʿīl*. Two readings of the pattern are linguistically possible:
  - **Intensive or habitual:** someone much given to disputing, a confirmed contender, like other *faʿīl* adjectives of intensity (*ʿalīm*, *raḥīm*).
  - **Equivalent to *mufāʿil* (*mukhāṣim*):** "one who disputes with another," an opponent or adversary, comparable to *jalīs* (one who sits with) and *ʿashīr* (companion).
- Both senses fit the ayah, and they are not mutually exclusive. "Adversary" (Saheeh International) reflects the second. "Contentious disputant" reflects the first.

**مُبِين (mubīn)**
- This is the active participle of Form IV *abāna*, which Arabic uses both intransitively and transitively.
  - **Intransitive:** "clear, manifest, evident." On this reading man is *plainly, openly* an adversary, and his contentiousness is unmistakable.
  - **Transitive:** "making clear, expressing articulately." On this reading man is a disputant who *sets out his case clearly*, eloquent and able to argue.
- The translation "clear adversary" follows the first reading. The second is grammatically equally available. Which one is meant depends on how the ayah as a whole is read (see below).

**فَإِذَا هُوَ (fa-idhā huwa)**
- *Idhā* here is the *idhā* of sudden occurrence (*al-fujāʾiyya*), conveying "and lo, he is…" or "then at once he is…".
- The *fa* marks sequence. Together they express a striking, almost abrupt transition from a drop of fluid to an arguing adversary.
- The construction itself does not mean the transformation is literally instantaneous. Man's development takes time, as the Qur'an describes elsewhere. The expression highlights the surprising disproportion between origin and outcome, as if nothing lay between them.

## Two main lines of interpretation

What the text clearly says is that man, created from a *nuṭfa*, becomes a *khaṣīm mubīn*. Whether this is said in **censure** or as a **reminder of favour** is a matter of interpretation. Both views are reported in the exegetical tradition (general statement; needs verification).

**1. Censure: man disputes against his Creator**
- On this reading, *khaṣīm* means an adversary against God: one who argues against His oneness, His messengers, or the resurrection, despite having been created from something so insignificant.
- *Mubīn* then means "manifest" in his hostility.
- Support from the immediate context: the preceding ayah ends with a declaration of God's transcendence above what is associated with Him:

>> خَلَقَ السَّمٰوٰتِ وَالۡاَرۡضَ بِالۡحَـقِّ​ؕ تَعٰلٰى عَمَّا يُشۡرِكُوۡنَ

  Read in sequence, 16:4 can be taken as exposing the ingratitude of those who commit *shirk*: the One who created heavens and earth also created them, yet they turn into opponents.
- Support from parallels: 36:77 contains an almost identical phrase, also following mention of creation from a *nuṭfa*. In that passage the following ayah (36:78) describes man striking a comparison against God and forgetting his own creation, while questioning how decayed bones could be revived. There the context of disputing the resurrection is explicit. Compare also 18:54, which describes man as the most argumentative of things.

**2. Favour: man is given the faculty of reasoned speech**
- On this reading, the ayah highlights God's power and generosity. From a mere drop He produced a being capable of thought, speech and argument, able to state and defend his position clearly.
- *Mubīn* is then taken in its transitive sense: articulate, expressing himself clearly.
- Support from the following context: 16:5 onward enumerates blessings, beginning with livestock:

>> وَالۡاَنۡعَامَ خَلَقَهَا​ ۚ لَـكُمۡ فِيۡهَا دِفۡ ٴٌ وَّمَنَافِعُ وَمِنۡهَا تَاۡكُلُوۡنَ

  If 16:4 belongs to this catalogue of favours, the faculty of articulate speech is itself a sign and a gift.

**Combining the two**
- Many readers see no strict contradiction between these views (general statement; needs verification). The same faculty that is a divine gift, the capacity to reason and argue, is what man then turns against its Giver.
- On this combined reading, the ayah simultaneously displays God's creative power, the dignity of the faculty He bestowed, and the irony of its misuse. This fits the passage's movement from *tawḥīd* (16:3) to blessings (16:5 ff.).

## Summary of what is clear and what is interpretive

- **Clear from the text:** the contrast between a lowly origin (*nuṭfa*) and a contentious, articulate outcome; the suddenness or unexpectedness expressed by *fa-idhā*; the generic reference to *al-insān*.
- **Interpretive:**
  - whether *khaṣīm* means "adversary against God" specifically or "disputant" in general;
  - whether *mubīn* means "manifest" or "articulate";
  - whether the tone is censure, reminder of favour, or both.
- **Uncertain:** whether *al-insān* here refers to humanity generally or primarily to the disbelievers addressed at the time. The article can be generic. Some exegetes may link the parallel at 36:77 to a specific individual or incident (needs verification). I cannot confirm the details from the text alone.

## To verify before saving

- That both the "censure" and "favour" interpretations of 16:4 are actually reported in classical tafsir.
- The claim that many readers combine the two views.
- 36:77: wording nearly identical to 16:4, including *khaṣīmun mubīn* after mention of *nuṭfa*.
- 36:78: content as described (man strikes a comparison, forgets his creation, questions the revival of bones).
- 18:54: describes man as the most argumentative of things.
- Any report linking 36:77 to a specific individual or incident, and whether such a report exists in reliable sources.
- The grammatical points:
  - *faʿīl* as intensive or as equivalent to *mufāʿil*;
  - *abāna* as both transitive and intransitive;
  - *idhā* in 16:4 as *idhā al-fujāʾiyya*.
- The root meaning of *nuṭfa* as a small quantity of fluid.

q.en: Explain KHASEEMUN MUBEEN

ans.en:
## What the text clearly establishes

>> وَلَكُمۡ فِيۡهَا جَمَالٌ حِيۡنَ تُرِيۡحُوۡنَ وَحِيۡنَ تَسۡرَحُوۡنَ

- **The object:** The pronoun in فِيۡهَا refers back to الۡاَنۡعَام, the grazing livestock of 16:5. The beauty is located *in the livestock*.
- **The beneficiary:** لَكُمۡ, "for you." The beauty is presented as something the human owners or observers receive, a benefit (niʿma) like warmth and food, not only an abstract quality of the animals.
- **The timing:** The beauty is tied to two specific moments, not to the animals in general:
  - **حِيۡنَ تُرِيۡحُوۡنَ**: from the root r-w-ḥ, the bringing back of herds in the evening to their resting place.
  - **حِيۡنَ تَسۡرَحُوۡنَ**: from the root s-r-ḥ, the sending out of herds, typically in the morning, to pasture.
- **The human agency:** Both verbs are second person. The beauty appears in the course of the owners' own activity of herding.

So, on the text alone, the jamāl is **a beauty that belongs to the livestock, accrues to their owners, and shows itself at the moments when the herd is in motion between pen and pasture.**

## Linguistic observations

- **The word جَمَال:** The root j-m-l denotes beauty, comeliness and goodliness. The ayah uses the noun, not an adjective. This frames beauty as a thing possessed or enjoyed, parallel to دِفۡءٌ and مَنَافِع in 16:5.
- **The indefinite form (jamālun):** The tanwīn may carry a sense of magnitude ("a great beauty") or of kind ("a certain sort of beauty"). Both readings are grammatically possible. Choosing between them is interpretation.
- **Sentence structure:** The predicate لَكُمۡ فِيۡهَا comes before the subject جَمَالٌ, which parallels لَـكُمۡ فِيۡهَا دِفۡءٌ in 16:5 and links the two ayahs as one list of blessings. The time adverbs حِيۡنَ … وَحِيۡنَ restrict *when* this beauty is enjoyed.
- **A lexical echo (my own observation):** s-r-ḥ appears elsewhere paired with the j-m-l root, in the phrase "a beautiful release" (33:28, 33:49). This is not evidence for the meaning of 16:6, but it shows the two roots sitting naturally together in Qur'anic diction.

## Context: where this ayah sits

- **16:5** lists material benefits: warmth, unspecified benefits, and food.

>> وَالۡاَنۡعَامَ خَلَقَهَا​ ۚ لَـكُمۡ فِيۡهَا دِفۡ ٴٌ وَّمَنَافِعُ وَمِنۡهَا تَاۡكُلُوۡنَ

- **16:6** adds a benefit of a different order: beauty.
- **16:7** returns to practical utility: carrying loads to distant lands.

>> وَتَحۡمِلُ اَثۡقَالَـكُمۡ اِلٰى بَلَدٍ لَّمۡ تَكُوۡنُوۡا بٰلِغِيۡهِ اِلَّا بِشِقِّ الۡاَنۡفُسِ​ؕ اِنَّ رَبَّكُمۡ لَرَءُوۡفٌ رَّحِيۡمٌۙ

- **16:8** (reference only) continues with horses, mules and donkeys, given for riding and as *zīna* (adornment).

The contextual point is clear. **The passage deliberately places an aesthetic, non-utilitarian benefit inside a list of practical ones.** Beauty is counted among God's favours alongside food and transport, and the sequence closes with the divine attributes of kindness and mercy.

## What kind of jamāl? Interpretive possibilities

The following are reasonable readings. None is stated explicitly by the text, and they are not mutually exclusive.

1. **Visual or aesthetic beauty.** The sight of a herd moving together at dawn and dusk is a spectacle. The tie to the moments of movement supports this, since that is when the animals are gathered and most visible.
2. **Social beauty: honour, standing, the dignity of wealth.** In a pastoral society a large, healthy herd passing through the settlement displays its owner's prosperity before others. The لَكُمۡ ("for you") and the public moments of departure and return fit this reading well. I understand this to be a common view among classical exegetes, but this needs verification.
3. **Inner or psychological beauty: contentment and delight.** The satisfaction of an owner watching his flock return safely, or set out healthy, is part of what makes the scene "beautiful" to him.

**My assessment:** The text most directly supports a beauty that is *seen and felt by the owners*, with a strong social dimension. Restricting it to bare visual appearance is narrower than the wording requires.

## The order: evening before morning

The evening return (تُرِيۡحُوۡنَ) is mentioned before the morning release (تَسۡرَحُوۡنَ), although morning comes first in the day.

- One explanation, which I believe is found in exegetical literature (needs verification), is that the animals are most beautiful on return: fed, full-uddered, and calm, with the owner's anxiety relieved.
- Another possibility is simple rhetorical or rhythmic choice.

I am uncertain which, if either, is intended. The order is notable, but its reason is interpretation.

## Wider Qur'anic theme (references only)

The idea that beauty and adornment are legitimate blessings appears elsewhere:
