- **16:8**: animals as *zīna*, directly continuing this passage.
- **7:32**: a rebuke to those who forbid the adornment God has brought forth.
- **18:7**: what is on earth made an adornment for it.

A possible distinction is that *jamāl* refers to inherent beauty and *zīna* to adornment or embellishment. If so, 16:6 and 16:8 speak of two related but different aesthetic benefits. This is a lexicographical claim and needs verification.

## Summary

- **Clear from the text:** a beauty residing in the livestock, granted to their owners as a blessing, and enjoyed at the times of the herd's evening return and morning departure.
- **Interpretation:** that this beauty is visual spectacle, social prestige, and inner contentment together, and that the evening is placed first because the animals look best then.

## To verify before saving

- Root meanings: r-w-ḥ (evening return of herds; *murāḥ*) and s-r-ḥ (sending to pasture, morning) in a standard Arabic lexicon.
- The claim that the indefinite *jamālun* can indicate magnitude or type (check a grammatical or rhetorical source).
- References 33:28 and 33:49: confirm both pair s-r-ḥ with j-m-l ("beautiful release").
- Reference 16:8: confirm wording on riding and *zīna*.
- Reference 7:32: confirm it concerns those forbidding God's adornment.
- Reference 18:7: confirm it speaks of earth's contents as adornment.
- The general statement that classical exegetes commonly explain the jamāl as honour or prestige among people.
- The general statement that exegetical literature explains the evening-first order by the animals' fuller condition on return.
- The *jamāl* vs *zīna* distinction (inherent beauty vs added adornment).

q.en: What kind of JAMAAL is being talked about?

ans.en:
## Practical Hidāyah Lessons from 16:1–9

**16:1: Patience with God's decree**
- Do not demand that God's promises or warnings come on your own timetable.
- Keep affirming God's transcendence over everything associated with Him.

**16:2: Revelation as the source of guidance**
- Seek guidance first in revelation, not in personal speculation alone.
- Make tawḥīd the centre of your belief.
- Let belief show itself in taqwā, conscious mindfulness of God in daily conduct.

**16:3: Creation as a sign**
- Reflect on the heavens and the earth as created with purpose, not in vain.
- Let this reflection strengthen your rejection of shirk. *(interpretive)*

**16:4: Humility about one's origin**
- Remember your humble beginning when tempted to argue against the truth.
- Watch for a contentious attitude in yourself, and approach truth with submission rather than dispute. *(interpretive)*

**16:5–8: Gratitude for blessings**
- Notice the everyday provisions you rely on, such as food, warmth, transport and comfort, and attribute them to God.
- Turn that recognition into gratitude in word and deed.
- Enjoy beauty and lawful adornment in creation without guilt, as part of God's provision.
- Remember God's kindness and mercy in the ease you are given (16:7).

**16:8: Humility in knowledge**

>> وَيَخۡلُقُ مَا لَا تَعۡلَمُوۡنَ

- Accept that human knowledge is always partial.
- Stay open to learning while recognising that God's creation exceeds what any generation knows.
- Treat new discoveries and inventions as further occasions for gratitude. *(interpretive application)*

**16:9: Choosing the straight path**

>> وَعَلَى اللّٰهِ قَصۡدُ السَّبِيۡلِ وَمِنۡهَا جَآٮِٕرٌ

- Recognise that God has made the straight path clear. Your task is to follow it, not to invent one.
- Be aware that many deviating paths exist, and test your choices against revelation.
- As you plan physical journeys, give equal or greater care to the direction of your life's journey toward God. *(interpretive link with 16:7–8)*

>> وَلَوۡ شَآءَ لَهَدٰٮكُمۡ اَجۡمَعِيۡنَ

- Ask God continually for guidance, since following the path depends on His will (compare 1:6).
- Take responsibility for your own choices, since you are addressed as one who chooses.
- Do not despair of others or try to force guidance on them. Convey the message and leave the outcome to God (compare 10:99). *(interpretive)*

## To verify before saving

- Summaries of 16:1–7 as implied in the lessons, including 16:7 mentioning God's kindness and mercy.
- 16:4 understood as describing a contentious disposition toward truth (commentators' view).
- The link between the physical travel of 16:7–8 and "the way" in 16:9 (commentators' view).
- Applying 16:8 to later inventions or discoveries (modern interpretive view).
- 1:6 as the request for guidance to the straight path.
- 10:99 as stating that, had God willed, all would have believed.
- The distinction between guidance as clarification and guidance as enablement, underlying the 16:9 lessons.

fu: Just list out practical lessons in points, not as detailed explanation

q.en: The Hidayah lesson from ayah 1-9

ans.en:
## The Text and Its Immediate Context

>> يُنۡۢبِتُ لَـكُمۡ بِهِ الزَّرۡعَ وَالزَّيۡتُوۡنَ وَالنَّخِيۡلَ وَالۡاَعۡنَابَ وَمِنۡ كُلِّ الثَّمَرٰتِ​ؕ اِنَّ فِىۡ ذٰ لِكَ لَاٰيَةً لِّـقَوۡمٍ يَّتَفَكَّرُوۡنَ

The ayah continues 16:10. The pronoun in *bihi* ("thereby") refers to the water sent down from the sky in that verse:

>> هُوَ الَّذِىۡۤ اَنۡزَلَ مِنَ السَّمَآءِ مَآءً​ لَّـكُمۡ مِّنۡهُ شَرَابٌ وَّمِنۡهُ شَجَرٌ فِيۡهِ تُسِيۡمُوۡنَ

It is followed by a shift from earthly to celestial phenomena:

>> وَسَخَّرَ لَـكُمُ الَّيۡلَ وَالنَّهَارَۙ وَالشَّمۡسَ وَالۡقَمَرَ​ؕ وَالنُّجُوۡمُ مُسَخَّرٰتٌۢ بِاَمۡرِهٖؕ اِنَّ فِىۡ ذٰ لِكَ لَاٰيٰتٍ لِّـقَوۡمٍ يَّعۡقِلُوۡنَۙ

**What the text states plainly:**
- God is the agent of growth (*yunbitu*, "He causes to grow").
- The water is the means (*bihi*).
- The produce is "for you" (*lakum*).
- Four items are named (*al-zarʿ*, *al-zaytūn*, *al-nakhīl*, *al-aʿnāb*), followed by "and from all the fruits."
- All of this is declared a sign (*āyah*) for those who reflect (*yatafakkarūn*).

**What is interpretation:** exactly what the sign points to, and why this vocabulary was chosen. The list below separates the two.

## Linguistic Observations Relevant to the Question

- **Singular *āyah* versus plural *āyāt*.** In 16:11 the word is singular (*la-āyatan*). In 16:12 it is plural (*la-āyātin*). This contrast is clearly in the text. Its significance is interpretive:
  - One reading takes the whole process (one water producing many kinds of growth) as a single unified sign.
  - Another reading treats the singular as generic or collective.
  - I am not certain which view predominates among exegetes.
- **The verb *yatafakkarūn*.** It is a Form V verb (*tafakkur*) from the root f-k-r. Such verbs often carry a sense of deliberate, effortful engagement. On that basis, *tafakkur* is commonly understood as reasoning from what is observed to what is not directly seen. The morphological pattern is clear; the precise semantic nuance should be confirmed in the Arabic lexicons.
- **Different closing phrases in this passage.** 16:12 closes with *yaʿqilūn* ("who reason"). 16:13, as I recall it, closes with a verb of remembrance or heeding (*yadhdhakkarūn*). The closings vary across consecutive signs. Whether each closing word is matched to the type of phenomenon described is a recognised line of rhetorical analysis, but its conclusions are interpretive.
- **The imperfect *yunbitu*.** The imperfect tense can convey ongoing or recurrent action. This suggests that growth is continually renewed rather than a single past event. That reading is linguistically reasonable but not compelled by the tense alone.
- **The partitive *min* in *min kulli al-thamarāt*.** It most naturally means "some of every kind of fruit." This signals that the four named items are illustrative, not exhaustive.
- **How the items are named.** *Al-nakhīl* names the palm *trees*, while *al-aʿnāb* names the grapes (the fruit). *Al-zaytūn* can denote either the tree or the fruit. Saheeh International's "grapevines" is a translational choice. Whether this variation carries meaning is uncertain.

## Probable Signs (*Āyāt*) for the *Mutafakkirūn*

Each item notes how firmly it rests on the text.

1. **Divine agency behind natural causation.**
   - *Text:* God is the grammatical subject of *yunbitu*; water is introduced with the instrumental *bi-*.
   - *Interpretation:* The thinker is invited to see that the means (water) is not the ultimate cause; growth is attributed to God working through it.
   - *Context:* The sūrah soon contrasts the One who creates with those who do not create (16:17), and states that those invoked besides God create nothing (16:20). This supports reading the sign as an argument for tawḥīd.

2. **One cause, many effects: diversity from a single water.**
   - *Text:* A single water (16:10) produces grain, olives, palms, grapes and every kind of fruit.
   - *Interpretation:* The variety of form, taste and use arising from one undifferentiated source points to a deliberate Originator, not blind uniformity.
   - *Cross-reference:* 13:4 makes this point explicitly: lands watered with one water, yet some produce is preferred over others in taste.

3. **Purposeful provision and care.**
   - *Text:* *lakum* ("for you") appears in both 16:10 and 16:11. In 16:12 the heavenly bodies are subjected "for you."
   - *Interpretation:* Creation is presented as oriented toward human benefit. This invites reflection on the Provider's care and on the gratitude owed.
   - *Context:* The sūrah's emphasis on enumerating blessings is widely noted. Some refer to it by a name connected with blessings; this should be verified.

4. **A gradation of provision across 16:10–11.**
   - *Text:* 16:10 mentions drink and vegetation for pasturing animals. 16:11 turns to crops and fruits for humans.
   - *Interpretation:* The ordering moves from water itself, to fodder, to human food. Some take this as a sign of an ordered, layered system of sustenance. The ordering is in the text; its intended significance is interpretive.

5. **The selection of the named crops.**
   - *Text:* Grain, olives, dates and grapes are named specifically, before the general category.
   - *Interpretation:* These were staples well known to the first audience. Some readers note their complementary uses: grain as staple food, olive as oil and fat, dates and grapes as sweet fruit and preserved provision. This nutritional reading is an inference and should not be presented as the text's explicit claim.
   - *Uncertain:* The significance of the precise order (grain first, then olive, then palm, then grape) is not obvious from the text alone. Views likely differ.

6. **Renewal of life as a pointer to resurrection.**
   - *Text:* 16:11 itself does not mention resurrection.
   - *Interpretation, supported by other passages:* Elsewhere the Qur'an explicitly draws the analogy from rain and plant growth to the raising of the dead. Examples include 50:9–11 (blessed water, gardens, harvest grain and tall palms, followed by "thus is the coming forth") and 35:9 (rain reviving dead land, "thus is the resurrection").
   - *Caution:* Applying this analogy to 16:11 is an intertextual inference. It fits the *tafakkur* closing, but the ayah does not state it.

7. **Interdependence with the cosmic order (16:11 → 16:12).**
   - *Text:* The next ayah turns to night and day, sun, moon and stars.
   - *Interpretation:* The sequence may invite the thinker to see that plant growth depends on a wider, regulated system of light, seasons and time, all under one command. This connection is suggested by the arrangement, not stated.

8. **Process and time as an object of reflection.**
   - *Interpretation:* The ayah describes growth: water, then sprouting, then fruiting. It does not describe a finished object. Some see this as particularly suited to *tafakkur*, which considers stages and processes leading to conclusions. This rests on the reading of *tafakkur* noted above and on the imperfect *yunbitu*, so it is suggestive rather than certain.

## Points of Uncertainty

- Whether the singular *āyah* is deliberately significant, and how, is debated or at least open. I cannot reliably attribute specific views.
- How tightly each closing verb (*yatafakkarūn*, *yaʿqilūn*, and the closing of 16:13) is tied to the type of sign is a matter of exegetical and rhetorical interpretation.
- The nutritional, ecological and scientific elaborations sometimes attached to this ayah go beyond the text. They should be presented, if at all, as later reflections, not as its meaning.

## To verify before saving

- The singular *la-āyatan* in 16:11 versus the plural *la-āyātin* in 16:12 (check against the muṣḥaf).
- The closing word of 16:13 (*yadhdhakkarūn*), cited from memory.
- 16:17: the contrast between the One who creates and one who does not.
- 16:20: those invoked besides God create nothing.
- 13:4: lands watered with one water, some produce preferred over others.
- 50:9–11: blessed water, gardens, grain, tall palms, then the analogy to "coming forth."
- 35:9: rain reviving dead land, analogy to resurrection.
- The claim that some refer to Sūrat al-Naḥl by a name relating to blessings.
- The semantic description of Form V *tafakkur* as deliberate reflection moving from the seen to the unseen (check the Arabic lexicons).
- Whether *al-zaytūn* denotes tree, fruit or both in classical usage.
- The general statement that exegetes hold differing views on the singular *āyah* and on the order of the named crops (unattributed; needs confirmation in tafsīr works).
- The general observation that the closing words of consecutive signs vary and are discussed in rhetorical analysis (needs confirmation in tafsīr or balāgha sources).

q.en: List out the probable AYAHS in this for the MUTAFAQQIRUN

ans.en:
## A note on the wording of the question

The ayah does not say *tahtadūn*. It reads:

>> وَعَلٰمٰتٍ​ؕ وَبِالنَّجۡمِ هُمۡ يَهۡتَدُوۡنَ

The verb is **yahtadūn** ("they are guided"), in the third person, with the explicit pronoun **hum** ("they"). The second-person form *tahtadūn* ("you may be guided") occurs at the end of the previous ayah:

>> وَاَلۡقٰى فِى الۡاَرۡضِ رَوَاسِىَ اَنۡ تَمِيۡدَ بِكُمۡ وَاَنۡهٰرًا وَّسُبُلًا لَّعَلَّكُمۡ تَهۡتَدُوۡنَۙ

So the question is really: **who is meant by *hum* in "wa bi-n-najmi hum yahtadūn"?**

## What the text clearly establishes

- **Grammar:** *hum* is the subject of *yahtadūn*. *Bi-n-najmi* ("by the star/stars") is the means of guidance. The phrase is fronted before the subject and verb.
- **Context:** 16:15 addresses the hearers directly ("with you", "that you may be guided"). 16:16 then switches to the third person ("they"). This kind of shift in person is a well-known feature of Qur'anic style.
- **Theme:** Mountains, rivers, roads, landmarks (*ʿalāmāt*) and stars are listed together as things God placed in creation so that people can find their way. 16:17 then asks whether the One who creates is like one who does not create. The passage therefore presents these means of orientation as **signs of the Creator's provision**, set against the powerlessness of false objects of worship.
- **Meaning of *yahtadūn* here:** In this context the primary sense is physical: finding one's way and direction. The root (h-d-y) also carries the sense of moral and spiritual guidance, and the passage arguably moves from the one to the other. That second layer, however, is an interpretive inference, not an explicit statement.

## Who "they" are: interpretation

The text itself does not name the referent. Possible readings, from most general to most specific:

1. **Human beings in general.** On this reading, "they" are the same people addressed in 16:15, now spoken of in the third person. It means anyone who travels and finds direction by the stars. This is the most economical reading linguistically.
2. **Travellers by land and sea, especially at night.** The pairing of landmarks (*ʿalāmāt*, typically visible by day) with the star(s) suggests a contrast between daytime and night-time navigation. This is a contextual inference.
3. **The Arabs, or Quraysh specifically.** Some exegetes are reported to have held that *hum* refers to the Arabs, who were renowned for navigating desert and sea by the stars. On this view, the emphatic *hum* and the fronted *bi-n-najmi* would carry a nuance of "they in particular," highlighting a favour well known to the first audience. *(Needs verification.)*

The shift from "you" to "they," together with the emphatic structure, is compatible with readings 1 and 3. The text alone does not decide between them.

## The meaning of *an-najm*

- *An-najm* is grammatically singular. It may be **generic** ("the stars" as a class), which is how Saheeh International renders it.
- Some exegetes are reported to have understood it as **a specific star used for orientation**. The Pole Star (known in Arabic tradition by names such as *al-Jady*) and the Pleiades (*ath-Thurayyā*) have been mentioned. *(Needs verification.)*
- There are also reported views on *ʿalāmāt*. Some take it as landmarks on earth (hills, paths, terrain features). Others take it as including the stars themselves, or as distinguishing different kinds of stars. *(Needs verification.)*

## Related ayah

- **6:97** states that God made the stars so that people may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea. This supports the navigational reading of 16:16 and its general application to people who travel. *(Check wording against the muṣḥaf.)*

## Summary

- **Clear from the text:** "They" are people who find their way by the star(s). The guidance is a divine favour, cited as evidence that the Creator alone deserves worship (16:17).
- **Interpretation:** Whether "they" means humanity in general, travellers at night, or specifically the Arabs/Quraysh is not stated in the text. Each view rests on context, style, or reported exegesis.
- **Uncertain:** Whether *an-najm* is generic or refers to a particular star.
- **Correction:** The ayah reads *yahtadūn* (third person), not *tahtadūn*.

## To verify before saving

- The exact Arabic text of 16:15 and 16:16 against a standard muṣḥaf, including the waqf mark after *wa-ʿalāmāt*.
- The reading *yahtadūn* in 16:16 and *tahtadūn* in 16:15 across the canonical readings (qirāʾāt).
- The reference 6:97 and the accuracy of my paraphrase of it.
- The claim that some exegetes identified *hum* as the Arabs or Quraysh.
- The claim that some exegetes took *an-najm* as a specific star, and the names *al-Jady* (Pole Star) and *ath-Thurayyā* (Pleiades) in that connection.
- The reported views on *ʿalāmāt* (earthly landmarks vs. stars).
- The grammatical analysis: the fronting of *bi-n-najmi* and the emphatic *hum*, and whether classical grammarians read this as specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ*) or emphasis.
- The description of the shift from second to third person as a recognised stylistic device (*iltifāt*) in this ayah.

q.en: Who are BINNAJMI TAHTADUUN ?

ans.en:
## Who is being described?

The subject of 16:21 continues directly from 16:20:

>> وَالَّذِيۡنَ يَدۡعُوۡنَ مِنۡ دُوۡنِ اللّٰهِ لَا يَخۡلُقُوۡنَ شَيۡــًٔا وَّهُمۡ يُخۡلَقُوۡنَؕ

>> اَمۡوَاتٌ غَيۡرُ اَحۡيَآءٍ​ ۚ وَمَا يَشۡعُرُوۡنَ اَيَّانَ يُبۡعَثُوۡنَ

**What the text says clearly:**
- **اَمۡوَاتٌ** is a predicate with an omitted subject, understood as "they are". Its nearest antecedent is "those they invoke besides Allah" in 16:20. The ayah is therefore describing the **objects of worship**, not, at least in its first clause, the worshippers.
- The passage argues against their divinity. They create nothing, they are themselves created (16:20), they are lifeless, and they do not know the time of resurrection (16:21). It then concludes in 16:22 that "your god is one God".

**Interpretation (the identity of the "invoked ones"):**
- **Idols (stone, wood, etc.).** This fits the immediate Meccan context. Applying "dead" to things that were never alive is natural in Arabic, where *mayyit* can mean simply "lifeless". Compare 2:28, where human beings before creation are called "dead".
- **Any being worshipped besides Allah.** This would include angels, jinn, or deceased righteous people. The grammar gives some support: the pronouns (هُمۡ, يَخۡلُقُوۡنَ, يَشۡعُرُوۡنَ, يُبۡعَثُوۡنَ) are masculine plurals normally used for rational beings. Two explanations are possible, and both may be meant:
  - The idols are spoken of in the way their worshippers treated them, as if they were rational.
  - The category includes rational beings.

**Note on the emphasis:** "dead, not alive" may look redundant. A plausible reading is that **غَيۡرُ اَحۡيَآءٍ** adds that life is not intrinsic to them at all. A god, by contrast, must be "living" in the full sense. This reading is interpretive.

## How can idols be "resurrected"?

The difficulty lies in the final clause, **وَمَا يَشۡعُرُوۡنَ اَيَّانَ يُبۡعَثُوۡنَ**. It contains two verbs, and the Arabic does not fix the referent of each pronoun. Three readings are grammatically possible, and views along these lines are reported in the exegetical tradition (needs verification).

**1. Both pronouns refer to the invoked ones.** They do not know when *they themselves* will be raised.
- On this view, even idols will be brought forth on the Day of Judgment. Other passages describe the false objects of worship being gathered with their worshippers and disowning them: 10:28–29, 25:17–18, 46:5–6. One passage states that worshippers and what they worship are fuel for Hell: 21:98.
- "Resurrection" here would mean being brought forth or gathered. Some also hold that God will grant the idols speech or perception so that they testify against their worshippers. That last point is interpretation and should be verified.
- If the invoked ones include angels, jinn or dead humans, there is no difficulty at all, since they will literally be raised.

**2. "Perceive" refers to the invoked ones, "resurrected" to the worshippers.** The idols do not even know when *those who worship them* will be raised.
- This removes the difficulty entirely, because the idols are not said to be resurrected.
- It also fits the argument well. A true deity would know the Hour of its servants' resurrection. These objects know nothing of it.
- The shift in pronoun reference is a recognised feature of Qur'anic style. Still, it is an interpretive choice that the text does not force.

**3. Both pronouns refer to the worshippers.** The polytheists do not perceive when they will be raised.
- This links neatly to 16:22, which immediately mentions "those who do not believe in the Hereafter".
- However, it breaks the flow from the description of the idols in the same ayah, so it seems the less natural reading of the immediate syntax.

## Summary

- **Clear from the text:** the ayah describes what is invoked besides Allah. Its purpose is to show that these cannot be gods: they are created, lifeless, and ignorant of the resurrection.
- **Your question:** whether idols "will be resurrected" depends on how the last clause is read.
  - Under reading 2, they are not said to be resurrected at all.
  - Under reading 1, "being raised" means being brought forth and gathered on the Day of Judgment, which other ayahs support.
  - If the invoked ones include rational beings, their literal resurrection is unproblematic.
- I cannot say from the text alone which reading is decisive. Reading 2 is the simplest solution to the difficulty you raise, while reading 1 has support from parallel passages.

## To verify before saving

- 2:28: humans described as "dead" before being given life.
- 10:28–29: the worshipped partners disown their worshippers on the Day of Judgment.
- 25:17–18: the worshippers are gathered with what they worshipped, and the worshipped are questioned.
- 46:5–6: those invoked are unaware of the invocation and become enemies of their worshippers.
- 21:98: worshippers and what they worship as fuel of Hell.
- The claim that all three pronoun readings are reported in the classical tafsir tradition.
- The view that God will grant idols life, speech or perception to testify against their worshippers.
- The grammatical explanation that rational-plural pronouns are used for idols because their worshippers treated them as rational.
- The explanation of غَيۡرُ اَحۡيَآءٍ as meaning that life is not intrinsic to them (not merely emphasis).
- Whether any variant readings (qirā'āt) of يَدۡعُوۡنَ or يُبۡعَثُوۡنَ affect the referent question. These are not addressed above.

q.en: Who are being talked? If idols, how they will be ressurected?

ans.en:
## What *lā jarama* is

*Lā jarama* (لا جرم) is a fixed expression of emphatic, conclusive affirmation. In the Qur'an it is **always followed by *anna* + a clause**, as here:

>> لَا جَرَمَ اَنَّ اللّٰهَ يَعۡلَمُ مَا يُسِرُّوۡنَ وَمَا يُعۡلِنُوۡنَ​ؕ اِنَّهٗ لَا يُحِبُّ الۡمُسۡتَكۡبِرِيۡنَ

By my count it occurs five times: 11:22, 16:23, 16:62, 16:109 and 40:43. That puts three of the five in Sūrat An-Nahl, and two of those are in near-identical wording (11:22 and 16:109).

The root *j-r-m* carries the senses "to cut off," "to earn or bring upon oneself," and, in the noun *jurm*, "crime." Classical grammarians analysed the phrase in several ways (needs verification):

- **Two-part reading:** *lā* negates a preceding or implied claim ("No! [It is not as they think]"), and *jarama* is a verb meaning "it has earned / brought about" or "it has become due." The *anna*-clause is then its subject or object: "it has become due that God knows…"
- **Verbal reading:** *jarama* means *ḥaqqa* or *wajaba*, "it is truly and necessarily the case that…"
- **Compound reading:** *lā jarama* functions as a single unit equivalent to *lā budda* ("inevitably") or *lā maḥālah*.
- **"Cutting" reading:** *lā jarama* means "there is no cutting it off," i.e., the matter is decisively settled.

Usage itself is clear: the phrase states a firm conclusion. Which etymology is correct is disputed, and I cannot settle it.

## Why this expression rather than the alternatives

The Qur'an has several other means of emphatic affirmation. What follows is an argument from the text and context, not a transmitted explanation.

**1. Versus *lā rayba* ("no doubt")**
- *Lā rayba* negates doubt about a matter presented for belief, such as the Book in 2:2 or the coming of the Hour.
- *Lā jarama* does something different. It draws a **settled conclusion from what precedes it**, and it often carries a note of rebuttal. Here the preceding ayah describes the deniers:

>> فَالَّذِيۡنَ لَا يُؤۡمِنُوۡنَ بِالۡاٰخِرَةِ قُلُوۡبُهُمۡ مُّنۡكِرَةٌ وَّهُمۡ مُّسۡتَكۡبِرُوۡنَ

- 16:23 then reads as the verdict that follows from that description. It is not an answer to a doubt in the listener's mind.

**2. Versus a bare *inna* or *anna***
- *Inna* gives emphasis without the sense of "therefore, inevitably."
- The ayah in fact uses both devices. *Lā jarama* governs the first clause, and *inna* introduces the second (اِنَّهٗ لَا يُحِبُّ الۡمُسۡتَكۡبِرِيۡنَ).
- This suggests the two are not interchangeable. The first statement, God's knowledge of their concealed and declared states, is framed as the **inescapable conclusion**. The second is a general principle given ordinary emphasis. (Interpretive.)

**3. Versus *ḥaqqan* or *laqad***
- *Ḥaqqan* typically affirms a promise or a truth positively, for example with God's promise.
- *Laqad* (an oath-*lām* with *qad*) emphasises the occurrence of an event.
- Neither carries the confrontational, conclusion-drawing force of *lā jarama*.

**4. The pattern of occurrences**
- In all five places, *lā jarama* appears in a setting of **confrontation with those who reject the message**:
  - the losers in the Hereafter (11:22, 16:109);
  - those assigned the Fire (16:62);
  - the believer of Pharaoh's people rebutting his own people (40:43).
- It seems reserved for verdicts against an opposing stance, not for neutral statements. This fits 16:23 exactly. (Observation from the occurrences; worth checking each in context.)

## Contextual fit in 16:22–24

**What the text states clearly:**
- The deniers have "disapproving hearts," an inner state.
- They are "arrogant," a state that shows outwardly.
- God knows "what they conceal and what they declare."
- He does not love the arrogant.

**Interpretation:**
- The pairing *yusirrūn / yuʿlinūn* maps onto the preceding description:
  - **concealed:** the hearts' denial (*qulūbuhum munkirah*);
  - **declared:** their arrogance, and their open dismissal of revelation in the next ayah:

>> قَالُـوۡۤا اَسَاطِيۡرُ الۡاَوَّلِيۡنَ

- If the "rebuttal" analysis of *lā* is accepted, the phrase answers an implied assumption: that inward denial stays hidden, or that open mockery carries no consequence. "No, it is settled: God knows both."
- The root sense "earned / brought upon oneself" (if accepted) would add a further resonance. The conclusion is something their own stance has **brought about**.
- This last point is a possible nuance. It is not a demonstrated intention of the text, and I am unsure how much weight it can bear.

## Caveat

We can describe how *lā jarama* functions differently from its near-synonyms. We cannot prove from the text alone why it was "chosen" over them. Arguments of this kind are rhetorical inference. Some classical scholars of *balāghah* and the grammarians discussed the expression, but I have not reproduced their wording here (needs verification).

## To verify before saving

- That *lā jarama* occurs exactly five times: 11:22, 16:23, 16:62, 16:109, 40:43.
- That it is always followed by *anna* in the Qur'an.
- The wording and context of 11:22, 16:62, 16:109 and 40:43, and that all are confrontational or verdict contexts.
- The four grammatical analyses of *lā jarama* (rebuttal + verb; *ḥaqqa/wajaba*; compound = *lā budda*; "no cutting off"), and which grammarians held each.
- The root meanings of *j-r-m* (cut, earn, crime) in standard lexicons.
- The characterisation of *lā rayba* (e.g., 2:2 and usage with the Hour), *ḥaqqan* and *laqad*.
- Whether classical *balāghah* or tafsir works explicitly discuss the choice of *lā jarama* in 16:23.

q.en: Why JARAMA instead of other similar quranic word?

ans.en:
## The two occurrences

The phrase the questioner refers to appears twice within a few verses of each other:

- **16:19** (not quoted here) states, in the second person, that God knows what "you" conceal and what "you" declare.
- **16:23** says:

>> لَا جَرَمَ اَنَّ اللّٰهَ يَعۡلَمُ مَا يُسِرُّوۡنَ وَمَا يُعۡلِنُوۡنَ​ؕ اِنَّهٗ لَا يُحِبُّ الۡمُسۡتَكۡبِرِيۡنَ

The two statements are close in wording but not identical, and each does different work in its own setting. Read in context, the second is not redundant.

## Differences in the text itself

These points are observable directly in the wording.

1. **Person and addressee.**
   - In 16:19 the verbs are second person ("you conceal… you declare"). It addresses the audience in general, within an argument about who deserves worship.
   - In 16:23 the verbs are third person (*yusirrūna*, *yuʿlinūna*). They refer specifically to the group just described in 16:22.

2. **The opening particle.**
   - 16:19, as commonly read, opens with a simple statement ("And Allah knows…").
   - 16:23 opens with **لَا جَرَمَ**, an emphatic expression of certainty ("assuredly, there is no doubt"), followed by the confirmatory **أَنَّ**.
   - The added emphasis suits a verse directed at people who are denying, not one simply stating a truth.

3. **What follows.**
   - 16:23 continues with a judgement: **إِنَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ الْمُسْتَكْبِرِينَ**.
   - The divine knowledge is thus tied immediately to God's disapproval of a specific moral fault.

## The function of each occurrence (interpretation)

The following is my reading of the context. It is reasoned from the text, not quoted from a source.

**16:19: knowledge as proof of divinity.**
The surrounding verses contrast God, who creates, with what is worshipped besides Him, which creates nothing (16:17, 16:20–21). Comprehensive knowledge of the hidden and the open is offered as one of the attributes that distinguish the true God from false objects of worship. Its function is **argumentative**: it supports *tawḥīd*. This leads directly to the conclusion in 16:22:

>> اِلٰهُكُمۡ اِلٰهٌ وَّاحِدٌ​​

**16:23: knowledge as warning to the deniers.**
Once 16:22 has described the deniers, the same truth is turned toward them. Its function is now **admonitory**: God knows exactly what they are, so they will be held to account. The point is no longer "God knows, therefore He alone is God". It is "God knows *you*, therefore beware".

## How 16:23 maps onto 16:22 and 16:24

This is a plausible but interpretive reading. The two halves of the knowledge statement appear to correspond to the description around it.

- **What they conceal (*mā yusirrūn*)** corresponds to their inner state in 16:22:

>> قُلُوۡبُهُمۡ مُّنۡكِرَةٌ

- **What they declare (*mā yuʿlinūn*)** corresponds to their outward conduct, their arrogance, and the open words reported in the next verse:

>> قَالُـوۡۤا اَسَاطِيۡرُ الۡاَوَّلِيۡنَۙ

- **The arrogance** named in 16:22 is picked up directly in the closing words of 16:23:

>> وَّهُمۡ مُّسۡتَكۡبِرُوۡنَ

>> اِنَّهٗ لَا يُحِبُّ الۡمُسۡتَكۡبِرِيۡنَ

On this reading, 16:23 sits between the description of the deniers' hidden disposition (16:22) and the example of their public speech (16:24). It declares that both are known to God.

## Summary

The repetition is a **re-application of one truth to a new purpose**:

- In 16:19 it is general, addressed to "you", and serves to prove God's uniqueness.
- In 16:23 it is specific, about "them", made emphatic by *lā jarama*, and serves as a warning that ends in God's disapproval of the arrogant.

This kind of restatement, where a theological principle is first established and then turned on a particular group, is a recognisable feature of Qur'anic discourse. I have not, however, checked how classical exegetes treat this particular pair.

**Uncertainties:**
- Exegetes have discussed the morphology and grammatical analysis of *lā jarama*. I cannot state the specific positions reliably from memory.
- I am also unsure whether variant readings (*qirāʾāt*) affect the person of the verbs in 16:19 or nearby verses. If they do, part of the contrast drawn above would need adjusting.

## To verify before saving

- That 16:19 is the earlier occurrence, and that its verbs are second person (*tusirrūna / tuʿlinūna*) and it opens with "wa-llāhu yaʿlamu", in the Ḥafṣ reading.
- Whether any *qirāʾa* reads 16:19 (or 16:20–21) with third-person verbs, which would affect the "you" vs "them" contrast.
- The description of 16:17 and 16:20–21 as contrasting the Creator with things that create nothing.
- The meaning of *lā jarama* as "assuredly / no doubt", and the grammarians' differing analyses of it.
- The claim that this restatement-then-application pattern is a recognised feature of Qur'anic style (general claim, not sourced).
- How classical *tafsīr* works explain the relationship between 16:19 and 16:23. None were consulted or quoted here.
- The mapping of *mā yusirrūn* to "hearts disapproving" and *mā yuʿlinūn* to arrogance and the words of 16:24. This is my interpretation and should be checked against exegetical sources.

q.en: Why YALAMU MA YUSIRRUNA WA YULINUNA is repeated in a short interval?

ans.en:
**Short answer:** The text does not settle the matter. It reads naturally either as a concrete report of real buildings collapsing on real people, or as a figurative image (*tamthīl*) for plots that collapse on those who make them. Even on the figurative reading, though, it is not *merely* a parable. It reports a real outcome, the downfall of earlier plotters, and only the building imagery is in question.

## What the text says clearly

>> قَدۡ مَكَرَ الَّذِيۡنَ مِنۡ قَبۡلِهِمۡ فَاَتَى اللّٰهُ بُنۡيَانَهُمۡ مِّنَ الۡقَوَاعِدِ فَخَرَّ عَلَيۡهِمُ السَّقۡفُ مِنۡ فَوۡقِهِمۡ وَاَتٰٮهُمُ الۡعَذَابُ مِنۡ حَيۡثُ لَا يَشۡعُرُوۡنَ

- **It is a past-tense report.** *Qad makara* ("had already plotted") presents a completed fact about "those before them." It is not framed as a hypothetical or an illustrative story.
- **The subject is plotting (*makr*).** The verse opens by naming the plotting, then moves to the building, the foundations and the roof. This sequence is what allows the building to be read as the structure of their scheming.
- **The final clause is general and plainly literal.** "The punishment came to them from where they did not perceive" states a real punishment, whatever one makes of the building imagery.
- **Context.** The surrounding verses address the Meccan opponents. Verse 16:24 has them dismiss the revelation as "legends of the ancients." In 16:25 they bear their own burdens and some of the burdens of those they misguide. In 16:27 comes their disgrace on the Day of Resurrection. Verse 16:26 is therefore a warning drawn from precedent: earlier plotters were undone, and so will these be.

## Linguistic points bearing on the question

- **No simile marker.** The verse has no *mathal*, *ka-*, or *ka-anna*. Contrast passages that explicitly label an image as a likeness. In 29:41, those who take protectors besides God are likened to the spider's house. In 14:18, deeds are likened to ashes in the wind. The absence of a marker weighs somewhat toward a literal reading. It does not exclude a figurative one, however, because Arabic rhetoric recognises the extended metaphor (*istiʿāra tamthīliyya*), which works without any explicit comparison.
- ***Atā* used for destruction.** "God came at their building" uses *atā* in the sense of assailing or undoing. Compare 59:2, where God "came to" a people from where they did not expect. There the phrase describes a real historical event, and its vocabulary resembles 16:26's final clause.
- ***Min al-qawāʿid* ("from the foundations").** The attack strikes at the base, so the whole structure fails. This fits a physical collapse and also fits the image of a scheme undermined at its root.
- ***Min fawqihim* ("from above them").** A roof can only fall from above, so the phrase looks redundant. Its function is debated, and I am unsure which view is stronger:
  - On a literal reading, it stresses that they were actually beneath the roof when it fell, so they were killed by it, not merely that their building fell.
  - On a figurative reading, it intensifies the image of being overwhelmed by one's own construction.
- ***ʿAlayhim* ("upon them")** may carry the sense of "against them," to their harm. That sense suits both readings.

## Interpretive positions (in general terms, all needing verification)

1. **Literal and specific.** Some exegetes are reported to connect the verse to a particular ancient ruler who built a lofty tower or structure to reach the heavens, which God destroyed. The ruler is often identified with the king associated with Abraham, and some link the story to the tower of Babel narratives. *(Needs verification: who holds this, and the reliability of the reports.)* For comparison, Pharaoh's order to build a tower appears in 28:38 and 40:36–37, though 16:26 does not name him.
2. **Figurative (*tamthīl*).** Others are reported to read the verse as an extended metaphor. The plotters built their schemes like a building, God undermined them at the base, and the schemes collapsed on their own makers. *(Needs verification.)* The Qur'an uses building imagery figuratively elsewhere. In 9:109–110 a building founded on the edge of a crumbling bank collapses with its builder, and the building of the hypocrites remains a source of doubt in their hearts.
3. **General and combined.** Some are reported to take "those before them" broadly, as all earlier deniers, while allowing that physical destruction of dwellings did occur among them. For example, 11:82 and 29:40 describe the overturning of cities and the varied punishments of past peoples. *(Needs verification.)*

## Assessment

- The plural, unnamed "those before them," the opening focus on *makr*, and the general closing clause favour reading 16:26 as a **pattern of divine response to plotting**, not a single anecdote. This leaves room for figurative imagery.
- The past-tense narrative frame, the lack of a simile marker and the concrete *min fawqihim* keep a **literal reading fully viable**.
- The **substance is the same either way**: plots against the truth recoil on their authors, and punishment arrives unforeseen. Calling it "just a parable" would understate that. At most, the imagery is figurative while the warning and the historical claim are real.

## To verify before saving

- That some exegetes link 16:26 to a specific ancient ruler or tower (Nimrod, Babel), and the reliability of those reports
- That some exegetes read the verse as *tamthīl* or *istiʿāra tamthīliyya*, and which ones
- That some take "those before them" generally, combining literal and figurative senses
- The explanations given for *min fawqihim*
- The reading of *ʿalayhim* as "to their detriment" in this verse
- The sense of *atā* as assailing or destroying, in the lexicons and tafsir
- References and descriptions: 16:24, 29:41, 14:18, 59:2, 28:38, 40:36–37, 9:109–110, 11:82, 29:40
- The rhetorical classification of an unmarked extended metaphor in Arabic *balāgha*

q.en: Is it just a Figurative speech?

ans.en:
**Short answer:** The word in this ayah is **السَّلَمَ (*as-salam*)**, not **السَّلَام (*as-salām*)**, "peace." In the idiom used here, *as-salam* means surrender, yielding or capitulation, and "submission" fits both the word and the context better than "peace."

## 1. The word itself

The ayah reads:

>> فَاَلۡقَوُا السَّلَمَ

- **Vocalisation:** The lām carries a fatḥa and is followed by no long vowel (no alif and no dagger alif). It is read *as-salam*, with two short vowels. This is morphologically different from *as-salām*, with a long ā, which is the familiar word for "peace" and the greeting.
- **Shared root:** Both words come from the root **s-l-m**. Its core sense is roughly safety, soundness, being free from harm, and, by extension, yielding or handing oneself over. Because the two words share a root, they overlap in meaning, which explains why some translations choose "peace." They are still not identical words.
- **Meaning of *salam*:** In classical Arabic usage, *salam* commonly denotes surrender and submissive compliance, especially giving up resistance. It also has commercial and other technical senses that are irrelevant here. *(This lexical claim should be checked in the standard dictionaries.)*

## 2. The idiom *alqā as-salam*

- The verb **أَلْقَى (*alqā*)** literally means "to throw, cast, lay down."
- Combined with *as-salam*, it forms an idiom close to "to lay down one's arms" or "to throw in the towel": to capitulate and declare that one is no longer resisting.
- A literal "they cast peace" would make little sense in English. "They offered submission" or "they surrendered" captures the idiom.

## 3. The context of 16:28 supports "submission"

What the text clearly says:

- The scene is the moment of death. The angels take these people while they are *ẓālimī anfusihim*, "wronging themselves."
- Their response is introduced by **fa-** ("then, thereupon"). They immediately "cast the *salam*" and then deny any wrongdoing:

>> مَا كُنَّا نَـعۡمَلُ مِنۡ سُوۡۤءٍ

- The denial is rejected at once:

>> بَلٰٓى اِنَّ اللّٰهَ عَلِيۡمٌۢ بِمَا كُنۡتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُوۡنَ

- The next ayah (16:29) sends them into Hell and calls them **al-mutakabbirīn**, "the arrogant."

Interpretive reading (reasonable, but interpretation):

- The people described are not in a position to "offer peace" to the angels, as if they were an equal party negotiating terms. What fits the scene is that their former arrogance and opposition (compare *tushāqqūna* in 16:27) collapses at death and they yield.
- There is a contrast. In life they were *mutakabbirūn* (16:29) and opposed God's messengers and believers (16:27). At death they abruptly surrender. Their surrender is accompanied by a false denial, which shows it is capitulation under compulsion rather than sincere peace-making or repentance.
- "Submission" here should therefore not be confused with *islām* in the sense of voluntary faith, even though the root is the same. It is forced, belated yielding. (Whether this yielding has any value is answered by the context: it does not.)

## 4. Usage elsewhere in the Qur'an (to be checked)

- **16:87**, in the same sūra, describes the polytheists on the Day of Judgment "casting *as-salam*" to God, after which their invented partners abandon them. This parallel strongly supports the sense of surrender or capitulation.
- **4:90–91** uses the same idiom in a military and political setting. It refers to people who withdraw from fighting and "cast *as-salam*" to the believers. There the sense is closer to offering peace or terms, that is, laying down arms. This shows that the idiom can lean toward "peace" when two parties face each other in conflict.
- **4:94** has a related expression about someone who greets or addresses the believers. I understand that the canonical readings differ here between *as-salam* and *as-salām*. If so, this would show that the two words were distinguished and that the reading affects the meaning. *(I am not certain of this; it needs verification.)*
- Related forms meaning "peace," such as *salm* and *silm*, occur in passages such as **8:61**, **47:35** and **2:208**. The exact vocalisations and readings in these verses should be checked.

**Inference:** The semantic range runs from "peace or truce" (between parties in conflict) to "surrender or submission" (from a defeated or powerless party). Context decides which sense applies. In 16:28 the party is helpless before the angels of death, so the "surrender" end of the range applies.

## 5. Is "peace" therefore wrong?

Not entirely, but it is less precise:

- Some English translations do render the phrase with "peace." *(Which translations do so needs checking.)* This may reflect the root's general meaning, or the idea that the defeated "sue for peace."
- I understand that exegetical works generally gloss *salam* here as surrender, submission or yielding, and treat the scene as the disbelievers' capitulation at death. *(This general characterisation needs verification against the tafsir literature; I am not quoting any specific scholar.)*
- "Submission" avoids two misleading implications of "peace": that the speakers are an equal party, and that their gesture is sincere or accepted. Both implications contradict the text, since the ayah immediately rejects them.

## To verify before saving

- That the standard Arabic dictionaries define *salam* (fatḥa on sīn and lām) as surrender, submission or yielding, and distinguish it from *salām* (peace).
- That the idiom *alqā as-salam* is understood classically as capitulating or laying down arms.
- 16:87: that it uses the same expression for the polytheists yielding to God on the Day of Judgment.
- 4:90–91: that they use *alqaw ilaykum as-salam* in a military context in the sense of withdrawing from fighting or offering peace.
- 4:94: whether the canonical readings differ between *as-salam* and *as-salām*, and which readers hold which reading.
- 8:61, 47:35 and 2:208: the exact words and readings (*salm*, *silm*) used for "peace."
- That some English translations render 16:28 with "peace," and which ones.
- That the tafsir literature in general glosses *as-salam* in 16:28 as surrender or submission.

q.en: Why SALAM is translated as submission instead of peace?

ans.en:
## The basic sense of حَرَصَ

Classical Arabic lexicography generally treats **حِرْص** as *intense, persistent eagerness for something, combined with effort to obtain it*. It is not simple wanting. It implies inner attachment and active pursuit, sometimes to the point of avidity or greed. (This summary of the lexical sense needs checking against the standard dictionaries.)

The Qur'anic data supports this reading. Every occurrence of the root involves strong attachment, and the object of that attachment is marked with **عَلَى**:

>> وَلَتَجِدَنَّهُمۡ أَحۡرَصَ ٱلنَّاسِ عَلَىٰ حَيَوٰةٖ

>> حَرِيصٌ عَلَيۡكُم بِٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ رَءُوفٞ رَّحِيمٞ

>> إِن تَحۡرِصۡ عَلَىٰ هُدَىٰهُمۡ

**What the text shows clearly:**
- The root is morally neutral. In 2:96 it is blameworthy clinging to life. In 9:128 it is praiseworthy concern for people.
- Its value depends entirely on its object. In 16:37 the object is the best possible one, **هُدَاهُم** ("their guidance").

## Comparison with the other verbal occurrences

The verb appears three times. All three share a striking pattern: **the verb always stands in a conditional or concessive clause, and the outcome it strives for is denied.**

>> وَلَن تَسۡتَطِيعُوٓاْ أَن تَعۡدِلُواْ بَيۡنَ ٱلنِّسَآءِ وَلَوۡ حَرَصۡتُمۡ

>> وَمَآ أَكۡثَرُ ٱلنَّاسِ وَلَوۡ حَرَصۡتَ بِمُؤۡمِنِينَ

>> إِن تَحۡرِصۡ عَلَىٰ هُدَىٰهُمۡ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَهۡدِي مَن يُضِلُّ

**What this shows about meaning.** In the Qur'an's usage, the verb seems to describe a maximal human effort that meets a limit beyond human control:
- In 4:129, perfect equality of feeling between wives cannot be achieved.
- In 12:103, most people do not believe.
- In 16:37, God does not guide those He leaves astray.

The word is well suited to this role. Because حرص denotes the *utmost* eagerness, saying that even this does not change the outcome closes off every lesser effort as well. This is a reading of the pattern, not a stated rule, but the consistency across all three verses is a textual fact.

**12:103 and 16:37 compared.** Both address the Prophet and both concern people's belief or guidance. Their grammar differs:
- **12:103: لَوْ + perfect (حَرَصْتَ).** This is a concessive aside: "even though you are eager." It is set inside a statement of fact about most people.
- **16:37: إِنْ + jussive imperfect (تَحْرِصْ).** The eagerness is the main condition of the sentence. The imperfect presents it as an ongoing, present disposition.

*Interpretation:* 16:37 makes the Prophet's eagerness the explicit topic and responds to it directly. That suits a verse whose function appears to be consolation.

**Grammar of the apodosis.** The clause after فَـ, **فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَهۡدِي مَن يُضِلُّ**, does not state the direct result ("you will not succeed"). It states the *reason* why the effort will not succeed. A common grammatical analysis treats this kind of clause as standing in place of an implied answer to the condition (needs verification). On that reading, the wording turns attention away from the Prophet's effort and toward God's decree.

## Comparison with the other words of the root

- **حَرِيص (9:128).** This adjective describes a *stable trait* of the Messenger: concern for his people. The verb in 16:37 refers to that same disposition in action.
  - *Interpretation:* read together, the two verses portray a consistent figure. The eagerness is affirmed as a virtue in 9:128, and its limits are marked in 16:37. Neither verse criticises the eagerness itself.
- **أَحْرَص (2:96).** This elative applies the same intensity to a worldly object, life itself. It confirms that the root carries a sense of intensity and attachment, not mild desire. That intensity is what gives 16:37 its force.

## Fit with the immediate context

16:36 divides people into two groups:

>> فَمِنۡهُمۡ مَّنۡ هَدَى اللّٰهُ وَمِنۡهُمۡ مَّنۡ حَقَّتۡ عَلَيۡهِ الضَّلٰلَةُ​

16:37 then takes up the second group:
- **هُدَاهُم** and **يَهۡدِي** echo **هَدَى**.
- **يُضِلُّ** echoes **الضَّلٰلَةُ**.

The two verses share both **عَلَى** constructions and the same lexical pair of guidance and misguidance. *Interpretation:* تحرص therefore marks the point where human effort meets the division already announced in 16:36.

The words **حَقَّتۡ عَلَيۡهِ** ("[deservedly] decreed") in 16:36 are often taken to qualify how يُضِلُّ in 16:37 should be understood. Theological schools differ on this, and the matter lies outside a word-fit analysis (views exist; needs verification).

16:38 then gives evidence of the obstinacy in question, the deniers' oath that God will not resurrect the dead. *Interpretation:* this shows the kind of resistance that even intense eagerness cannot overcome.

## Why this word and not another

Other Qur'anic words cover nearby meanings. The contrasts below are interpretive, and the references should be checked.

- **أَحْبَبْتَ (28:56).** This verse also tells the Prophet that he does not guide whom he wishes. It uses a verb of *love* directed at a person. حرص in 16:37 is directed at *their guidance* as an object of effort. 28:56 speaks of affection, while 16:37 speaks of exertion.
- **طَمِعَ (2:75).** Here believers are asked whether they hope that certain people will believe. طمع suggests *hopeful expectation*. حرص suggests *active, anxious striving*, which fits a verse about the Prophet's mission.
- **أَرَادَ / وَدَّ.** These are general verbs of will and wish. They lack حرص's sense of intensity and persistent effort, so they would weaken the concessive force.
- **Self-consuming grief (18:6; 26:3; 35:8).** These passages describe the Prophet's sorrow over his people's rejection. حرص names the *drive* that precedes such grief. *Interpretation:* 16:37 addresses the striving itself, not its emotional aftermath.

**Sound.** **تَحۡرِصۡ** is short, and its final sukūn on the emphatic ص gives a firm, clipped close before **عَلَىٰ هُدَىٰهُمۡ**. Any claim that this sound is deliberately expressive is speculative.

**Readings.** Variant readings exist for **لَا يَهۡدِي** (an active versus a passive reading). Variant vocalisations of the verb (تَحۡرِصۡ / تَحۡرَصۡ) may also be reported, reflecting the two lexical forms of the verb. Both points need verification against the qirāʾāt literature.

## To verify before saving

- The lexical definition of حِرْص (intense eagerness with effort, bordering on avidity) against the standard Arabic lexicons.
- That the verb حَرَصَ occurs exactly three times (4:129, 12:103, 16:37), أَحْرَص once (2:96) and حَرِيص once (9:128).
- The exact Arabic text of every quoted line against a standard muṣḥaf.
- The grammatical analysis of فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يَهۡدِي as a causal clause standing in place of the implied answer to the condition.
- The general statement that views differ on how حَقَّتۡ عَلَيۡهِ الضَّلٰلَةُ relates to يُضِلُّ.
- 28:56: wording and theme (the Prophet does not guide whom he loves).
- 2:75: wording and theme (hope that certain people would believe).
- 18:6, 26:3, 35:8: that these concern the Prophet's grief over his people's disbelief.
- The variant readings of لَا يَهۡدِي (active/passive) and any reported vocalisation تَحۡرَصۡ, and which readers are associated with each.
- The existence of both verb forms حَرَصَ يَحۡرِصُ and حَرِصَ يَحۡرَصُ in the lexicons.

q.en: How does the word «تَحْرِصْ» fit in this ayah (16:37) compared with similar Qur'anic words used elsewhere? Why this word here and not another?

ans.en:
## The occurrences

The full formula, the command *kun* ("Be") followed by *fa-yakūn* ("and it is/was"), appears in **eight places**:

| Ref. | Wording (described) | Immediate context |
|---|---|---|
| **2:117** | He is the Originator of the heavens and earth; when He decrees a matter, He only says to it "Be," and it is. | Refutation of the claim that God has taken a son (2:116) |
| **3:47** | Allah creates what He wills; when He decrees a matter, He only says to it "Be," and it is. | Maryam asks how she can have a child when no man has touched her |
| **3:59** | The likeness of ʿĪsā with God is that of Ādam: He created him from dust, then said to him "Be," and he was. | Argument with those who deify ʿĪsā (the Najrān context is a traditional report and needs verification) |
| **6:73** | He created the heavens and earth in truth; on the day He says "Be," it is. His word is the truth, and His is the dominion on the day the Horn is blown. | Creation and the Last Day |
| **16:40** | The ayah under study | Denial of resurrection (16:38–39) |
| **19:35** | It is not befitting for God to take a son; when He decrees a matter, He only says to it "Be," and it is. | Birth of ʿĪsā; rejection of divine sonship |
| **36:82** | His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it "Be," and it is. | The man who asks who can revive decayed bones (36:77–81) |
| **40:68** | He gives life and causes death; when He decrees a matter, He only says to it "Be," and it is. | Stages of human creation, life and death (40:67–68) |

**Related, but not the same formula** (useful for comparison, not counted above):
- Creative or transformative commands without *fa-yakūn*: 2:65 and 7:166 ("Be apes"), 21:69 (the fire told to be cool and safe for Ibrāhīm).
- The same idea of an instantaneous command in other words: 54:50 (God's command is but one, like the twinkling of an eye).

## Variation in the formula

The text shows four distinct frames:

1. **"When He decrees a matter (*qaḍā amran*)…"**: 2:117, 3:47, 19:35, 40:68.
2. **"When He intends a thing (*arāda*)…"**: 36:82 (third person) and 16:40 (first person plural).
3. **Narrative past**: 3:59, which reports a specific completed act (the creation of Ādam).
4. **Eschatological time-frame**: 6:73, "on the day He says…".

**16:40 is the only occurrence in the divine first person plural:**
>> اِنَّمَا قَوۡلُـنَا لِشَىۡءٍ اِذَاۤ اَرَدۡنٰهُ اَنۡ نَّقُوۡلَ لَهٗ كُنۡ فَيَكُوۡنُ

This places the statement directly in God's own voice, as a reply to the oath of the disbelievers in 16:38.

## Thematic analysis: where the phrase is used

Grouping the eight contexts gives three clusters:

**1. The birth of ʿĪsā and the rejection of divine sonship** (2:117, 3:47, 3:59, 19:35)
- A birth without a father is presented as no harder than any other act of creation.
- 3:59 extends the argument a fortiori: Ādam had neither father nor mother.
- In 2:117 and 19:35 the formula follows directly on the denial that God has a son. The implied reasoning (an inference from context) is that a Being who creates by mere command has no need of offspring or partners.

**2. Resurrection and the Last Day** (6:73, 16:40, 36:82)
- 16:40 and 36:82 each answer an explicit denial of resurrection. 16:38 is an oath that God will not raise the dead; 36:78 asks who can revive bones.
- 6:73 links the command to the Day the Horn is blown.

**3. Creation in general, life and death** (2:117, 40:68)
- 2:117 joins the formula to God as Originator of the heavens and earth.
- 40:68 joins it to giving life and causing death, after the stages of human development.

**What the text clearly shows:** the formula almost never appears as a bare cosmological statement. It typically comes as a **response to an objection or a doubt about possibility**:
- Maryam's "how?"
- The claim of a son
- The denial of resurrection
- The wonder at revived bones

Its function is **argumentative (ḥujja)**. Whatever humans judge impossible, extraordinary, or in need of means is, for God, a single command.

**Common semantic core:**
- **Effortlessness and absence of intermediary**: nothing more than the command is needed.
- **Immediacy**: the *fa* expresses sequence without interval.
- **Absolute will**: the formula is tied to God's decreeing (*qaḍā*) or intending (*arāda*).
- **The unusual made ordinary**: the formula collects the "hard cases" (virgin birth, creation from dust, resurrection) under one rule.

## Linguistic notes on 16:40

- **Restriction (*innamā*)**: God's word to a thing, when He intends it, is limited to this: nothing beyond the command is involved.
- **The thing addressed (*li-shayʾin*)**: the thing is called *shayʾ* and addressed *before* it exists.
  - A theological debate exists over whether the non-existent can be termed a "thing," and whether the address is literal or a figure for the instantaneous effect of the divine will (*tamthīl*).
  - Different schools held different positions (needs verification). The text itself does not settle the question.
- **The verb *kun***: here it is naturally read as *kāna tāmma* ("come into being"), not the incomplete *kāna* that needs a predicate.
- **The ending *fa-yakūnu***:
  - The common reading has the indicative (*rafʿ*), usually explained as a resumptive clause: "and so it is."
  - A reading with the subjunctive (*fa-yakūna*) is reported in some of these places, including 16:40 and 36:82. In this ayah it can be explained as joined to *an naqūla*.
  - The exact distribution among the canonical readers needs verification.
- **Context in Sūrat al-Naḥl**: 16:39 states the purpose of resurrection:
>> لِيُبَيِّنَ لَهُمُ الَّذِىۡ يَخۡتَلِفُوۡنَ فِيۡهِ وَلِيَـعۡلَمَ الَّذِيۡنَ كَفَرُوۡۤا اَنَّهُمۡ كَانُوۡا كٰذِبِيۡنَ

  16:40 then answers the implied question of *how* the dead will be raised: by the same command that brings anything into being.

## The tense in 3:59

In 3:59, a past narrative ("He said to him") is followed by an imperfect, *fa-yakūn*. Grammarians and exegetes have explained this in various ways, for example:
- as a vivid present (*ḥikāyat al-ḥāl*), or
- as expressing the general rule underlying the event.

These views exist, but their attribution needs verification. Textually, it shows the formula keeping its fixed shape even inside a narrative.

## Conclusion

On the evidence of the text:

1. **"Kun fa-yakūn" is a fixed Qur'anic formula for the unmediated, effortless efficacy of the divine will.**
2. **It is deployed polemically.** It appears where something is denied or doubted as impossible: chiefly the fatherless birth of ʿĪsā (with the rejection of divine sonship) and the resurrection of the dead, and also creation, life and death in general.
3. Its rhetorical role is to **remove the grounds of the objection**. If all existence follows from a single command, then a virgin birth, creation from dust, and the revival of bones are not harder cases.
4. **Matters of interpretation, not textual statement:**
   - whether *kun* is a literal utterance or a figure for instantaneous willing;
   - whether an addressed "thing" exists in some sense before creation.

   The text affirms the command and its immediate result. It does not specify the metaphysics.

## To verify before saving

- The count of eight occurrences and the list: 2:117, 3:47, 3:59, 6:73, 16:40, 19:35, 36:82, 40:68
- My English paraphrases of each of these ayahs and their surrounding contexts (2:116, 16:38, 36:77–81, 40:67)
- The related ayahs 2:65, 7:166, 21:69, 54:50 and their descriptions
- The claim that 16:40 is the only first-person-plural occurrence
- The traditional Najrān context for 3:59
- The variant reading *fa-yakūna* (subjunctive): which canonical readers, and in which ayahs
- The grammatical explanations: resumptive *rafʿ*, subjunctive by joining to *an naqūla*, *kāna tāmma*
- Explanations of the past/imperfect shift in 3:59, and who held them
- Theological positions on whether the non-existent is a *shayʾ*, and literal vs. figurative readings of *kun*, with their attribution to particular schools

q.en: Analyze all the occurances of KUN FAYAKUN in the Quran and reach conclusion on where or for what purpose this phrase is used.

ans.en:
## The apparent tension

Ayahs 16:45–47 list ways in which Allah could seize those who plot evil, yet 16:47 closes with two names of compassion rather than names of power or retribution. The ending makes sense once one sees what the passage *does*: it threatens, but it describes punishment that **has not yet happened**. The closing names explain why.

>> اَوۡ يَاۡخُذَهُمۡ عَلٰى تَخَوُّفٍؕ فَاِنَّ رَبَّكُمۡ لَرَءُوۡفٌ رَّحِيۡمٌ

## 1. What the text clearly says

- **The passage is a rhetorical warning, not a report of punishment carried out.** It continues the question begun in 16:45, which asks, in substance, whether those who plot evil feel secure that Allah will not cause the earth to swallow them or bring punishment from where they do not perceive. Ayahs 16:46–47 add further possibilities, each introduced by اَوۡ ("or"). All of these remain possibilities. The plotters are still alive, still active (فِىۡ تَقَلُّبِهِمۡ), and still being addressed.
- **The ending is introduced by فَـ**, which connects it causally or explanatorily to what precedes it, and it is emphasised with إِنَّ and the lām of emphasis (لَرَءُوۡفٌ). The sentence therefore asserts strongly that your Lord *is* compassionate and merciful, as the ground or explanation of the situation just described.
- **The pronoun shifts from "them" to "you".** The seizing is described in the third person (يَاۡخُذَهُمۡ), but the Lord is described as رَبَّكُمۡ, "your Lord". The mercy is announced directly to the audience, including the people being warned.

## 2. How the ending relates to the threat (interpretation)

The following readings are drawn from the wording and context. They are not mutually exclusive.

**(a) Mercy explains the delay.** The natural question behind the passage is: if Allah is able to seize them in all these ways, and they cannot frustrate Him (فَمَا هُمۡ بِمُعۡجِزِيۡنَ), why have they not already been seized? The فَـ clause answers that it is because your Lord is Ra'ūf and Raḥīm. The respite is itself the expression of these names.

This fits a pattern elsewhere in the Qur'an, which can be compared by reference:
- 16:61 states that if Allah were to seize people for their wrongdoing, He would not leave a single creature on the earth, but He defers them to an appointed term.
- 18:58 links the description of the Lord as Forgiving and possessor of mercy to His not hastening the punishment people have earned.
- 35:45 is similar in content to 16:61.

**(b) Mercy within the mode of seizing itself.** This reading depends on how تَخَوُّف is understood.
- **From *khawf* (fear):** seizing them "while in a state of dread", meaning after they have become apprehensive and have seen warning signs. This contrasts with the sudden seizures in 16:45–46. On this reading, gradual or forewarned seizure leaves room for people to take heed, which is a form of mercy compared with sudden destruction.
- **In the sense of *tanaqquṣ* (gradual diminishing):** taking them away bit by bit, through loss of people, wealth or strength, rather than all at once. Classical lexicography is generally said to record this meaning (needs verification). Here too, gradualness gives time for return.

Saheeh International's rendering ("gradually [in a state of dread]") combines both senses. On either sense, the final mode in the list is the least abrupt one, and the ayah closes with compassion immediately after it. That placement seems meaningful, although the text does not state the link explicitly.

**(c) The warning itself is mercy.** A Lord who simply destroyed would not need to warn. The fact that these possibilities are *announced* to people still able to respond is consistent with رَءُوۡفٌ رَّحِيۡمٌ. The next ayah supports this. Ayah 16:48 turns at once to inviting reflection on creation, which is an invitation, not an execution.

>> اَوَلَمۡ يَرَوۡا اِلٰى مَا خَلَقَ اللّٰهُ مِنۡ شَىۡءٍ يَّتَفَيَّؤُا ظِلٰلُهٗ عَنِ الۡيَمِيۡنِ وَالشَّمَآٮِٕلِ سُجَّدًا لِّلَّهِ وَهُمۡ دٰخِرُوۡنَ

## 3. Why *Ra'ūf* specifically

- Arabic lexicographers and exegetes are often said to distinguish *ra'fa* from *raḥma*. On this view, *ra'fa* is a more intense or tender compassion, especially associated with warding off harm, while *raḥma* is broader (needs verification). If this distinction holds, *Ra'ūf* is especially apt here: the harm described is real and fully within Allah's power, and it is being held back.
- The identical phrase إِنَّ رَبَّكُمۡ لَرَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ also occurs earlier in this sūrah at 16:7, closing a passage on the blessing of livestock that carry burdens. A similar phrase about Allah's compassion toward people closes 22:65, in a context of Allah holding back something that could fall on them. The repetition within Sūrat An-Nahl, which is rich in enumerated blessings, suggests the phrase works as a recurring reminder. The very respite of the wrongdoers is counted among Allah's favours. This thematic link is my inference.

## 4. Where caution is needed

- The text does not state *which* of the readings above is intended. The causal force of فَـ is clear, but whether it explains the delay, the gentleness of the last mode, or both is a matter of interpretation.
- The ayah does not say punishment is cancelled. Mercy here means respite and opportunity, not a guarantee of safety for those who persist. The surrounding verses keep the threat fully in force.
- Exegetes are generally reported to have discussed this ending in terms of respite and the opportunity for repentance (needs verification against the tafsir literature). I am not citing any specific scholar.

## To verify before saving

- The paraphrase of 16:45: whether its wording matches the description of the earth swallowing them and punishment from where they do not perceive.
- The paraphrase of 16:61: seizing people for wrongdoing would leave no creature, and deferral to an appointed term.
- The paraphrase of 18:58: forgiveness and mercy linked to not hastening punishment, with an appointed time.
- The claim that 35:45 is similar in content to 16:61.
- The claim that 16:7 ends with the identical phrase إِنَّ رَبَّكُمۡ لَرَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ in the context of livestock.
- The claim that 22:65 closes with a similar phrase in the context of withholding something from falling on people.
- The lexical meaning of تَخَوُّف as *tanaqquṣ* (gradual diminishing) in classical lexicons.
- The lexical distinction between *ra'fa* and *raḥma* (intensity, warding off harm).
- The general statement that exegetes explain this ending in terms of respite and opportunity for repentance.
- The grammatical description of فَـ as causal/explanatory and the shift from third to second person (iltifāt), to be checked against a grammatical source on the ayah.

q.en: How RAUFUR RAHEEM is relevant to the ayah of punishment?

ans.en:
## The Text and What It Clearly Says

>> اَوَلَمۡ يَرَوۡا اِلٰى مَا خَلَقَ اللّٰهُ مِنۡ شَىۡءٍ يَّتَفَيَّؤُا ظِلٰلُهٗ عَنِ الۡيَمِيۡنِ وَالشَّمَآٮِٕلِ سُجَّدًا لِّلَّهِ وَهُمۡ دٰخِرُوۡنَ

The ayah does the following:

- **It calls for observation.** *A-wa-lam yaraw* ("Have they not seen/considered") presents what follows as something visible and checkable, not a hidden doctrine.
- **It names the objects.** These are "whatever things Allah has created" (*mā khalaqa Allāhu min shay'*), meaning physical bodies that cast shadows.
- **It describes a visible movement.** Their shadows shift (*yatafayya'u*) to the right and to the left.
- **It interprets that movement.** It is prostration to Allah (*sujjadan li-llāh*) carried out in humility and submission (*wa-hum dākhirūn*).

The text does **not** say that a shadow is a substance, that it has a will, or how its prostration takes place. Those questions belong to interpretation.

## The Objection Stated Precisely

The question assumes that a shadow is "just absence of light," so it is not a thing that could do anything, prostration included. This objection merges two separate claims:

1. **Ontological:** a shadow is a privation (*'adam*) and not a positive entity.
2. **Semantic:** only a positive entity can be the subject of *sujūd*.

The first claim can be granted without accepting the second. The sections below explain why, from the grammar, the vocabulary, the wider Qur'anic usage, and the context.

## 1. Grammar: Who Exactly Is Prostrating?

The phrase *sujjadan* is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*). Grammatically it can attach to one of two things:

- **(a) "their shadows" (*ẓilāluhu*).** The shadows shift while prostrating.
- **(b) the created things themselves (*mā khalaqa Allāh*).** The things are prostrating, and the movement of their shadows is the visible sign of it.

The clause *wa-hum dākhirūn* uses *hum*, a pronoun normally reserved for rational beings. Grammarians commonly explain such usage as personification, or as the inclusion of rational beings among the things described. It refers most naturally to the objects, possibly including humans, rather than to the shadows. This supports reading (b), at least as a live possibility. Both attachments are discussed in the grammatical and tafsir literature (*needs verification*).

**Consequence:** on reading (b), the objection largely falls away. The ayah would not be claiming that an absence acts. It would be saying that **bodies submit, and their shadows display that submission.** The shadow would be the evidence of the prostration, not its agent.

## 2. Vocabulary: What *Sujūd* and the Other Words Mean

**Sujūd (root s-j-d).** The root's basic meaning in Arabic is lowering, inclining and yielding. Classical lexicons are generally reported to apply it beyond ritual prayer, for example to lowering the head or to plants and trees bending (*needs verification against lexicons*). Ritual prostration is a specialised case of this wider meaning. "Prostration" in the ayah therefore need not mean the bodily ritual. It can mean total yielding and lowliness.

**The visual fit.** A shadow is, by its nature:

- always cast on the ground;
- always lower than the object that casts it;
- lengthened along the earth, especially at the start and end of the day.

Whatever the shadow is metaphysically, its *form* is the posture of prostration. Every upright body therefore carries with it a flattened counterpart lying on the ground. The image works because the shadow is seen this way. Its physics is irrelevant to that.

**Yatafayya'u (form V of f-y-').** The root carries the sense of *returning*. *Fay'* is often reported by lexicographers to mean specifically the shadow that "returns" or shifts after midday, as distinct from *ẓill* (*this distinction needs verification*). The verb expresses repeated, gradual turning. The ayah thus describes a **regulated, daily, unresisting motion**, which is the kind of motion that fits submission.

**Dākhirūn (root d-kh-r).** The root signifies abasement and humble submission. It describes a state of yielding, not a chosen act of worship.

**Al-yamīn (singular) and al-shamā'il (plural).** The asymmetry is deliberate in the Arabic. Explanations offered in the literature include the following (*all need verification*):

- the singular refers to one direction or phase, and the plural to the shadow's gradual, multiple stages;
- the singular is generic;
- the variation is stylistic.

What "right" and "left" are measured from (the observer, the object, or a fixed orientation) is also interpreted differently. I am not certain which view is dominant.

## 3. The Qur'anic Pattern: Prostration of Non-Rational Things

This ayah belongs to a consistent Qur'anic theme. It is not an isolated poetic image.

- **The next ayah (16:49)** widens the claim at once: everything in the heavens and earth, every creature, and the angels prostrate to Allah, without arrogance.

>> وَلِلّٰهِ يَسۡجُدُ مَا فِى السَّمٰوٰتِ وَمَا فِى الۡاَرۡضِ مِنۡ دَآبَّةٍ وَّالۡمَلٰۤٮِٕكَةُ وَهُمۡ لَا يَسۡتَكۡبِرُوۡنَ

- **13:15** states that whoever is in the heavens and earth prostrates to Allah, willingly or unwillingly, and **their shadows too**, in the mornings and evenings. This is the closest parallel. Its contrast between willing and unwilling shows that the Qur'an itself recognises a kind of prostration that does not depend on choice.
- **22:18** lists the sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees and animals as prostrating, along with many, though not all, people.
- **17:44** states that everything glorifies Allah, but that people do not understand the manner of that glorification.
- **25:45–46** describes Allah extending the shadow, making the sun a guide to it, and then drawing it back gradually. The shadow is presented as something Allah actively governs.
- **6:1** speaks of Allah making the darknesses and the light. The verb is one of making or appointing. Whether that implies darkness is an existent is precisely what theologians debated.

Two broad interpretive positions are reported regarding the prostration of non-rational things (*needs verification*):

1. **Subjugation (*sujūd taskhīr*).** Their prostration is their complete subjection to Allah's decree. It is expressed through their state (*lisān al-ḥāl*) rather than through speech or intention.
2. **A real act of unknown manner.** Their prostration is real but its manner is unknown to us. This is often supported by 17:44's statement that people do not comprehend their glorification.

Neither position requires a shadow to be a substance with a will. Position 1 needs only that the shadow is fully governed. Position 2 explicitly declines to specify the mechanism.

## 4. Why "Absence of Light" Does Not Undercut the Ayah

Even granting that a shadow is a privation, three points follow.

**(a) A privation can still be real, structured and created.** A shadow is not mere nothing. It is a *determinate* absence, with:

- an exact shape set by the object;
- an exact length and direction set by the sun's position;
- an exact rate of change.

This determinacy is why sundials could tell time from shadows. A hole, a silence or a pause is likewise "absence," yet each has boundaries and properties and can be described truthfully. Whether privations are "things" was itself a debated question in classical *kalām* (*needs verification for specific positions*). The Qur'an, however, speaks of shadows being extended and withdrawn by Allah (25:45–46), so it treats them as within His governance whatever their ontological status.

**(b) The privative nature actually strengthens the image.** A shadow has:

- no existence independent of its object;
- no existence independent of the light source;
- no capacity to deviate by a single degree from the path these determine.

It is the purest picture of **total dependence and zero resistance**, which is what *dākhirūn* expresses. An entity with its own substance might be imagined as resisting. A shadow cannot. As a symbol of submission it is therefore apt precisely *because* it has nothing of its own.

**(c) The shadow belongs to the object.** The text says *ẓilāluhu*, "*its* shadows." Through the shadow the ayah shows the submission of the casting body itself. This includes the human being who casts it. The ayah's force lies in that point.

## 5. The Context: The Rhetorical Point

The preceding ayahs (16:45–47) warn those who plot evil that Allah could seize them suddenly or gradually. Ayah 16:47 ends:

>> اَوۡ يَاۡخُذَهُمۡ عَلٰى تَخَوُّفٍؕ فَاِنَّ رَبَّكُمۡ لَرَءُوۡفٌ رَّحِيۡمٌ

Ayahs 48–49 then set up a contrast:

- Shadows, objects, creatures and angels all submit without arrogance (*lā yastakbirūn*).
- The addressees, who are meant to "see" this, are the ones resisting.

On this reading, the implicit argument is as follows. Even a person who refuses to prostrate is accompanied all day by his own shadow, which lies on the ground and turns exactly as Allah's order of sun and earth dictates. His body is already within that order. Only his will refuses. Some exegetes are reported to have drawn this point about the disbeliever's shadow prostrating while he does not (*needs verification*). The context makes it a reasonable reading, but it remains interpretation.

## Summary

| Level | Status |
|---|---|
| Shadows of created things shift right and left | Clear in the text; observable |
| This shifting is described as prostration in humility | Clear in the text |
| *Sujjadan* may attach to the objects, not only the shadows | Grammatical possibility; interpretation |
| *Sujūd* here means subjugation or yielding, not ritual | Interpretation, supported by linguistic usage and 13:15 |
| A shadow's being a privation makes it an ideal sign of dependence | Interpretive argument (mine), not a stated tafsir position |
