Against this background, the first part of 16:118 most plausibly works as a **contrast and clarification**. The wider prohibitions known among the Jews were a specific imposition on them, already explained to the Prophet. They are not part of the law addressed to him and his community. The second part explains why: those restrictions came from their own wrongdoing, not from divine injustice.

16:119 then opens the door of repentance for anyone who did wrong out of ignorance:

>> ثُمَّ اِنَّ رَبَّكَ لِلَّذِيۡنَ عَمِلُوا السُّوۡۤءَ بِجَهَالَةٍ ثُمَّ تَابُوۡا مِنۡۢ بَعۡدِ ذٰ لِكَ وَاَصۡلَحُوۡۤا

This reading of the passage's flow is widely held in the exegetical literature as I understand it, but that general claim needs verification.

**In short:** the first part says that God forbade to the Jews specific things, which He had previously described to the Prophet. Most likely these are the items in 6:146, and the prohibition was particular to them.

## To verify before saving

- That 6:146 lists the prohibitions as described (undivided hoof/claw; fat of cattle and sheep with the stated exceptions) and calls them a recompense for transgression.
- That 6:146 is the passage commonly identified by exegetes as the referent of *mā qaṣaṣnā ʿalayka min qabl*.
- The relative revelation order of al-Anʿām and an-Naḥl (al-Anʿām earlier), and that both are classed as Meccan.
- That 4:160 is Medinan and concerns prohibitions on the Jews due to their wrongdoing.
- The content attributed to 16:114, 16:115 and 16:116.
- The use of a related form of *h-w-d* in 7:156 in the sense of "turning back," and the etymological link to *hādū*.
- The grammatical points: *qablu* indeclinable with omitted complement; possible attachment of *min qabl* to either verb; the fronting of *ʿalā alladhīna hādū* and of *anfusahum* for specification or emphasis.
- The general claim that exegetes read 16:118 as contrasting Jewish dietary law with the law addressed to the Prophet's community.

q.en: What does this ayah actually say in the first part?

ans.en:
## 1. What the text itself establishes

>> اِنَّ اِبۡرٰهِيۡمَ كَانَ اُمَّةً قَانِتًا لِّلَّهِ حَنِيۡفًاؕ وَلَمۡ يَكُ مِنَ الۡمُشۡرِكِيۡنَۙ
>> شَاكِرًا لِّاَنۡعُمِهِ​ؕ اِجۡتَبٰٮهُ وَهَدٰٮهُ اِلٰى صِرَاطٍ مُّسۡتَقِيۡمٍ

The following points can be read directly from the text, without relying on interpretation.

- **A single person is called an *ummah*.** The subject of *kāna* is Ibrāhīm alone, and *ummatan* is its predicate. In every other occurrence supplied in the data, *ummah* refers to a plurality of people, or of creatures in 6:38.
- **The grammar keeps Ibrāhīm, not *ummah*, as the reference point.** *Ummah* is grammatically feminine, but the descriptors that follow, *qānitan* and *ḥanīfan* (and *shākiran* in 16:121), are masculine. They therefore describe Ibrāhīm, not *ummah*. If they had been adjectives of *ummah*, the expected forms would have been feminine (compare *ummatun qāʾimatun* in 3:113 below). So *ummatan* works as a noun-predicate, a designation of what Ibrāhīm *was*. The masculine words form a chain of further predicates or descriptions of him.
- **The verse frames the description against *shirk*.** It ends with *wa-lam yaku mina l-mushrikīn*. Whatever *ummah* means here, it stands in contrast to the people of *shirk*.

## 2. The same word elsewhere: what the comparison shows

**(a) *Ummah* as a collective, the dominant usage.** The word denotes a group joined by a common bond, such as religion, time or messenger, as in 7:34, 10:47 and 6:42. Several occurrences describe a *righteous* group with qualities close to those given to Ibrāhīm:

>> ۞لَيۡسُواْ سَوَآءٗۗ مِّنۡ أَهۡلِ ٱلۡكِتَٰبِ أُمَّةٞ قَآئِمَةٞ يَتۡلُونَ ءَايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِ ءَانَآءَ ٱلَّيۡلِ وَهُمۡ يَسۡجُدُونَ
>> وَمِن قَوۡمِ مُوسَىٰٓ أُمَّةٞ يَهۡدُونَ بِٱلۡحَقِّ وَبِهِۦ يَعۡدِلُونَ

*What this shows (interpretation):* in these verses a whole *ummah* is needed to carry the qualities of standing in obedience, devotion and guidance by truth. In 16:120 the same word is predicated of one man described as *qānit* (devoutly obedient). This reads as a deliberate compression: one individual is presented as carrying what a whole righteous community carries.

**(b) Ibrāhīm and the *ummah* in Sūrat al-Baqarah.** In 2:128, Ibrāhīm (with Ismāʿīl, per the surrounding context, to be verified) prays for an *ummah*:

>> رَبَّنَا وَٱجۡعَلۡنَا مُسۡلِمَيۡنِ لَكَ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِنَآ أُمَّةٗ مُّسۡلِمَةٗ لَّكَ وَأَرِنَا مَنَاسِكَنَا وَتُبۡ عَلَيۡنَآۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلتَّوَّابُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ

Shortly afterwards, a past group is called an *ummah*:

>> تِلۡكَ أُمَّةٞ قَدۡ خَلَتۡۖ لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتۡ وَلَكُم مَّا كَسَبۡتُمۡۖ وَلَا تُسۡـَٔلُونَ عَمَّا كَانُواْ يَعۡمَلُونَ

In the surrounding passage of 2:133–140, "that *ummah*" appears to refer to the patriarchs: Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and their descendants. This identification needs to be checked against the context.

*What this shows (interpretation):*
- In al-Baqarah, Ibrāhīm *asks for* an *ummah* and is *counted within* one.
- In an-Naḥl, he *is* one.

The two usages fit together well. The man who prayed for a *muslim ummah* was himself its seed and its first full instance.

**(c) *Ummah* as "one way or religion".** In 2:213 and 10:19 (*kāna n-nāsu ummatan wāḥidatan*), the translation renders *ummah* as "one religion" or "one community [united in religion]". This shows that the word can lean toward the *shared path* that unites a group, not only the group itself. If this sense is heard in 16:120, Ibrāhīm embodies a whole *way*. This fits the later command in the same sūrah to follow the *millah* of Ibrāhīm, at 16:123, which is not quoted in the data.

**(d) Other senses outside the supplied list (references only; verify):**
- In 12:45 the word appears to mean "a period of time".
- In 43:22–23 it appears to mean "a way or creed of the forefathers".

These confirm that *ummah* is semantically wide, which helps explain why it can be extended to a single person.

## 3. The root family (أ م م)

The common thread of the root appears to be *aiming at, heading toward, and that which is a source or point of orientation*.

**Āmm, "heading for" (5:2).** The phrase *āmmīna l-bayta l-ḥarām* means "those heading for the Sacred House". This preserves the verbal core: *amma* means "to aim for, make for". On this basis, a proposed reading of *ummah* in 16:120 is "one who is aimed at, made for, followed". This is a reading of the root, not a certainty. Morphologically, it is often compared to *fuʿlah* forms that carry a passive sense, meaning "one who is done-to". That morphological comparison needs verification.

**Imām, "leader, one in front" (2:124).** God makes Ibrāhīm an *imām*:

>> ۞وَإِذِ ٱبۡتَلَىٰٓ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمَ رَبُّهُۥ بِكَلِمَٰتٖ فَأَتَمَّهُنَّۖ قَالَ إِنِّي جَاعِلُكَ لِلنَّاسِ إِمَامٗاۖ قَالَ وَمِن ذُرِّيَّتِيۖ قَالَ لَا يَنَالُ عَهۡدِي ٱلظَّـٰلِمِينَ

- This is the closest root neighbour, and it is applied to the same person.
- The Saheeh International rendering of 16:120, "a [comprehensive] leader", clearly draws on this connection.
- The difference: *imām* stresses *precedence and being followed*, whereas *ummah* adds *collectivity and comprehensiveness*.

**Amām, "in front" (75:5).** This supports the spatial sense of "front, the direction one faces" that underlies *imām*.

**Umm, "mother, source, foundation" (e.g. *umm al-kitāb*, 3:7).** This supports the sense of *origin to which things return*. As an interpretation, calling Ibrāhīm an *ummah* may echo his role as the *origin* of a believing lineage and of the *millah*. This is suggestive, not provable from the text.

**Ummī (2:78, 3:20, 3:75).** This lemma is related to *umm* or *ummah*. It is less directly relevant here. It shows the root's association with belonging to a people or to a native, original state.

## 4. Why *ummah* here and not another word (interpretation)

The following reasons are readings of the text and context, not certainties.

1. ***Ummah* says more than *imām*.** *Imām* already appears for Ibrāhīm in 2:124. *Ummah* can carry, at once:
   - "leader or exemplar" (through the root's sense of *aiming at* and its link with *imām*);
   - "a whole community in one person" (through its dominant collective usage);
   - "a way or creed embodied" (through 2:213 and 10:19).

   No single synonym combines all three.

2. **Fit with the context of *shirk* and polemic.**
   - The verse closes by stating that he was not of the *mushrikūn*.
   - The surrounding passage (16:118 on what was forbidden to the Jews, 16:123 on the *millah* of Ibrāhīm; references only, verify) contests who truly belongs to Ibrāhīm.

   Calling him an *ummah* implies that he stood for the true community even when alone among his people. A widely cited exegetical view holds that he was the only believer in his land, a "community of one". This is a general view that needs verification and should not be cited without a source.

3. **Fit with the sequence of praise.** *Ummah* opens a list: *qānit*, *ḥanīf*, not a *mushrik*, *shākir*, chosen, guided. As the first and only noun of collective meaning, it reads like a heading that summarises the qualities that follow. This matches a view found in classical lexicography that *ummah* can mean "a man who gathers all qualities of good". That view needs verification and attribution before use.

4. **Alternatives from other roots (references only; verify):**
   - *Uswah*, "model to be imitated", is used of Ibrāhīm in 60:4. It stresses imitation by others but lacks the collective sense.
   - *Qudwah*/*iqtadi*, "follow the guidance of", appears in 6:90 of the prophets generally.

   Neither would carry the "whole community in one" dimension that *ummah* seems to bring here.

## 5. Sound and structure

- The verse and its continuation form a run of indefinite accusatives with *tanwīn*: *ummatan, qānitan, ḥanīfan* and, in 16:121, *shākiran*. *Ummatan* sets the pattern of this cadence.
- The doubled *mīm* gives the first predicate a weighty, emphatic opening.

These are observations about the recited text. Any claim that they *explain* the word choice is interpretive.

## To verify before saving

- That 16:120 is the only occurrence of the lemma *ummah* (among the 64) predicated of a single individual. Check the full list, not only the first 25 shown.
- The grammatical analysis: *qānitan* and *ḥanīfan* (and *shākiran* in 16:121) are masculine predicates or descriptions of Ibrāhīm, not adjectives of *ummah*.
- That "that *ummah*" in 2:134 and 2:141 refers to Ibrāhīm and the patriarchs (check 2:133–140), and that 2:128 is spoken by Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl (check 2:127).
- The sense of *ummah* in 12:45 ("a period of time") and in 43:22–23 ("a way or creed").
- The content of 16:118 and 16:123 as described.
- 60:4 (*uswah ḥasanah* in Ibrāhīm) and 6:90 (*iqtadi*) as described.
- The morphological claim that *ummah* follows a *fuʿlah* pattern with a passive sense, meaning "one aimed at or followed".
- The lexicographical view that *ummah* can mean a man combining all qualities of good. Find and cite a specific dictionary entry.
- The exegetical view that Ibrāhīm was called *ummah* because he was the sole believer of his time. Find and cite a specific tafsīr before attributing it.
- That the root's core sense is "aiming or heading toward" (supported by *āmmīn* in 5:2). Confirm against a standard Arabic lexicon.
- The Saheeh International rendering "[comprehensive] leader" for 16:120, as given in the data.

q.en: How does the word «أُمَّةً» fit in this ayah (16:120) compared with similar Qur'anic words used elsewhere? Why this word here and not another?

ans.en:
## Short answer

The ayah answers an implied question raised by the one before it. If the Prophet is told to follow the religion of Abraham (16:123), and the Sabbath was a central law among the People of the Book, should he observe it too? The ayah's answer is no. The Sabbath was **not** part of Abraham's religion. It was a specific obligation **imposed on a particular people**, those "who differed over it." Their dispute will be settled by God on the Day of Resurrection, not by argument now.

## What the text clearly says

>> اِنَّمَا جُعِلَ السَّبۡتُ عَلَى الَّذِيۡنَ اخۡتَلَفُوۡا فِيۡهِ​ؕ وَاِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَيَحۡكُمُ بَيۡنَهُمۡ يَوۡمَ الۡقِيٰمَةِ فِيۡمَا كَانُوۡا فِيۡهِ يَخۡتَلِفُوۡنَ

- **إِنَّمَا (innamā)** is a particle of restriction (ḥaṣr). It limits the Sabbath to "those who differed over it." This excludes it from the universal, Abrahamic core just mentioned in 16:123.
- **جُعِلَ ... عَلَى (juʿila ... ʿalā)**: the passive "was made/appointed" with *ʿalā* ("upon") suggests an obligation or burden placed on someone, rather than something granted *for* (*li-*) them. The agent is unstated but clearly God.
- **الَّذِيۡنَ اخۡتَلَفُوۡا فِيۡهِ**: the people concerned are identified only by their having "differed over it." The text does not name them. Given the Qur'an's usage elsewhere, the reference is almost certainly to the Israelites/Jews (see the Context section).
- **The second clause** uses emphatic *inna* and *la-* (*la-yaḥkumu*): God *will certainly* judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. The root *kh-l-f* ("differ") is repeated (*ikhtalafū ... yakhtalifūn*). This frames the whole ayah around their disagreement and defers its resolution to God.

## Context in the passage

- **16:123** establishes that the Prophet follows *millat Ibrāhīm*, the upright (*ḥanīf*) and non-polytheist religion of Abraham.
- **16:124** then separates the Sabbath from that Abrahamic religion. It was a later, people-specific law. So the Prophet's not observing it does not contradict his following Abraham.
- **16:125** turns to method: call to God's way with wisdom and good admonition, and argue in the best manner, because God knows best who has strayed and who is guided. This fits the end of 16:124. Since final judgement on disputes belongs to God, the Prophet's role is invitation and courteous argument, not settling every sectarian dispute.
- Slightly earlier in the sūrah, **16:118** speaks of things God made unlawful specifically for the Jews, also using *ʿalā*. This appears to set up the same theme: certain laws were particular to them and not part of the Abrahamic baseline. *(The exact wording and the connection should be checked.)*
- Elsewhere the Qur'an refers to the Sabbath and the Israelites' violation of it, for example **2:65**, **4:154**, and **7:163–166** (the town by the sea whose people transgressed regarding the Sabbath). These support identifying "those who differed" with the Israelites.

## What is interpretation: the meaning of "differed over it"

The text does not specify the nature of the disagreement. Exegetes have proposed several readings. These are stated here in general terms only, and each needs verification against the tafsīr literature:

1. **They differed over the day itself.** On this reading they were meant to honour a different day (often said to be Friday), disagreed, and chose Saturday, so Saturday was imposed on them. This view is commonly linked to prophetic reports about the communities differing over the weekly day of gathering. I am not quoting those reports. *(Needs verification.)*
2. **They differed in observing it.** Some kept the Sabbath and some violated it, as in the episode alluded to in 7:163–166. *(Needs verification.)*
3. **They differed with their prophet, or among themselves, about its rulings**, such as what exactly was forbidden on it. *(Needs verification.)*

Readings 1 and 2 are the ones most often cited, as far as I am aware. Grammatically, all three fit *ikhtalafū fīhi*. The context of 16:123 (Abraham vs. later laws) is compatible with any of them. I cannot confirm from the text alone which is preferred.

## Summary of the ayah's point

- The Sabbath is not part of the original, universal religion of Abraham that the Prophet is commanded to follow.
- It was a specific law laid upon a particular people (by strong contextual indication, the Israelites), connected with their disagreement.
- God, not human debate, will decide their disagreement on the Day of Resurrection. This leads directly into 16:125's instruction to invite and argue graciously.

## To verify before saving

- The grammatical points: *innamā* as restriction; the nuance of *juʿila ʿalā* (imposition/burden) vs. *li-*; emphatic *la-* in *la-yaḥkumu*.
- That 16:118 speaks of things made unlawful specifically for the Jews, and its use of *ʿalā*.
- That 2:65, 4:154 and 7:163–166 refer to the Sabbath and its violation by the Israelites.
- The identification of "those who differed over it" with the Israelites/Jews in the tafsīr tradition.
- Interpretive view 1 (differing over the day, Friday vs. Saturday) and its connection to prophetic reports. Check sources and authenticity.
- Interpretive view 2 (some observed, some violated).
- Interpretive view 3 (differing with their prophet or over its rulings).
- The claim that views 1 and 2 are the most commonly cited.
- The reading that 16:124 answers an implied objection arising from 16:123 (link between millat Ibrāhīm and the Sabbath).

q.en: What this ayah is saying actually?

ans.en:
## Core meaning of the root and the verb

The root **س ر ي** denotes movement by night. The Qur'anic data supports this:

- In **89:4** the night itself is the subject:
>> وَٱلَّيۡلِ إِذَا يَسۡرِ
Here the root describes the night's own quiet passage, which suggests that the root's core is unobtrusive, continuous movement associated with night.

- In **19:24** the noun:
>> قَدۡ جَعَلَ رَبُّكِ تَحۡتَكِ سَرِيّٗا
is glossed as "stream." Classical lexicographers are generally reported to link this to flowing movement, and some to a separate sense of "nobility." *(Views exist; needs verification.)* If the flowing sense is correct, it reinforces the idea of smooth, quiet motion.

**أَسْرَىٰ** is the Form IV perfect. Arabic lexicography is generally reported to discuss whether **سَرَىٰ** (Form I) and **أَسْرَىٰ** (Form IV) are synonyms meaning "to travel by night." *(Needs verification.)* In every Qur'anic occurrence of this lemma, the verb is followed by **بِ** plus a person:

- بِأَهۡلِكَ (11:81, 15:65)
- بِعِبَادِي (20:77, 26:52, 44:23)
- بِعَبۡدِهِۦ (17:1)

The Qur'anic usage is therefore consistent: the verb means "to move by night **with / taking** someone."

## Comparison with the other five occurrences

**1. Context: deliverance at night.**
All five other occurrences come in rescue narratives. Lot is told to leave with his family before the punishment falls at dawn (11:81, 15:65). Moses is told to lead the Israelites out from Pharaoh (20:77, 26:52, 44:23). The surrounding words stress danger and pursuit:
>> إِنَّكُم مُّتَّبَعُونَ
*(Interpretation:)* By using this verb in 17:1, the Qur'an places the Prophet's night journey within a recognisable pattern: God moving His chosen servant by night, under divine protection, toward a destined place. The difference is that in 17:1 the purpose is stated as revelation of signs (لِنُرِيَهُۥ مِنۡ ءَايَٰتِنَآ), not escape.

**2. Grammar: who performs the action.**
The five other occurrences are **imperatives** (أَسۡرِ) addressed to a prophet, who carries out the journey himself. In 17:1 the verb is **perfect**, and **God is the subject**. The servant is the one taken.
*(Interpretation:)* This shift is significant. In the other passages the prophet acts on God's command. Here the journey is presented wholly as God's act, which fits the opening praise formula سُبۡحَٰنَ ٱلَّذِيٓ, a declaration of transcendence that introduces an extraordinary divine deed. Grammarians are reported to discuss whether transitivity through **بِ** (rather than a direct object) implies that the agent accompanies the one moved. Some commentators apply this to 17:1 in terms of divine care or company. *(View exists; needs verification; theologically sensitive, so treat with caution.)*

**3. Lexical echo: عَبۡد / عِبَاد.**
The three Moses verses say بِعِبَادِي ("with My servants," plural). The Lot verses say بِأَهۡلِكَ ("your family"). 17:1 says بِعَبۡدِهِۦ ("His servant," singular).
*(Interpretation:)* The near-identical phrasing (أَسۡرِ بِعِبَادِي / أَسۡرَىٰ بِعَبۡدِهِۦ) links the Prophet's journey to the Exodus. The link is strengthened by the very next verse, which turns to Moses and the Children of Israel:
>> وَءَاتَيۡنَا مُوسَى ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَجَعَلۡنَٰهُ هُدٗى لِّبَنِيٓ إِسۡرَٰٓءِيلَ
Read this way, the choice of أَسۡرَىٰ prepares the transition into the Israelite material that follows in the sūrah. Calling the Prophet عَبۡد at the moment of his greatest honour is also widely noted as significant. *(View exists; needs verification.)*

**4. The added word لَيۡلٗا.**
If the verb already implies night, لَيۡلٗا looks redundant. It appears with this verb only in 17:1 and 44:23. The Lot verses use the more specific بِقِطۡعٖ مِّنَ ٱلَّيۡلِ ("a portion of the night").
Commentators are reported to explain the indefinite لَيۡلٗا in 17:1 as stressing that the journey took only part of a single night, which heightens the miracle. *(View exists; needs verification.)* What the text itself clearly shows is emphasis: the night setting is made explicit twice, once in the verb and once in the adverb.

## Why not another verb?

Other verbs of movement exist in the Qur'an. The comparisons below are suggestive and should be checked.

- **سَارَ بِـ** ("travelled with"): used, for example, of Moses travelling with his family (28:29, as I recall). It denotes journeying generally and carries no inherent night sense. *(Verify.)*
- **Verbs of ascent from the root ع ر ج** (e.g., 70:4, of angels ascending). 17:1 does not use ascent vocabulary. It describes only a horizontal journey from one masjid to the other. The ascension (miʿrāj) is not named in this verse; whether other passages allude to it is a matter of interpretation. *(Verify.)*
- **رَفَعَ** ("raised"), used of Jesus (4:158), denotes elevation and removal, not a journey between two places. *(Verify.)*

*(Interpretation:)* أَسۡرَىٰ uniquely combines three elements:
1. night;
2. movement *with* a person under divine direction;
3. an established Qur'anic association with prophetic deliverance narratives.

No general verb of travel carries all three.

## Sound and structure

- **Sibilance** *(interpretation):* سُبۡحَٰنَ … أَسۡرَىٰ … ٱلۡمَسۡجِدِ … ٱلۡمَسۡجِدِ repeats the **s** sound, which some may hear as suiting the hush of night. This is an impressionistic observation only.
- **Shift of person (iltifāt):** The verse moves from third person (أَسۡرَىٰ، عَبۡدِهِۦ) to first person plural (بَٰرَكۡنَا، لِنُرِيَهُۥ، ءَايَٰتِنَآ) and then back to third (إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ). The verb أَسۡرَىٰ sits within the third-person praise frame introduced by سُبۡحَٰنَ ٱلَّذِيٓ. Who the pronoun in إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ refers to is reportedly debated. *(Needs verification.)*
- **Name of the sūrah:** The sūrah's common name, al-Isrāʾ, is the verbal noun of this verb, which shows how central the word is to the sūrah's identity.

## Summary: what is clear and what is interpretation

**Clear from the text:**
- The verb means night travel with someone (بِ + person).
- It occurs only in divinely ordered night journeys.
- Only in 17:1 is God the subject and the verb perfect.
- 17:1 alone uses the singular عَبۡد.
- لَيۡلٗا adds explicit emphasis.
- 17:2 immediately turns to Moses.

**Interpretation:**
- The Exodus echo.
- The idea of divine accompaniment through بِ.
- The "one night" emphasis.
- The sound effects.
- The contrast with ascent vocabulary.

## To verify before saving

- The Arabic quotations from 11:81, 15:65, 17:1, 17:2, 20:77, 26:52, 44:23, 19:24, 89:4 against a reliable muṣḥaf.
- Lexicographers' views on سَرَىٰ vs أَسۡرَىٰ (synonymy or distinction).
- The lexical link of سَرِيّ (19:24) to "flowing" and its alternative "noble" sense.
- The grammatical view that transitivity through بِ implies the agent's accompaniment, and its application to 17:1.
- Commentators' explanation of indefinite لَيۡلٗا as "part of one night."
- The claim that the use of عَبۡد in 17:1 is commonly noted as significant.
- 28:29: whether it uses سَارَ بِأَهۡلِهِۦ of Moses.
- 70:4: use of the root ع ر ج for ascent.
- 4:158: use of رَفَعَ for Jesus.
- Whether any other Qur'anic passage is held to allude to the miʿrāj.
- The debate over the referent of إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ in 17:1.
- That "al-Isrāʾ" is the sūrah's common name (it is also known as Banī Isrāʾīl).
- That لَيۡلٗا with this verb occurs only in 17:1 and 44:23 (based on the data supplied).

q.en: How does the word «أَسْرَىٰ» fit in this ayah (17:1) compared with similar Qur'anic words used elsewhere? Why this word here and not another?

ans.en:
## The word itself

**Dhurriyyah** means "offspring, progeny, descendants." It is a collective noun that can refer to one person or many, though here it clearly means a whole line of descent.

The root is disputed, and the classical lexicographers record several derivations (to be verified):
- from **ذ-ر-أ** ("to create, bring forth"), with the hamzah dropped in ordinary use, so that the word means "those brought forth";
- from **ذَرّ** ("tiny particles, small ants"), suggesting small, numerous offspring;
- from **ذ-ر-و/ي** ("to scatter, disperse"), suggesting progeny spread across the earth.

These are etymological proposals. None of them changes the plain meaning in this ayah.

## What the text says clearly

>> ذُرِّيَّةَ مَنۡ حَمَلۡنَا مَعَ نُوۡحٍ​ؕ اِنَّهٗ كَانَ عَبۡدًا شَكُوۡرًا

- The *dhurriyyah* is defined by its ancestors: **"those We carried with Noah."** The ayah does not say "the descendants of Noah." It says the descendants of those carried *with* him.
- The verb **حَمَلۡنَا** ("We carried") credits God with the rescue. The descendants exist only because their forebears were saved by God's act.
- The ayah ends by describing Noah as **عَبۡدًا شَكُوۡرًا**, "a servant much given to gratitude" (an intensive form). Most naturally the pronoun refers to Noah. A different referent has occasionally been proposed (to be verified), but Noah is the obvious antecedent.

## The grammatical problem: why is it *dhurriyyata* (accusative)?

The accusative ending is the main interpretive issue, because the word has no obvious governing verb. Grammarians and commentators give several analyses (to be verified in the i'rāb literature):

1. **Vocative with the particle omitted** ("O descendants of…"). Saheeh International follows this. It fits smoothly with the second-person reading of the previous ayah:

>> اَلَّا تَتَّخِذُوۡا مِنۡ دُوۡنِىۡ وَكِيۡلًا

   The sense is: "…that you not take any disposer of affairs other than Me, O descendants of those We carried with Noah."

2. **First object of تَتَّخِذُوا**, with وَكِيۡلًا as the second object. The sense is: "that you not take the descendants of those carried with Noah as disposers of affairs besides Me." On this reading, the warning is against relying on *any human being*, since all humans are only descendants of rescued people.

3. **Apposition (badal)** to وَكِيۡلًا. The meaning is close to (2): the "disposer" that must not be taken is any member of humanity.

4. **Specification or praise (ikhtiṣāṣ)**, governed by an implied verb such as "I mean…".

There is also a reported variant in the previous ayah, **يَتَّخِذُوا** (third person), attributed to Abū ʿAmr (to be verified). If that reading holds, the vocative analysis would involve a shift of address (iltifāt) from speaking *about* the Israelites to speaking *to* them. A nominative reading, *dhurriyyatu*, is also reported as non-canonical (to be verified).

**Where I am unsure:** I cannot confirm from memory which analysis particular commentators preferred. Readings (1) and (2) are the ones most often discussed.

## Interpretation: the point of the phrase in context

These points are interpretive, not explicit in the text:

- **An argument from origins.** Your very existence goes back to a rescue that God alone accomplished. It is therefore incoherent to take another *wakīl* (guardian, one entrusted with your affairs). The ayah grounds the command of 17:2 in history.
- **Gratitude as the expected response.** Your ancestor-in-rescue, Noah, responded to God with intense gratitude. His descendants should do the same. Taking another *wakīl* is the opposite of gratitude.
- **Humbling lineage.** The Children of Israel are about to be addressed with the warnings of 17:4. Calling them "descendants of those carried with Noah" places them within universal human descent, rather than an exclusive lineage. This prepares for the warning that they are accountable like anyone else.
- **Who is addressed?** The immediate context (17:2 and 17:4) points to the Children of Israel. The wording, however, describes all post-Flood humanity. Some read it as addressing the Israelites specifically, others as a general address. Both views exist (to be verified).

## Related ayahs (described, not quoted)

- **37:77** states that God made Noah's own offspring the survivors. Read alongside 17:3, this raises the question of whether post-Flood humanity descends from Noah alone or also from others on the ark. Commentators discuss this (to be verified).
- **36:41** speaks of God carrying "their *dhurriyyah*" in the laden ship. It is often cited because *dhurriyyah* there seems to refer to *forebears* carried in the ark. This has prompted discussion of whether the word can sometimes include ancestors (to be verified).
- **19:58** mentions prophets from the progeny of Adam and of those carried with Noah, which is a close parallel phrase.

## To verify before saving

- The three proposed etymologies of *dhurriyyah* (ذرأ / ذرّ / ذرو) and their attribution to classical lexicographers.
- The four grammatical analyses of the accusative *dhurriyyata* (vocative, first object, badal, ikhtiṣāṣ) in the i'rāb works and tafsīrs.
- The variant reading **يَتَّخِذُوا** in 17:2 and its attribution to Abū ʿAmr.
- The reported non-canonical nominative reading *dhurriyyatu*.
- Whether any commentator refers the pronoun in اِنَّهٗ to someone other than Noah.
- The existence of the two views on the addressees (Israelites specifically vs. all humanity).
- The content of 37:77, 36:41 and 19:58 as described, and the discussion of their relation to 17:3.

q.en: What's actually being said about DHURRIYAH?

ans.en:
## Short answer

**أُولِي is in fact *manṣūb*, not *majrūr*.** The ending *-ī* (ـِي) is the accusative form of this word as well as the genitive form. The words in the phrase that really are *majrūr* are بَأْسٍ and شَدِيدٍ, not أُولِي.

>> بَعَثۡنَا عَلَيۡكُمۡ عِبَادًا لَّنَاۤ اُولِىۡ بَاۡسٍ شَدِيۡدٍ

## Why the form looks genitive

- **أُولُو / أُولِي** means "possessors of" and works as the plural counterpart of ذُو / ذِي.
- It is not a true sound masculine plural (*jamʿ mudhakkar sālim*), because it has no singular from its own root. Grammarians class it as *mulḥaq bi-jamʿ al-mudhakkar al-sālim*, a word attached to that category and inflected like it.
- It therefore follows the inflection of the sound masculine plural:
  - **Nominative (*rafʿ*):** with wāw → أُولُو
  - **Accusative (*naṣb*) and genitive (*jarr*):** with yāʾ → أُولِي
- In the sound masculine plural, *naṣb* and *jarr* always share the yāʾ form (compare مُسْلِمِينَ in both cases). The yāʾ alone therefore cannot tell us whether the word is accusative or genitive. Its syntactic position decides that.
- The *nūn* of the plural is dropped because the word is *muḍāf* (in an *iḍāfa* construction) to بَأْسٍ.
- The wāw written after the alif (اُوۡلِى) is orthographic only and is not pronounced. The word is read *ūlī*.

## Parsing the phrase (*iʿrāb*)

| Word | Function | Case and sign |
|---|---|---|
| عِبَادًا | object of بَعَثۡنَا | *manṣūb*, *fatḥa* (with tanwīn) |
| لَنَا | prepositional phrase functioning as a first qualifier (*naʿt*) of عِبَادًا | in the position of *naṣb* |
| أُولِي | second qualifier (*naʿt*) of عِبَادًا | *manṣūb*, sign: **yāʾ**, as with the sound masculine plural; *muḍāf* |
| بَأْسٍ | *muḍāf ilayh* | *majrūr*, *kasra* |
| شَدِيدٍ | qualifier (*naʿt*) of بَأْسٍ | *majrūr*, *kasra* |

So the adjective agrees with its noun exactly as expected:
- أُولِي agrees with عِبَادًا in case (accusative), number (plural) and gender (masculine).
- شَدِيدٍ agrees with بَأْسٍ (genitive, singular, masculine).

The *kasra* the questioner notices belongs to بَأْسٍ شَدِيدٍ. It is the result of the *iḍāfa*, not the case of أُولِي.

## Contrast within the Qurʾān (for checking)

- **27:33:** Bilqīs's counsellors describe themselves with nearly the same expression, "possessors of strength and possessors of severe might." There the word stands in the nominative, as the predicate of نحن, and so takes the wāw form (أُولُو). This is a useful minimal pair with 17:5.
- **Genitive yāʾ form:** this occurs after a preposition, e.g. the phrase "for those of understanding" in 3:190.

The same yāʾ form therefore serves for the accusative in 17:5 and the genitive in 3:190. Only the syntax distinguishes them.

## Clear text vs. interpretation

- **Clear from the language:** أُولِي is accusative with the yāʾ sign and qualifies عِبَادًا. This is standard morphology and is not disputed.
- **A matter of analysis:** whether أُولِي is best called a second *naʿt*, or could also be analysed differently (e.g. as *badal*). The case would be *naṣb* under any of these analyses. My statement that some grammarians may allow alternative analyses is from general knowledge and needs verification.

## To verify before saving

- The classification of أُولُو/أُولِي as *mulḥaq bi-jamʿ al-mudhakkar al-sālim* and its inflection (wāw in *rafʿ*; yāʾ in *naṣb* and *jarr*), in a standard grammar reference.
- The parsing of لَنَا as a first *naʿt* in the position of *naṣb*, and of أُولِي as a second *naʿt*, in an *iʿrāb al-Qurʾān* work.
- Whether any grammarians allow أُولِي here to be *badal* or another function (stated only in general terms above).
- 27:33: that the phrase appears there with أُولُو in the nominative, spoken by Bilqīs's counsellors.
- 3:190: that it contains أُولِي in the genitive after a preposition ("for those of understanding").
- That the wāw in the spelling of أُولِي is orthographic and not pronounced.

q.en: Why sifah of ABDAN is ULI, majroor instead of mansub?

ans.en:
## What the data shows first

The root **ج و س** occurs in the Qur'an **only here**. The data gives a single occurrence of the lemma جاسَ (17:5) and no other derivatives. No internal Qur'anic comparison within the root is therefore possible. The word's fit has to be judged from three things:

- its lexical meaning in Arabic,
- its immediate syntax (especially خِلَالَ الدِّيَارِ),
- its contrast with words of related meaning from other roots, above all the parallel description in 17:7.

That a word is unique (a *hapax*) is a fact about the text. It does not prove by itself that the word was chosen for a special effect. Any such claim is interpretation.

## Lexical meaning of جاسَ

In classical Arabic lexicography, جاسَ يَجُوسُ (جَوْسًا / جَوَسانًا) is generally described as follows (to be verified in the standard lexica):

- going to and fro through a place;
- treading through it thoroughly;
- searching it out, often for people or plunder, and typically in the context of a raid.

The core idea is therefore **not simple "entering"**. It combines three features:

1. **Penetration**: being inside the place.
2. **Repeated or thorough movement**: going back and forth, covering it.
3. **Search**: seeking out what or who is there.

This is why the gloss "and they entered" (from the word data) is too thin. Saheeh International's "probed [even] into the homes" captures the searching sense better. Renderings such as "ransacked" or "went searching through" are also defensible.

It is generally reported that lexicographers treat جاسَ as close to حاسَ (with ḥāʾ) and to داسَ (to trample). It is also reported that a non-canonical reading with ḥāʾ (فَحَاسُوا) exists. Both claims need verification, and the canonical reading is فَجَاسُوا.

## How the word fits its syntax

>> فَجَاسُوا۟ خِلَٰلَ ٱلدِّيَارِۚ

- **The fāʾ** links the action directly to بَعَثْنَا ("We sent"). The text presents the sending and the roaming as one swift sequence, with no battle narrated in between. The ayah does not mention resistance. That this silence implies no effective resistance is a reasonable reading, but it is an inference.
- **The object خِلَٰلَ ٱلدِّيَارِ** means "the in-between spaces of the dwellings": the gaps, streets and interiors. خِلَال is used elsewhere for the space *between or within* things:
  - 9:47: hypocrites hastening about *among* the believers;
  - 18:33: a river made to flow *between* two gardens;
  - 24:43 and 30:48: rain coming out from *within or between* the clouds.

  A verb meaning "move to and fro, searching" pairs naturally with a noun meaning "the in-between spaces." The verb supplies the back-and-forth motion, and خِلَال supplies the interstices through which it passes. This lexical fit is the strongest textual argument for the word.
- **The agents** are described as عِبَادًا لَّنَآ أُو۟لِى بَأْسٍ شَدِيدٍ, "possessors of severe might." Thorough, unhurried searching through a city is what forces of overwhelming strength can do. Their might explains why they can move this way.

## Comparison with near-synonyms from other roots

Each word below has a different focus. All references should be checked.

- **دَخَلَ (to enter)**
  - 27:34: the Queen of Sheba says that kings, when they *enter* a town, corrupt it.
  - 17:7: the second punishment is described with entering the *masjid* "as they entered it the first time."

  دَخَلَ marks crossing a boundary. It says nothing about thoroughness or searching.
- **نَقَّبُوا فِي الْبِلَادِ** (50:36): earlier nations *bored through / ranged through the lands*. The verb stresses wide-ranging exploration across territory, here in a context of seeking escape. It is not focused on searching inside a single city's homes.
- **سِيحُوا / سِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ** (for example 9:2, and many "travel in the land" ayahs such as 3:137). These denote free or general travel and carry no hostile or searching sense.
- **وَطِئَ (to tread)**
  - 33:27: land "you had not trodden," given as inheritance after a defeated enemy.
  - 9:120: treading ground that enrages the disbelievers.

  وَطِئَ stresses setting foot on territory, a sign of possession or dominance. It does not express the to-and-fro search.
- **تَبَّرَ / تَتْبِير (to destroy utterly)** (17:7): this verb describes the outcome of the second punishment, the destruction of whatever they had risen over.

**What the comparison suggests (interpretation):** جاسَ is the only one of these that combines hostile entry, thorough coverage and searching within the dwellings themselves. If the text had said "they entered the homes," it would have conveyed only intrusion. If it had said "they destroyed," it would have conveyed only ruin.

## The contrast with 17:7

The pair 17:5 and 17:7 sets two punishments side by side.

- **First punishment (17:5):** the enemy *roams searching through the dwellings*. This is invasion, exposure and humiliation, with the inner, private space of the community penetrated.
- **Second punishment (17:7):** the enemy *disgraces their faces*, *enters the masjid*, and *destroys utterly*.

Read together, the two passages appear to show **an escalation**. The first is penetration and domination of the homes. The second is desecration of the sanctuary and total destruction. جاسَ suits the first stage because it depicts thorough, unopposed occupation without yet speaking of annihilation.

This escalation is a **reading of the text's structure**. It is plausible, but the ayahs do not state it explicitly. Which historical events these punishments refer to is a separate matter, on which commentators hold differing views (to be verified). The linguistic argument here does not depend on resolving it.

## Sound (tentative)

The word has a long ā after jīm, followed by a sibilant (sīn). One may suggest that the long vowel and the hissing consonant give an impression of drawn-out, prowling movement. Such sound-symbolism is **impressionistic** and should not be presented as a proven reason.

## Conclusion

The textual evidence firmly supports the following:

- فَجَاسُوا means more than "entered." It denotes moving to and fro through a place, searching it thoroughly.
- It is grammatically and semantically matched to خِلَٰلَ ٱلدِّيَارِ ("the in-between spaces of the dwellings").
- It is consistent with agents of "severe might" sent in immediate sequence by the fāʾ.

**Interpretation, well-grounded but not certain:**

- The word was chosen to portray a thorough, unresisted penetration of the community's private spaces.
- It is distinguished from plain *entering* (دَخَلَ) and from *destruction* (تَتْبِير). The latter is reserved for the second, graver punishment in 17:7, producing a deliberate gradation.

Since the root is unique in the Qur'an, no internal parallel can confirm this further. The case rests on lexical meaning, syntax and the contrast with 17:7.

## To verify before saving

- That root ج و س occurs only once in the Qur'an (17:5).
- Lexical definitions of جاسَ يَجُوسُ, its verbal nouns (جَوْس / جَوَسان), and its "searching / going to and fro" sense, in the standard lexica.
- The claimed closeness of جاسَ to حاسَ and داسَ.
- The reported non-canonical reading فَحَاسُوا.
- The wording and sense of 17:7 (entering the masjid, disgracing faces, تَتْبِير).
- 27:34: kings entering a town and corrupting it.
- 50:36: نَقَّبُوا فِي الْبِلَادِ.
- 9:2 (سِيحُوا) and 3:137 (سِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ).
- 33:27 and 9:120: uses of وَطِئَ.
- 9:47, 18:33, 24:43, 30:48: uses of خِلَال.
- That commentators differ on the historical identification of the two punishments.
- The sound-symbolism remark (impressionistic, not sourced).

q.en: How does the word «فَجَاسُوا۟» fit in this ayah (17:5) compared with similar Qur'anic words used elsewhere? Why this word here and not another? Give a conclusive answer

ans.en:
## The clause in context

>> وَجَعَلۡنٰكُمۡ اَكۡثَرَ نَفِيۡرًا

The phrase **اَكۡثَرَ نَفِيۡرًا** is the second half of a clause built on **جَعَلۡنٰكُمۡ**. The وَ joins this clause to the two before it in the same ayah (رَدَدۡنَا … وَاَمۡدَدۡنٰـكُمۡ …). All three describe what God granted after the first punishment in 17:5.

## 1. The governing verb: جَعَلَ

- **جَعَلۡنٰ** is a past-tense verb attached to the pronoun نا (the subject, "We").
- Here جَعَلَ means **"to make something into / to render"** (Arabic grammarians call this جَعَلَ التصييرية). In this sense it takes **two objects** that were originally a subject and predicate. Underlying the clause is the nominal sentence "أنتم أكثرُ نفيرًا" ("you are greater in number of men").
- **ـكُمۡ** is the **first object** (مفعول به أول), an attached pronoun in the accusative position.
- **اَكۡثَرَ** is the **second object** (مفعول به ثانٍ), in the accusative (منصوب).

The text supports this analysis clearly. A two-object reading of جَعَلَ is the natural one, since the sense is "We made you [into] more numerous," not "We created you."

## 2. اَكۡثَرَ: the elative (اسم التفضيل)

- **Form:** أَفۡعَل from the root ك ث ر ("to be many"). It is the comparative/superlative pattern, "more numerous."
- **Case ending:** It ends in a single fatḥa without tanwīn, **اَكۡثَرَ**, because it is diptote (ممنوع من الصرف). It is an adjectival form on the verbal pattern أَفۡعَل (الوصفية + وزن الفعل), so in the accusative it takes fatḥa with no nunation.
- **Unexpressed object of comparison:** An elative used indefinitely normally takes مِن ("more … than …"). Here no مِن-phrase appears. Arabic regularly omits it when context supplies it. Two readings are possible:
  - "more numerous **than you were before**" (compared with your weakened state after the defeat in 17:5), or
  - "more numerous **than your enemies**" (the عِبَادًا لَّنَا of 17:5, over whom the كَرَّة was given in this ayah).

  The grammar allows both. Choosing between them is a matter of interpretation. Both views are reported in the exegetical literature *(needs verification)*.

## 3. نَفِيۡرًا: specifying accusative (تمييز)

- **Function:** **تمييز** (specification), in the accusative, marked by fatḥa with tanwīn. In pause it is read *nafīrā*.
- **Why tamyīz:** "More numerous" is vague: more numerous in what? نَفِيۡرًا removes the ambiguity by specifying the respect in which the comparison holds.
- **Type:** Grammarians class this as a **tamyīz of relation (تمييز نسبة)**, a common pattern after an elative. It is often explained as "transformed" (محوَّل) from what would logically be a subject. Underlying it is something like "نفيرُكم أكثرُ" ("your نفير is greater"). The construction moves the logical subject into the tamyīz slot and makes the people themselves the subject of the comparison. Compare the familiar pattern زيدٌ أكثرُ منك مالًا.

## 4. The word نَفِيۡر: morphology and meaning

The root ن ف ر has the core sense of **going forth / setting out quickly**, especially to war. The same verb appears in the command to "go forth" for fighting in 9:41 and in 9:122, and in 4:71.

The morphology of نَفِيۡر is analysed in more than one way *(needs verification)*:

- **A collective noun** for the men who go out with a person to fight, i.e. one's mobilised fighting force. On this reading the tamyīz means "in fighting men / manpower."
- **A plural of نَفَر** ("a group of men"), on a pattern comparable to عَبۡد → عَبِيد. On this reading it means "in men / in numbers of people."
- **A فَعِيل adjective with the sense of فاعِل** ("one who goes forth"), used collectively.
- **A verbal noun (مصدر) of نَفَرَ** ("going forth"). This is less likely here, because a quantity of people is being counted.

Whichever analysis is adopted, the sense is much the same: **"greater in manpower / in men who mobilise."** Saheeh International's "more numerous in manpower" reflects this. A well-known Arabic proverb uses نفير in the sense of a war-party set against a caravan (عِير) *(needs verification)*.

## 5. Summary i'rāb (إعراب)

- **وَ**: conjunction (حرف عطف).
- **جَعَلۡ**: past verb, built on sukūn because of the attached subject pronoun.
- **نا**: attached pronoun, subject (فاعل).
- **كُمۡ**: attached pronoun, first object.
- **اَكۡثَرَ**: second object, accusative, fatḥa without tanwīn (diptote). The مُفَضَّل عليه is omitted.
- **نَفِيۡرًا**: tamyīz, accusative, fatḥa with tanwīn.

## 6. Rhetorical observation (interpretive)

The three verbs form a progression:

1. رَدَدۡنَا: the turn of fortune is restored.
2. اَمۡدَدۡنٰـكُمۡ بِاَمۡوَالٍ وَّبَنِيۡنَ: you are reinforced with resources and offspring.
3. جَعَلۡنٰكُمۡ اَكۡثَرَ نَفِيۡرًا: those resources turn into a larger mobilisable force.

The elative with an unstated term of comparison keeps the reversal relative to 17:5. The verbs in the first person plural keep the agency with God throughout. The warning in 17:7 then makes clear that this restored strength is conditional on conduct. This is a reading of the structure, not a grammatical necessity.

## To verify before saving

- That جَعَلَ here is classed as التصييرية taking two objects, and the standard i'rāb given above (check a reference i'rāb work).
- The diptote status of اَكۡثَرَ (وصفية + وزن الفعل).
- The classification of نَفِيۡرًا as تمييز نسبة, and specifically the "محوَّل" explanation.
- The competing morphological analyses of نَفِير (collective noun / plural of نَفَر / فَعِيل as فاعِل / masdar) and which lexicographers or grammarians hold each.
- The two readings of the omitted مُفَضَّل عليه ("than before" vs. "than your enemies") and their attribution in the tafsir literature.
- The references 9:41, 9:122 and 4:71 for the root ن ف ر in the sense of going forth to fight.
- The proverb involving العِير and النَّفِير, its wording and meaning.

q.en: Explain grammar of AKTHARA NAFEERA

ans.en:
## Short answer

The ayah does not say the night or its sign was removed from existence. It says that, within the created order, the night's sign was made "effaced" (dark, without light to see by), while the day's sign was made light-giving. On the plainest reading, this is a **lasting feature of how the night was made**, not a one-time event after which the night vanished. It holds for as long as the alternation of night and day continues.

## What the text says clearly

>> وَجَعَلۡنَا الَّيۡلَ وَالنَّهَارَ اٰيَتَيۡنِ​ فَمَحَوۡنَاۤ اٰيَةَ الَّيۡلِ وَجَعَلۡنَاۤ اٰيَةَ النَّهَارِ مُبۡصِرَةً

- **Both remain signs.** The ayah opens by calling the night and the day two signs (*āyatayn*). The effacing happens *within* the night's status as a sign. It does not cancel it.
- **The effacing has a counterpart.** *Fa-maḥawnā āyata al-layl* is set against *wa-jaʿalnā āyata al-nahāri mubṣiratan*. The day's sign is made *mubṣira* (enabling sight). The natural sense of the contrast is that the night's sign was made non-illuminating. The effacing describes a *quality* of the night, not its removal.
- **The purpose requires the night to continue.** The ayah gives the aim as *li-taʿlamū ʿadada al-sinīna wa-al-ḥisāb*, knowing the count of years and the reckoning. Counting time depends on night and day continuing to alternate. A night erased out of existence would undermine the very purpose the ayah states.
- **The closing phrase stresses fixed order.** *Wa-kulla shayʾin faṣṣalnāhu tafṣīlā* presents this as part of a detailed, deliberately set arrangement. That points to a standing design, not a passing incident.

## Linguistic observations

- **The verb *maḥā*** basically means to efface, blot out or remove the trace of something, as with writing. Here it is in the past tense and joined by *fa* to *jaʿalnā*. It describes how God set up the arrangement when He made the two signs. Grammatically it is an act of ordering in creation.
- **The phrase *āyat al-layl*** can be read in two ways:
  1. **As the night itself** ("the sign that is the night"), an explicative construct (*iḍāfa bayāniyya*). The opening clause, which calls the night and day themselves the two signs, supports this. The effacing is then the night's darkness.
  2. **As a sign belonging to the night**, usually understood as the moon. The day's sign is then the sun. The effacing is then the moon's lesser or non-intrinsic light, or something about its appearance.
- **The word *mubṣira*** literally means "seeing" or "making see." Applied to the day, it is commonly explained as "a time in which one sees," a figurative attribution of the action to the time. *(Treat this rhetorical classification as needing verification against works on balāgha.)*

## Interpretive views (in general terms; verify each)

- **Night-itself view.** The effacing is the darkness of night as opposed to the brightness of day. On this view "permanent" means a constant property, experienced again every night. *(Verify which exegetes hold this.)*
- **Moon view.** The effacing concerns the moon's light compared with the sun's. Some reports, as I recall, describe the moon as once having had light like the sun's before it was effaced. Others link the effacing to the dark marks on the moon or to its phases. *(I cannot confirm the wording, chains or authenticity of any such reports. Check them in the tafsir literature before relying on them.)*
- Even on the moon view, the moon plainly continues to exist and to function for reckoning. So again, "effaced" does not mean "removed."

## Support from other passages (described, not quoted)

- **10:5** describes the sun as radiance and the moon as light, with the moon given measured stages so that people may know the number of years and the reckoning. This is very close to the purpose clause of 17:12, and it fits the reading that both luminaries stay in operation.
- **36:37** describes the night as a sign from which the day is stripped away, leaving people in darkness. This supports linking the night's sign with darkness.
- **28:71–72** asks what would happen if God made the night, or the day, perpetual until the Day of Resurrection. This shows that alternation, not the permanent dominance or disappearance of either, is the established order.
- Passages on the end of the world, such as **75:9** and **81:1**, describe the sun and moon being disrupted at the Hour. If accepted as relevant, these suggest the present arrangement is "permanent" only within this world's order.

## Context

- The previous ayah, 17:11, speaks of human haste. The next ayah, 17:13, speaks of each person's fate bound to him and a record laid open on the Day of Resurrection. One possible link is that the measured, orderly succession of night and day, by which time and deeds are counted, contrasts with human impatience and leads into the theme of reckoning. This connection is my interpretation, not something the text states.

## Where I am unsure

- I cannot say from the text alone which reading of *āyat al-layl* (the night itself, or the moon) is stronger. The opening clause favours the first, but the second has a long history in the tafsir tradition. *(Verify.)*
- "Permanent" is ambiguous in the question. The text supports permanence as a *fixed quality* for the duration of the worldly order. It does not support a permanent *disappearance*. Whether the effacing refers to a past change in the moon depends on reports I cannot verify here.

## To verify before saving

- The general meaning of *maḥā* (efface, blot out, remove a trace): check in standard Arabic lexicons.
- The classification of *āyat al-layl* as an explicative construct (*iḍāfa bayāniyya*) on the first reading.
- The rhetorical analysis of *mubṣira* as a figurative attribution to the time.
- That exegetes hold the "night-itself / darkness" view, and which ones.
- That exegetes hold the "moon / sun" view, and which ones.
- Reports that the moon once had light like the sun and was effaced: their existence, wording and authenticity.
- Views linking the effacing to the moon's dark marks or phases.
- 10:5: moon given stages for knowing the number of years and the reckoning.
- 36:37: day stripped from the night, leaving darkness.
- 28:71–72: the hypothetical of perpetual night or day until the Resurrection.
- 75:9 and 81:1: their content concerning the sun and moon at the Hour, and whether they are relevant here.
- The suggested thematic link between 17:11, 17:12 and 17:13 (my own interpretation).

q.en: فَمَحَوۡنَاۤ اٰيَةَ الَّيۡلِ - is it permanently erased?

ans.en:
## Short answer

The repetition is only apparent. **ʿadad al-sinīn** (the number of years) and **al-ḥisāb** (the reckoning) are two separate objects of the verb *taʿlamū*, and they refer to different things. The first is the *count* of a single large unit, years. The second is the wider activity of *calculating* time in all its units and for all its practical purposes. The second term widens the scope of the first rather than restating it.

## 1. What the text shows clearly

>> وَلِتَعۡلَمُوۡا عَدَدَ السِّنِيۡنَ وَالۡحِسَابَ

- **Grammar:** *al-ḥisāba* has a *fatḥa*, so it is accusative. It is therefore coordinated with *ʿadada* (the object of *taʿlamū*), not with *al-sinīna*. Had it been coordinated with *al-sinīna*, it would be genitive, *al-ḥisābi*, giving "the number of the years and of the reckoning." The verse instead names two objects of knowledge:
  1. the number of years
  2. the reckoning
- **Lexical difference:**
  - *ʿadad* means a number or tally. It answers "how many?" Here it is restricted by *al-sinīn* to years.
  - *ḥisāb* is a verbal noun from the root ḥ-s-b, meaning to calculate or compute. It names a process, not a quantity, and it carries no restricting genitive, so its scope is open.
- **Context of the verse:** The signs named are the **night and the day**, the smallest natural cycle. Years come from adding up these days, while *ḥisāb* covers every reckoning built on them.

## 2. Interpretive readings (plausible, not stated explicitly)

**(a) Specific followed by general.** *Al-ḥisāb* may be a general term following a specific one (*ʿaṭf al-ʿāmm ʿalā al-khāṣṣ*). Years are one product of reckoning. *Al-ḥisāb* takes in everything else: days, months, hours, and the times tied to them, such as prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, debts, contracts and waiting periods. On this reading, mentioning years first singles out the largest and most memorable unit, and *al-ḥisāb* then extends the benefit to all of time-keeping.

**(b) Two distinct functions.** On a slightly different reading, the two terms do not overlap:
- *ʿadad al-sinīn*: knowing how many years have passed, for ages, eras and history.
- *al-ḥisāb*: calculating within and across shorter periods, for dates, deadlines and appointed times.

This reading fits the observation that the verse is built on night and day, the base units from which finer reckoning starts.

**(c) Link to what follows.** The next verse turns to each person's record brought out on the Day of Resurrection:

>> وَنُخۡرِجُ لَهٗ يَوۡمَ الۡقِيٰمَةِ كِتٰبًا يَّلۡقٰٮهُ مَنۡشُوۡرًا

The verse after that (17:14) speaks of the person being sufficient as a reckoner against himself, using the same root ḥ-s-b. The word *al-ḥisāb* in 17:12 therefore may also prepare for the theme of accountability. Measured time, in which every day is counted, leads into the measured record of deeds. This is a thematic observation about the sequence of verses. In 17:12 itself, *al-ḥisāb* refers most directly to the reckoning of time.

**(d) Fit with the close of the verse.**

>> وَكُلَّ شَىۡءٍ فَصَّلۡنٰهُ تَفۡصِيۡلًا

The move from the broad (years) to the detailed (all reckoning) matches the closing statement that everything has been set out in detail. This too is a reading of the verse's coherence, not an explicit statement.

## 3. Parallel usage

- **10:5** uses the same pairing, the number of years and the reckoning, in connection with the sun and moon and the moon's stations. That the pair recurs as a set phrase supports reading the two as distinct and complementary.
- **6:96** and **55:5** use the related form *ḥusbān* for the sun and moon as instruments of calculation. These verses support the sense of *ḥ-s-b* as computation.

## 4. Points of uncertainty

- Classical exegetes have offered views on how the two terms differ, for example years versus months and days, or general versus specific. These are mentioned here only in general terms. Specific attributions need checking against the tafsir sources.
- Some exegetes are said to identify the "sign of the night" with the moon and the "sign of the day" with the sun. If so, this would bear on whether lunar reckoning is in view. **This needs verification.**
- Reading (c), the accountability link, is suggestive, but the text does not state it.

## To verify before saving

- That *wa-l-ḥisāba* is accusative (*fatḥa*) in the standard reading, and whether any variant reading has the genitive
- The wording and context of 10:5 (number of years and reckoning; sun, moon, stations)
- The wording of 6:96 and 55:5 and their use of *ḥusbān*
- The wording of 17:14 and its use of the root ḥ-s-b
- The lexical senses of *ʿadad* and *ḥisāb* in standard Arabic lexicons
- Which exegetes distinguish *ʿadad al-sinīn* from *al-ḥisāb*, and how
- The view that the signs of night and day refer to the moon and sun, and who holds it
- Whether *ʿaṭf al-ʿāmm ʿalā al-khāṣṣ* is the analysis that grammarians or exegetes actually apply to this verse

q.en: Why HISAAB is mentioned again after ADADA SINEEN?

ans.en:
## The question the ayah raises

Saheeh International's rendering, "We have imposed his fate upon his neck," can suggest that each person's outcome is fixed and laid on him from outside, which would seem to sit uneasily with personal responsibility. Read in its own wording and context, however, the ayah is better understood as a statement *about* responsibility: each person's outcome is inseparably attached to him and is documented in a record that is his own.

>> وَكُلَّ اِنۡسَانٍ اَلۡزَمۡنٰهُ طٰۤٮِٕرَهٗ فِىۡ عُنُقِهٖ​ؕ وَنُخۡرِجُ لَهٗ يَوۡمَ الۡقِيٰمَةِ كِتٰبًا يَّلۡقٰٮهُ مَنۡشُوۡرًا

## 1. What the key words say (linguistic level)

**ṭāʾir (طائر)**
- Literally "bird" or "that which flies."
- The term is linked to the pre-Islamic practice of *taṭayyur*, reading good or ill fortune from the flight of birds. By extension, *ṭāʾir* came to mean a person's lot, omen or fortune.
- The Qur'an uses this vocabulary elsewhere in polemical contexts, where people blame a prophet for their misfortune and are told that their "omen" is really with God, or with themselves (see 7:131, 27:47, 36:19).
- Against that background, the ayah redirects the idea. A person's fortune is not something flying about in the world to be read from birds. It is fastened to the person himself.
- "Fate" is therefore one translation choice, not the only one. Other English translations render *ṭāʾir* as "deeds," "destiny," or "augury." The word itself is open, and context has to decide.

**alzamnāhu (ألزمناه)**
- This is Form IV of *l-z-m*, "to cling, to be inseparable": "We have made it cling to him, made it inseparable from him."
- God's stated act is the *binding* of the ṭāʾir to the person. The verb does not say that God compels the person's deeds. It says that whatever the ṭāʾir is, it cannot be detached from its owner.

**fī ʿunuqihi (في عنقه), "on his neck"**
- The neck is where a collar or necklace sits: visible, always carried, and impossible to shed.
- Arabic uses the idiom of something being "on one's neck" for an obligation or liability one bears. This image points towards *liability*, not towards a force that overrides the will. This is an interpretive reading of the idiom, but a natural one.

**kitāban yalqāhu manshūran (كتابا يلقاه منشورا)**
- The record is "brought out for him" and he "meets it spread open." Nothing about it is hidden from him.
- The second half of the ayah explains the first. Whatever is bound to the person's neck in this life becomes the open record of the Day of Resurrection.

## 2. What the following ayah adds (contextual level)

>> اِقۡرَاۡ كِتٰبَك َؕ كَفٰى بِنَفۡسِكَ الۡيَوۡمَ عَلَيۡكَ حَسِيۡبًا ؕ

This ayah is the strongest textual evidence for responsibility in the passage:

- **"Your record" (kitābaka).** The possessive suffix makes the record the person's own. It is not a record of what was done *to* him.
- **"Read."** The person is invited to read it himself. The evidence is presented to the one it concerns.
- **"Sufficient is yourself against you as reckoner"** (*kafā bi-nafsika … ʿalayka ḥasīban*). The self is made the reckoner (*ḥasīb*) against itself. This only makes sense if the deeds recorded are truly the person's own. A person cannot meaningfully be his own prosecutor for acts that were not his.

## 3. What the preceding ayah adds (structural level)

>> وَكُلَّ شَىۡءٍ فَصَّلۡنٰهُ تَفۡصِيۡلًا

Two features link 17:12 to 17:13. Both are my own observations and should be checked against grammatical and rhetorical works:

- **Parallel grammar.** *wa-kulla shayʾin faṣṣalnāhu* ("everything We have detailed") is followed by *wa-kulla insānin alzamnāhu* ("every human We have bound"). Both appear to use the same construction, an accusative noun governed by an implied verb that the following verb explains (*ishtighāl*).
- **The theme of reckoning.** 17:12 speaks of knowing "the number of years and the account" (*al-ḥisāb*). 17:14 ends with *ḥasīban*, from the same root.

The movement of thought appears to be this. God has made time measurable and detailed, so human life unfolds in a countable, recorded span, and every person's deeds within that span are bound to him and later presented in detail.

## 4. The wider passage (by reference only)

The immediately following ayah, **17:15**, states three things:
- whoever is guided is guided only for his own benefit, and whoever strays strays only against himself;
- no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another;
- God does not punish until He has sent a messenger.

This frames the whole passage in terms of individual moral consequence and fair warning. A system in which deeds were not genuinely the person's own would make these statements difficult to read coherently.

Related ayahs develop the same theme:
- **18:49:** the record leaves nothing small or great unaccounted for.
- **99:7–8:** even an atom's weight of good or evil will be seen.
- **41:46:** whoever does good does it for himself, and whoever does evil does it against himself.
- **53:38–39:** no one bears another's burden, and a person has only what he strives for.
- **81:28–29:** the Qur'an is for whoever wills to go straight, and human willing does not occur unless God wills. Human will and divine will are affirmed together, not set against each other.

## 5. What is clear and what is interpretation

**What the text states clearly:**
- Every individual (*kulla insān*) has a ṭāʾir bound inseparably to him.
- A record is brought out for him on the Day of Resurrection, open before him.
- The record is called *his*, he is told to read it, and he himself suffices as reckoner against himself.

**What is interpretation:**
- **The meaning of *ṭāʾir*.** Exegetical views are generally reported to fall into three groups: (a) the person's deeds; (b) the good and evil decreed for him; (c) a combination, such as deeds together with their consequences. *(Needs verification against the tafsir literature.)* The link to the "record" in the same ayah and the next favours a strong connection with deeds, but it does not exclude the idea of decree.
- **How divine decree relates to human agency.** This ayah does not settle that question in theological terms. The theological schools gave different accounts:
  - one position (associated with the Ashʿarīs) holds that God creates acts and the human "acquires" them (*kasb*);
  - another (associated with the Muʿtazila) holds that humans produce their own acts;
  - the Māturīdī account gives a distinct role to human choice.
  
  *(These general characterisations need verification.)*

## 6. Conclusion

On the ayah's own terms, people remain responsible for their deeds for five reasons:

1. **Binding is not compulsion.** What God does here is *make the ṭāʾir cling* to the person. The verse does not describe God producing the deeds against the person's will.
2. **The image is one of liability.** The neck idiom portrays something carried and answerable, not something imposed from outside.
3. **The record belongs to the person.** It is "your record," read by the person himself, and his own self is the reckoner against him. This presupposes real ownership of the acts.
4. **Responsibility is individual.** Every human is addressed one by one, and 17:15 adds that no one carries another's burden.
5. **Justice is a stated condition.** 17:15 makes punishment conditional on a messenger having been sent, so accountability rests on guidance actually received.

On honest limits: the passage strongly affirms accountability, but it is not a complete treatise on how divine decree and human choice relate metaphysically. That question belongs to *kalām*, where Muslim theologians disagreed. What can be said with confidence is that this passage gives no support to the idea that decree cancels responsibility. Its whole movement, from the binding of the ṭāʾir to the open record to self-reckoning, runs in the opposite direction.

## To verify before saving

- Exact Arabic text of 17:12, 17:13 and 17:14 as quoted, including the rasm and orthography used.
- The meaning of *ṭāʾir*, and its link to *taṭayyur* (bird augury), in classical Arabic lexicons.
- The content of 7:131, 27:47 and 36:19 as described (ṭāʾir/omen usage).
- That other English translations render *ṭāʾir* as "deeds," "destiny," or "augury."
- The sense of Form IV *alzama* from *l-z-m* as "to make inseparable."
- The Arabic idiom of an obligation being "on one's neck."
- The grammatical analysis of *wa-kulla insānin* and *wa-kulla shayʾin* as *ishtighāl*.
- The suggested *ḥisāb*/*ḥasīban* link between 17:12 and 17:14 (my own observation).
- The grammatical status of the *bāʾ* in *kafā bi-nafsika* (commonly described as an extra *bāʾ*).
- The content of 17:15 as described.
- The content of 18:49, 99:7–8, 41:46, 53:38–39 and 81:28–29 as described.
- The claim that exegetes held three general views on *ṭāʾir* (deeds; decreed good and evil; a combination).
- The general characterisations of Ashʿarī (*kasb*), Muʿtazilī and Māturīdī positions on human acts.

q.en: Give a conclusive analysis of how still people are responsible for their own deeds?

ans.en:
## Short answer

**No. *ihtadā* (اهتدى) is not a passive verb.** It is an **active-voice Form VIII (*iftaʿala*)** verb from the root ه-د-ي. Its meaning is *reflexive-resultative*: it describes the subject receiving and accepting guidance. That is why English translators often render it "is guided," which makes it look passive in translation even though it is active in Arabic.

## The morphology

- **Form I:** *hadā* (هدى), "he guided [someone]." Transitive and active.
- **Form I passive:** *hudiya* (هُدِيَ), "he was guided." This is the true passive.
- **Form VIII:** *ihtadā* (اهتدى), formed by adding a prefixed *alif* and an infixed *tāʾ* after the first radical: ا + ه + **ت** + د + ى. It is active, and its subject is the doer of the verb.

The vowelling in the muṣḥaf confirms the active voice:

>> مَنِ اهۡتَدٰى فَاِنَّمَا يَهۡتَدِىۡ لِنَفۡسِهٖ

The *tāʾ* carries a *fatḥa* (اهۡتَدٰى), and the imperfect is *yahtadī* (يَهۡتَدِىۡ) with a *kasra* on the *dāl*. A passive Form VIII would be vowelled differently, along the lines of *uhtudiya / yuhtadā*. Neither form appears here.

## Why it feels passive: *muṭāwaʿa*

One of the standard functions of Form VIII in Arabic grammar is ***muṭāwaʿa***: the subject "yields to" or "accepts" the effect of an action done to it. The classic pattern is:

- *hadāhu fa-htadā*: "he guided him, and he became guided / accepted the guidance."

The verb is therefore grammatically active, because the person is the agent of *ihtidāʾ*. Semantically, though, it presupposes a prior act of guiding (*hidāya*) by someone else. This is the reason for the ambiguity behind the question. *Ihtadā* does **not** mean "he guided himself" in the sense of generating guidance from nothing. It means "he took the guidance and became rightly guided."

Compare 7:178, where God is the one who guides and the person so guided is described with the participle of this same Form VIII verb (*al-muhtadī*). The two sides of the *muṭāwaʿa* pair appear together in that verse.

## Parallel within the ayah

The ayah balances *ihtadā* against *ḍalla* (ضلّ):

>> وَمَنۡ ضَلَّ فَاِنَّمَا يَضِلُّ عَلَيۡهَا

*Ḍalla* is an active, intransitive Form I verb: "he went astray." The parallelism treats both verbs as things the person does, one for the self (*li-nafsihi*) and one against it (*ʿalayhā*). Reading *ihtadā* as a pure passive would break this balance.

The conditional structure is also worth noting. *Man* here is the conditional particle (*man al-sharṭiyya*), the perfect *ihtadā* carries conditional or general sense, and the answer (*jawāb*) is introduced by *fa-* plus the restrictive *innamā*. The restriction stresses that the benefit returns to the self and to no one else.

## Context: why the active form fits

The surrounding ayahs are about **personal accountability**:

- 17:14 tells the person to read his own record and says his own self suffices as reckoner against him.
- 17:15 continues: no bearer of burdens bears another's burden.
- 17:15 then closes:

>> وَمَا كُنَّا مُعَذِّبِيۡنَ حَتّٰى نَبۡعَثَ رَسُوۡلًا

This last clause fits the *muṭāwaʿa* reading well, though that connection is my interpretation rather than an explicit statement in the text. Guidance is first *offered* through a messenger, and the human response (*ihtidāʾ* or *ḍalāl*) is then counted to the person. The active form puts responsibility on the individual, which is the theme of the passage.

## Text versus interpretation

- **What the text and grammar show clearly:** *ihtadā* is active Form VIII, and the person is its grammatical subject.
- **Standard grammatical analysis, though not stated in the ayah itself:** that its function here is *muṭāwaʿa*, the acceptance of guidance given by another.
- **Theological interpretation:** how human *ihtidāʾ* relates to divine *hidāya*. Elsewhere the Qur'an attributes guidance to God (e.g. 28:56, 7:178). Muslim theological schools are generally reported to have differed on how to reconcile divine agency with human acts. *(Needs verification against kalām and tafsīr sources; I am not citing any specific scholar.)* The grammar alone does not settle that question. It only shows that the Arabic presents the human as the one who "takes up" guidance.

## To verify before saving

- That *ihtadā* is Form VIII (*iftaʿala*) of ه-د-ي and active in voice (check a morphology reference or *ṣarf* manual).
- That *muṭāwaʿa* is a recognised function of Form VIII, and the pattern *hadāhu fa-htadā* as an illustration.
- The suggested passive Form VIII vowelling (*uhtudiya / yuhtadā*). Confirm the correct forms.
- The vowelling of اهۡتَدٰى and يَهۡتَدِىۡ as quoted, against a standard muṣḥaf.
- 7:178: that it pairs God's guiding with *al-muhtadī*.
- 28:56: that it attributes guidance to God.
- The analysis of *man* as conditional and of *fa-* plus *innamā* as the *jawāb* with restriction.
- The general statement that theological schools differed on divine versus human agency in guidance.
- The interpretive link between "until We send a messenger" and guidance being offered before it is accepted (my reading, not an explicit claim of the text).

q.en: MAN IHTADA - can a person by IHTADA by himself? Isn't it a passive verb?

ans.en:
## Immediate context

The phrase only makes sense against the two groups set out just before it. Ayah 17:18 (paraphrased) describes whoever desires *the immediate* (al-ʿājila), that is, this world: Allah hastens to him in it what He wills, for whom He wills, and his end is Hell. Ayah 17:19 then describes the opposite group:

>> وَمَنۡ اَرَادَ الۡاٰخِرَةَ وَسَعٰى لَهَا سَعۡيَهَا وَهُوَ مُؤۡمِنٌ فَاُولٰۤٮِٕكَ كَانَ سَعۡيُهُمۡ مَّشۡكُوۡرًا

Ayah 17:20 then says that **both** groups receive worldly provision:

>> كُلًّا نُّمِدُّ هٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ وَهٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ مِنۡ عَطَآءِ رَبِّكَ​

## Grammatical function

- **كُلًّا** is the direct object of **نُمِدُّ**, placed before the verb. Its tanwīn is generally analysed as *tanwīn al-ʿiwaḍ*, a nunation that stands in for an omitted noun in iḍāfa. The sense is roughly "each [of the two groups]."
- **هٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ وَهٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ** is most naturally parsed as a *badal* (apposition) from كُلًّا. As an indeclinable demonstrative, it is in the accusative position (*fī maḥall naṣb*). The second هٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ is joined to the first by wāw.
- The plural demonstrative fits the sense of the antecedents. Although مَن in 17:18–19 is singular in form, it is plural in meaning, and 17:19 already resumes it with the plural اُولٰۤٮِٕكَ.

## What the phrase does

**1. Detail after a summary (tafṣīl baʿd ijmāl).** كُلًّا states the point in summary form ("each"). The appositive then spells it out ("these and those"). This removes any doubt about whom "each" covers. The structure of the text clearly establishes this function.

**2. Explicit inclusion of both groups.** Naming each group separately makes it unmistakable that the people of 17:18, whose end is described as Hell, are not cut off from worldly provision. The believers of 17:19 are equally included. This is reinforced by the ayah's closing statement:

>> وَمَا كَانَ عَطَآءُ رَبِّكَ مَحۡظُوۡرًا

**3. Separating worldly provision from final reward.** The context sets 17:18–19 (opposite ends) against 17:20 (shared provision). This suggests the point is that receiving worldly provision is no sign of divine approval. The difference between the groups lies in the outcome, not in whether they are provided for here. 17:21 then confirms that the real distinction lies in the Hereafter:

>> وَلَـلۡاٰخِرَةُ اَكۡبَرُ دَرَجٰتٍ وَّاَكۡبَرُ تَفۡضِيۡلًا

This reading follows closely from the context, but it remains interpretation rather than explicit statement.

**4. Order of reference.** The demonstratives do not themselves identify which group is which. The natural reading takes the first هٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ as the seekers of this world (mentioned first, in 17:18) and the second as the seekers of the Hereafter (17:19). This is an inference from word order. Since the ayah affirms provision for both alike, the point does not depend on it.

## Why هٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ twice, and not هٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ … اُولٰۤٮِٕكَ?

- **Linguistic usage.** Repeating the same near demonstrative to distinguish two parties ("these and these," meaning "these and those") is a recognised Arabic idiom. In such usage the repetition marks distinct referents, not physical distance, so the choice need not carry special meaning.
- **A possible rhetorical nuance (interpretation, tentative).** Both groups are pointed to with the *near* demonstrative, just as both are equally within reach of worldly provision. By contrast, 17:19 refers to the believers with the *far* demonstrative اُولٰۤٮِٕكَ, which is sometimes read as a mark of elevated status. On this reading, the shift to هٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ in 17:20 levels the two groups with respect to *this world only*. This is suggestive but speculative, and I would not present it as established.
- **Deixis and the addressee.** The demonstratives present the two groups as if displayed before the addressee, who is the one addressed in رَبِّكَ. This prepares for the visual imperative that opens 17:21:

>> اُنْظُرۡ كَيۡفَ فَضَّلۡنَا بَعۡضَهُمۡ عَلٰى بَعۡضٍ​

The thread of "pointing out" and then "looking" is a coherence observation of mine, not a claim drawn from a source.

## Relation to "for whom We will" in 17:18

17:18 limits what is hastened in this world to "what We will, for whom We will." 17:20 says both groups are given provision. A common way of reconciling the two is that *provision in general* is given to all, while *the fulfilment of a particular worldly desire* is subject to divine will. That reconciliation is interpretive, and the views of exegetes on it should be checked.

## Points of uncertainty

- Whether عَطَآءِ رَبِّكَ here refers only to worldly provision, or also includes guidance and similar gifts. Most readings take it as worldly provision; this needs verification.
- Alternative parsings of هٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ (other than badal) may exist in the iʿrāb literature; I have not reproduced any.

## To verify before saving

- Paraphrase of 17:18 (content: desiring al-ʿājila; hastening "what We will, for whom We will"; end in Hell). Check against the muṣḥaf.
- كُلًّا as object placed before the verb, and its tanwīn as tanwīn al-ʿiwaḍ. Check in iʿrāb works.
- هٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ وَهٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ as badal from كُلًّا, and whether other parsings are recorded.
- That repeating the same near demonstrative for two groups is a recognised Arabic idiom. Check grammar or balāgha sources.
- The claim that اُولٰۤٮِٕكَ (far demonstrative) can signal elevated status. Check balāgha sources.
- The order of reference (first هٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ = seekers of this world; second = seekers of the Hereafter). Check tafsir.
- That عَطَآءِ رَبِّكَ is understood by most as worldly provision. Check tafsir.
- The reconciliation between 17:18 ("for whom We will") and 17:20. Check tafsir.
- The interpretive points (levelling nuance; deictic link to اُنْظُرۡ in 17:21) are my own observations and are not attributed to any source.

q.en: هٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ وَهٰٓؤُلَاۤءِ - explain the use of this phrase.

ans.en:
